exp40v2-tech.security:
Security and privacy: what a senior product manager must command

How would someone attack this, and what would stop them?

1. Two decisions, twelve days apart

On Tuesday 15 September 2026 Sharvari Velankar, director of product at Sankalan Settlement Network in Pune, found a line in an access review she could not explain away. Sankalan runs reconciliation and bulk-payout infrastructure for 340 client organisations, holds 92,00,000 beneficiary records and moves ₹18,400 crore of payouts in an average month. A service account created in 2023 held standing read access to every tenant’s beneficiary table, granted once because granting per client was harder. Louder, on the same desk: two clients worth ₹14.6 crore of annual recurring revenue had made customer-managed encryption keys a condition of renewal. Vedant Salvi, the chief information security officer, thought the demand theatre; Shalini Vartak, general counsel and data-protection officer, thought it the cheapest way to bound a catastrophe. The council met on Wednesday 30 September.

Sixteen days after that access review, at 21:40 on Thursday 1 October 2026, a build-integrity monitor at Vatayan Device Works in Bengaluru flagged an artefact whose hash did not match the pipeline’s record. Vatayan makes a connected home cardiac monitor — 4,20,000 in Indian homes — with an app used by 2,80,000 people a month and an AI triage feature. By 23:05 engineers had confirmed unauthorised code in one Android SDK build, drawn in through an unmaintained open-source package tampered with upstream. Supriya Vaze took incident command; Vaibhav Sule, the group product manager, had until Monday 12 October to decide on a ₹3.40 crore field-update programme.

2. The idea, and the six camps that disagree about it

Security maintains stated properties of a system — confidentiality, integrity, availability, accountability — against an adversary who chooses his moves after seeing yours. That clause separates it from reliability: a disk fails at a rate, an adversary only until he learns. Privacy is distinct: whether to hold the data at all, and for which purpose.

Anderson’s 1972 study established that security must be designed in, not tested in. Saltzer and Schroeder in 1975 gave the field its spine, including least privilege and complete mediation — every access to every object checked, with no cached shortcut. STRIDE arrived in 1999, the OWASP Top Ten in 2003, Microsoft’s Security Development Lifecycle in 2004. Cavoukian’s privacy-by-design formulation in 2009 and the LINDDUN taxonomy in 2010 did the same for privacy; NIST codified zero trust in 2020; Gordon and Loeb in 2002 moved the field into economics.

Six camps emerge; confusing them turns a dispute about method into one about facts. Design principles signs that serious weaknesses are decisions, not defects, and refuses that a ranked list of exploitable findings best guides spending. Adversarial empiricism signs that nothing is safe until someone competent has tried to break it, and refuses that a threat model is evidence. Economics signs that security is an investment problem with diminishing returns, and refuses that expected loss is measurable to that precision. Assurance signs that a control leaving no evidence did not happen. Architectural mistrust signs that position on a network confers no trust. Privacy engineering signs that the safest data is the data never collected. Sankalan’s argument was camps five and six against camp three.

3. Mechanics: where the plaintext actually is

Expert practice begins with an inventory and a classification. At Sankalan the tier that matters holds beneficiary bank details, constrained in location by the Reserve Bank of India’s 2018 directive on payment system data and in purpose by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Then come trust boundaries, and here is the step left implicit: most teams draw one, between the internet and themselves. Sankalan’s map has five zones and five trust boundaries, three of them internal: service to service, service to the key plane, and third-party code inside its own services.

The expert’s granularity is STRIDE-per-interaction: the six questions asked of every arrow in Figure 1, not every box. The decisive one is elevation of privilege as cross-tenant access, and the discipline is to ask where tenant identity comes from. As a request parameter it means the system trusts the caller; derived from the authenticated session it cannot be forged. Sankalan’s gateway did the latter, its 2023 internal calls the former. Then separate the policy decision point from the enforcement point: logic living only at the gateway cannot see object ownership, not knowing which client a payout batch belongs to.

Encryption is where vocabulary flatters. In transit it protects the wire; at rest, media — a stolen disk, a copied backup, a forgotten snapshot. Neither protects against the application handing a record to an authorised-but-wrong caller, where the data is decrypted by design. So the question is not whether it is encrypted but where the plaintext is: Sankalan’s answer listed seven places, two of them missed. Envelope encryption gives each tenant a data-encrypting key wrapped by a key-encrypting key held in a hardware module that performs operations but never exports.

The second-order effect in Figure 2 changed Shalini Vartak’s mind: a per-tenant key is also an erasure device. The DPDP Act obliges a data fiduciary to erase personal data when consent is withdrawn, and erasure across replicas and backups is hard to prove; destroying the key makes the records unreadable everywhere. Two mechanics complete the picture. Machine identity: service accounts and build jobs outnumber people several times over, and their credentials historically had no expiry or owner. And the supply chain, where Vatayan’s story lives — a bill of materials, provenance attestations binding each artefact to its source and builder, and verification at installation, not only at upload.

4. When the apparatus applies, and when it misleads

Four claims are usable only as tests. One: if a holder of one valid credential can name another tenant’s object and receive an answer, encryption changes nothing. At Sankalan the test passed at the gateway and failed on two internal paths. Two: if you cannot bound an affected cohort within seventy-two hours from logs you already keep, the notification duty will be discharged badly. Test: list every identity that read a named record last Tuesday. Vatayan could, but it took 36 hours and 40 minutes. Three: if one credential controls both the data and the key protecting it, the key gives detection value but almost no containment value — the strongest argument for customer-managed keys, and the one Vedant Salvi conceded. Four: where the ceiling on consequence is statutory, expected-value reasoning understates the right spend. The DPDP Act’s Schedule sets penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards and up to ₹200 crore for failing to give notice of a breach.

It misleads in three situations. Threat modelling over a system with no inventory diagrams only the part somebody remembered. Least privilege without a fail-safe path starves responders when they need breadth, so mature programmes pair narrow standing access with time-boxed emergency grants. And the OWASP Top Ten as a test plan lists categories seen across an industry, not weaknesses in yours.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product companies fail at the identity seam: Sankalan’s payout and reporting products share a login but classify data differently, so a reporting-only administrator can inherit, through role nesting nobody audits, a view the payout product would refuse. The answer is a periodic query listing every identity whose effective permissions exceed its nominal role. Marketplaces fail at the support seam: the role allowed to see both sides is the most socially engineered.

Regulated settings produce contradictions: payment records must be retained unaltered for statutory periods while personal data must be erased when its purpose ends. The resolution most Indian financial firms reach is to hold the person’s identifying attributes separately, under a key that can be destroyed. Hardware adds time: Vatayan’s device has an eleven-year field life, secure-boot keys burned at manufacture, and a population that will never all update.

AI-native features move the boundary again. Vatayan’s triage model has three new properties: its inputs may contain instructions as well as data, so a model that can both read a user’s record and call a tool is a confused deputy and must run with the user’s privileges, not the service’s; its training data are personal data with a purpose attached, so improving the model is a second purpose needing consent; and its inference logs are the most sensitive store nobody classified. At the organisational seam the failure is ownership: a finding in shared code belongs to no team and sits.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert from the competent

One: the vocabulary of encryption hides the location of plaintext. The tell is a team answering a logical-access question with a cipher name; an expert asks which of the seven plaintext locations “AES-256 at rest” covers.

Two: the authorisation check must live at the layer that owns the data. The tell is permission logic in the client or the gateway. The reading that checking early is checking well is wrong: an early check is bypassed by any path that avoids it.

Three: tenant identity taken from the request is not identity. The tell is an internal interface accepting a tenant identifier as a parameter — a declaration that the service trusts its callers, so the expert asks how many there are.

Four: machine identities are the larger population and the weaker one. The tell is a credential with no expiry and no named owner. The obvious reading is that service accounts are safer because no human is careless with them; the expert’s is that none is watching.

Five: logs are a liability as well as an asset. The tell is a log retention period longer than that of the data described. Logging bounds a cohort, and also copies personal data into a system with weaker access control.

Six: severity scores describe components, not products. The tell is a backlog sorted by published severity score. A high score on a function your code never calls is not a risk; a medium score in the authentication path may be your most urgent item. Exhibit 3 prices it.

Seven: consent is an architecture, not a screen. The tell is a consent flag in one table that no downstream job reads. DPDP consent must be purpose-bound and withdrawable with effect, so withdrawal must propagate to every warehouse, model and processor that received the data. Vendors pose the same question: which fields cross, and how fast can you revoke? Varenya Analytics Partners gets aggregate counts, no identifiers.

Eight: security debt is discovered by adversaries, not by you. The tell is a risk register with no tail scenario. Technical debt announces itself through slowing velocity; security debt is silent until catastrophic, so mean-based prioritisation under-invests.

7. The quantitative treatment, worked

The first quantity: Sankalan closed 162 findings in the twelve months to 31 August 2026.

Exhibit 1. Sankalan findings closed in the twelve months to 31 August 2026; the mean-days column is weighted by findings per row.

The counts say one thing, the severities another. Third-party libraries gave the most findings and the mildest: 9 of the 57 were high or critical. Service-to-service calls and the data-and-key plane produced 43 of the 162 findings, or 26.5 per cent, but 21 of the 46 high or critical ones, which is 45.7 per cent, and took 26 and 34 days to close against 9 at the edge. Vendor systems were slowest at 41 days. The company is fast where it is watched.

The second quantity is how much spend is defensible. Gordon and Loeb’s 2002 result is the rare piece of formal economics a PM can use: optimal investment never exceeds 1/e, about 0.368, of expected loss. Sankalan put the annual probability of a material data-exposure event at 0.14 and the loss if it happened at ₹3,000 lakh — an expected annual loss of ₹420 lakh, so a ceiling of ₹420 lakh ÷ e = ₹154.5 lakh. Its loss-avoidance engineering, the first two security lines of Exhibit 2, runs at 113 person-weeks a quarter, or 452 a year, which at a loaded ₹1.6 lakh per person-week is ₹723.2 lakh — nearly five times that ceiling. So invert the model. For ₹723.2 lakh to sit at the ceiling, expected loss must be at least ₹723.2 lakh × e = ₹1,966 lakh a year; at 0.14 that implies a single-event loss of ₹1,966 lakh ÷ 0.14 = ₹14,043 lakh, about ₹140 crore — below the ₹250 crore statutory ceiling, above anything Sankalan’s history suggests.

Exhibit 2. Sankalan engineering capacity, quarter to 31 December 2026: 46 engineers × 12 weeks = 552 person-weeks gross, less 99 person-weeks of on-call, leave and unplanned support (17.9 per cent of gross), leaving 453 net.

Security-attributable work is 145 of the 453 net person-weeks, which is 32.0 per cent — more than most teams assume, because two of its three lines are invisible: design work disappears into feature estimates, and compliance evidence is revenue-enabling work done by security engineers. Counting compliance as risk reduction would have made the comparison worse still, which is why only the first two lines entered it. The third quantity is reachability, censused at Vatayan on Monday 28 September 2026.

Across 732 components there were 48 open advisories, 6.6 per hundred components, of which 14 of the 48 were reachable — 29.2 per cent. A backlog built from advisory counts would have been three times larger than the work that mattered, and the effort is not where the count is. Firmware carries 18 person-days for three reachable items, six days each, against 11 person-days for five mobile items, 2.2 days each: a ratio of about 2.7 to one, because a firmware fix must be signed, staged and verified in the field.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

The first worked. Sankalan’s identity census on 31 July 2026 found 1,180 identities — 310 human, 870 machine, so machines were 73.7 per cent of the estate. Standing read access to production beneficiary data sat with 214: 38 human, 176 machine. The review after Sharvari’s finding cut that to 63, 9 human and 54 machine, so 151 of the 214 standing grants were withdrawn, 70.6 per cent. Of the 63, only 11 kept permanent credentials.

The second failed. Vatayan had an integrity monitor and an artefact store recording hashes, which is why the problem was caught at all. What it lacked was provenance: nothing bound an artefact to the source and builder that produced it, so the team could tell something was wrong but not what. That gap cost 36 hours and 40 minutes between detection and a bounded cohort.

Exhibit 4. Vatayan affected-cohort chain, 3 October 2026. Each rate is measured against the step immediately above.

The notifiable cohort was 43,200 people: 43,200 of the 4,20,000 devices in homes, 10.3 per cent, and 15.4 per cent of monthly active users. Of those, 28,080 of the 43,200 bundles carried health readings, 65.0 per cent, and 1,404 of the 28,080 belonged to accounts registered as a child’s, 5.0 per cent, which brought the Act’s stricter treatment of children’s data into the response. Vatayan notified all 43,200 rather than the 28,080, the narrower cohort being indefensible on the log coverage available. The direct cost was ₹79.64 lakh — exactly ₹79,63,920 — being ₹4.75 lakh of intimation at ₹11 a head for 43,200 people, ₹7.39 lakh of support for the 7,776 who made contact (18 per cent of those intimated) at ₹95 each, ₹36 lakh of forensics and counsel, ₹22 lakh for the withdrawal and re-release, and ₹9.50 lakh for signing-key rotation. The ₹3.40 crore field update was not triggered, the firmware signing path being intact.

The third is the decision Sharvari had to price, over three years.

Exhibit 5. Sankalan key-custody options: alternatives, not additive. Three-year cost is the one-time build plus three annual runs.

A to B costs ₹67 lakh over three years and cuts the blast radius of one data-key compromise from 92,00,000 records to a mean of 27,059 — a factor of 340. B to C costs a further ₹128 lakh and cuts blast radius hardly at all, B’s residual exposure being the key-encrypting key, which never leaves the hardware module. What C buys is different in kind: it removes Sankalan from the trust chain, which is what the clients are paying for. Against three-year revenue of ₹4,380 lakh the ₹128 lakh increment is 2.9 per cent. It imposes two costs they had not considered: a lost or revoked client key makes that client’s data unrecoverable, and Sankalan cannot decrypt to investigate an incident without the client’s participation.

9. Failure modes, with early warning and the cost of lateness

The perimeter-only threat model. Sign: one diagram, one dashed line. Diagnostic: name the three internal boundaries and show the check at each. Late, one weak service exposes every tenant.

Supply-chain blindness. Sign: no bill of materials, or one produced on request rather than every build. Diagnostic: for the artefact in production now, which source and builder made it? Vatayan’s cost of answering late was the 36 hours and 40 minutes in Figure 4.

Logging that misses authorisation decisions. Sign: logs record requests but not which identity read which object. Diagnostic: bound a cohort for last Tuesday. Late, you notify far more people than were affected — 43,200 rather than 28,080.

Consent unenforced, and no named decider. Signs: a withdrawal flow returning success in under a second; a plan naming roles but not who decides to notify at two in the morning. Diagnostics: trace a withdrawal into the warehouse and each processor; drill at an awkward hour. Late, the second spends the six-hour window assembling a committee.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether quantified risk helps or harms. The quantitative camp argues that unquantified registers are ordinal theatre in which “high” means the author cared; its evidence is organisations that under-invested exactly where their own registers were red. Critics answer that the inputs are invented, and that real decisions turn on the tail events an expectation averages away. They would be wrong if quantified teams allocated demonstrably better than ordinal ones — a comparison never run at scale.

Whether customer-managed keys are protection or liability transfer. Vedant Salvi, steelmanned: in most incidents the attacker obtains application-level access, at which point data is decrypted for him whoever holds the key, so the control meets a rare threat while adding an availability failure mode. Shalini Vartak, steelmanned: it bounds the worst case rather than the common one, alone makes erasure provable across backups, and makes an open-ended trust relationship terminable. Vedant is wrong if incidents with separately controlled key and data planes prove a material share of serious ones; Shalini is wrong if the key plane is always reachable from the same credentials as the data plane.

Whether to shift left or chase exploitability. The design camp’s evidence is that the costliest incidents trace to decisions made before any code existed. The exploitability camp’s is Exhibit 3: most of what a scanner reports is unreachable, and treating design review as a gate builds a queue that delays everything while two dangerous items wait. Both need the same scarce senior engineers, which is why the positions are rarely reconciled.

11. What mastery looks like

In a design review the master asks where the plaintext is and who makes the authorisation decision, not whether the feature is secure: the first questions have checkable answers. In an incident she treats the notification clock as a product requirement — log coverage, cohort queries, a named decider — because response quality is settled weeks beforehand. With a vendor she asks for the field-level data map before the certificate. Underneath sits an asymmetry: this work is funded on events that do not happen, so anyone demanding that security prove itself in a metric funds too little of it.

12. What each of them decided

On Wednesday 30 September 2026 Sharvari recommended option B, with a commitment to deliver option C for the two clients within two quarters and the identity reduction as a precondition. Her reasoning: B buys the factor-of-340 reduction in blast radius for ₹67 lakh over three years and delivers cryptographic erasure, which Sankalan needs for DPDP compliance anyway; C’s further ₹128 lakh buys almost no containment but protects ₹4,380 lakh of three-year revenue, so it should be sold as a commercial feature, not argued as a security control.

On Monday 12 October 2026 Vaibhav declined the ₹3.40 crore field update, the device images and firmware signing path being unaffected and the exposure confined to diagnostic uploads. He committed instead to provenance attestation across the release path in Figure 3, closing the gap that cost 36 hours and 40 minutes; to logging sufficient to bound a cohort in hours; and to a review of what the triage model’s inference logs retain. He refused to name a date by which this could not recur.

Discussion questions. First: Sharvari treated cryptographic erasure, not containment, as the decisive benefit of per-tenant keys. Is that a sound basis for ₹67 lakh? Second: Vatayan notified 43,200 when the evidence supported 28,080. Was that right, and what would its logs have had to show for the narrower figure to be defensible? Third: Exhibit 2 shows 32.0 per cent of capacity attributable to security, defensible on the Gordon–Loeb inversion only if one event could cost about ₹140 crore. Which number would you challenge?

13. Going deeper

APIs and integration basics comes next: the interfaces in Figure 1 are where tenant identity is derived or trusted. Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions unlocks the authorisation model proper. Security compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001 says what the assurance camp attests to. Device security treats field life and secure boot. Privacy-preserving architecture takes minimisation into aggregation and on-device processing. How web and mobile apps work and Reading an architecture diagram precede any credible boundary map. Data modelling for PMs and Databases, storage and caching show where the plaintext hides. Cloud infrastructure basics covers the services that make option B buildable. Scalability and performance matters because every control costs latency.
exp20v2-tech.security:
Security basics for product managers

How would someone attack this, and what would stop them?

1. A feature, a deadline and a finding

On Monday 5 October 2026, Tanvi Gadre, the product manager for invoicing at Tijori Systems, opened a message from the company's security engineer, Tejas Gawde. Tijori sells billing and GST-filing software to small merchants across Pune, Nashik and Kolhapur. It holds 1,80,000 merchant accounts, and each account stores business tax numbers, customer names, phone numbers and invoice histories. The feature Tanvi had championed for two quarters, "share invoice by link", was due to launch on Monday 19 October, fourteen days away. A distributor network had made it a condition of a ₹90 lakh renewal.

Tejas's message was short. In an internal review, he had found that the shared links were built from invoice numbers that ran in sequence, and that nothing checked whether the person opening a link was entitled to see that invoice. A reader who could see one invoice could reasonably expect to see its neighbours.

Tanvi's first instinct was to ask whether the problem was serious enough to move the date. Her second was to notice that she could not rank the weakness, price a fix, or say what the law would require if it were exploited. Girish Tendulkar, the chief technology officer, and Gita Thakkar, head of legal, awaited her recommendation.

Exhibit 1. The decision as Tanvi found it on 5 October 2026.
ItemPosition
Merchant accounts on the platform1,80,000
Launch dateMonday 19 October 2026 (14 days after the finding)
Commercial pressure₹90 lakh distributor renewal tied to the feature
Weakness reportedPredictable link identifiers; no entitlement check on the invoice
Statutory exposureUp to ₹250 crore under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, for failing to take reasonable security safeguards

2. The idea: security as structured pessimism

Security, for a product manager, is the discipline of deciding in advance who might want to misuse a system, what they could reach, and which controls make misuse costly or visible. A threat is a way harm could happen. A vulnerability is a weakness that lets it happen. A control is anything that prevents, limits or reveals the harm. Risk is the combination of how likely a threat is and how much it would cost.

The field grew from a problem: systems built to work were not built to resist. In 1975 two researchers, Jerome Saltzer and Michael Schroeder, published design principles that still anchor the subject, among them least privilege: every person and program should hold only the access its task requires. In 1999 Loren Kohnfelder and Praerit Garg at Microsoft proposed STRIDE, a checklist for threat modelling, meaning the structured exercise of drawing a system and asking what could go wrong at each point. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, known as OWASP and founded in 2001, began publishing its "Top Ten" list of common web-application weaknesses in 2003. It catalogues categories such as broken access control, cryptographic failures, insecure design and misconfiguration.

The sentence Tanvi could repeat in a meeting: "We are not asking whether this is secure; we are asking who could reach what, how we would know, and what it costs us if they do."

3. How it actually works

Tejas began the way every threat model begins: with a drawing. He sketched the invoice-sharing flow as boxes and arrows, then marked the trust boundaries, the lines across which data passes from something the company controls to something it does not. A merchant's phone, the public internet, Tijori's application servers, its database, and a third-party text-message vendor, Gajra Messaging Services, each sat on a different side of a boundary.

Step two is to walk each arrow and each box and ask STRIDE's six questions: could someone spoof an identity, tamper with data, repudiate an action (deny doing it, with no record to prove otherwise), disclose information, deny service, or elevate privileges beyond what they were granted? Arrow two, the customer opening a link, raised the disclosure question at once. The system accepted a request from an unknown person and returned an invoice. What decided that the person was entitled to it? The honest answer was: nothing except knowing the address.

Step three, which practitioners often leave implicit, is to separate authentication (who are you?) from authorisation (what may you see?). Tijori's links had a crude version of the first and none of the second. This is OWASP's broken access control, and it is a design decision, not a coding slip: someone chose that a link would be enough. Steps four and five are to rank the threats and to decide on controls: encryption in transit (scrambling data between devices so that eavesdroppers on the network see nothing useful), encryption at rest (scrambling stored data so a stolen disk or copied file is unreadable without keys), and logging, so that misuse leaves evidence. Encryption protects against a stolen file. It does not help when the application itself hands the invoice to the wrong person, which is precisely Tijori's case.

4. A worked example

Tejas and Tanvi listed four threats and scored each by annual likelihood (their estimate of the chance it occurs in a year) and impact (rupees lost if it does: remediation, notification, legal costs and lost merchants). Expected loss is likelihood multiplied by impact. These are estimates, but multiplying them forces the team to argue about the right things.

Exhibit 2. Pass one: expected annual loss before any new control (₹ lakh).
ThreatLikelihood per yearImpact (₹ lakh)Expected loss (₹ lakh)
A. Invoices reached through predictable links0.3012036.0
B. Staff login stolen and reused0.1030030.0
C. Leak at the text-message vendor0.05804.0
D. Misconfigured file storage exposes documents0.1520030.0

Threat A looks largest, but only just; B and D together are worth more (60.0 against 36.0). Two controls were priced. Replacing sequential identifiers with long random tokens that expire, and checking entitlement on every request, costs ₹6 lakh and cuts A's likelihood from 0.30 to 0.03. Requiring a second login factor for staff (multi-factor authentication) costs ₹4 lakh and cuts B's likelihood from 0.10 to 0.02.

With both controls the total falls from 100.0 to 43.6 (3.6 + 6.0 + 4.0 + 30.0), a reduction of 56.4 lakh for ₹10 lakh. The second input to change was the impact of threat D. Suppose the exposed storage held bank-statement uploads, doubling D's impact from 200 to 400; its expected loss becomes 60.0 and the total after both controls rises to 73.6. Now the ranking flips: the unfixed storage is the largest remaining risk, and the right next hour belongs to a storage review, not the launch date.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Encryption is not access control

Data encrypted at rest is still shown in plain form to any user the application authorises. If the authorisation is wrong, the encryption is irrelevant.

Compliance is not security

Certifications such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 attest that a company runs defined processes. They do not certify that a particular feature is safe.

Likelihood is a judgement, not a measurement

The 0.30 in Exhibit 2 came from a conversation. Use it to order risks, not as a forecast.

Least privilege has a price

Narrow access slows support work. The question is not whether to restrict but which roles need which data, and how long access lasts. Figure 3 shows the shape of a sensible answer.

Privacy and security overlap but differ

Security asks who can reach data. Privacy asks whether the company should hold it, for what purpose, and with whose consent. Under the DPDP Act, 2023, a company processing personal data is a data fiduciary: it decides why and how the data is used and carries the duty of care. A person whose data it is, the data principal, must generally give free, specific, informed consent, and consent can be withdrawn.

Vendors inherit your duty

Gajra processes data on Tijori's behalf; the statute treats Tijori as accountable regardless. Vendor risk means asking what data a supplier sees and how fast it will tell you of a problem.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

Exhibit 4. Where the weight of security falls by product type.
Product typeMain exposureWhat changes in practice
ConsumerAccount takeover at scale; consent for personal dataLogin protection and clear consent screens dominate the roadmap
B2BTenant isolation; staff and customer-administrator permissionsBuyers send security questionnaires and ask for SOC 2 or ISO 27001 before signing
MarketplaceTwo sides who do not trust each other; fraud; paymentsIdentity checks on both sides and tight limits on what each can see of the other

Tijori is B2B with a consumer-like edge, since merchants' own customers appear in the data. Company size matters as much as product type. A ten-person start-up should buy secure defaults (managed login, encrypted storage, automatic patching) and name one owner for incidents. A large company has review boards and audits, and its danger is reviews that arrive after the date has been promised to a customer. At either scale, the cheapest moment to ask is during design.

7. Common mistakes

"We will add security after launch"

Symptom: the launch checklist has a performance line and no security line. Misunderstanding: security as a coat of paint, when many weaknesses are design decisions. Diagnostic: ask at design review, "Who may see this object, and where is that checked?"

Treating the penetration test as the finish line

Symptom: a single annual report is cited as proof of safety. Misunderstanding: a test is a snapshot of one version. Diagnostic: ask how many releases have shipped since the last test.

Collecting everything, just in case

Symptom: forms ask for fields no feature uses. Misunderstanding: data as an asset without a liability side. Diagnostic: for any field, ask which feature breaks if it is deleted.

No rehearsed incident plan

Symptom: nobody can say who decides to notify. Misunderstanding: that incidents are rare enough to improvise. Diagnostic: run a two-hour tabletop drill and see who is unreachable.

8. What good looks like

The same decision, handled well, begins on the day the feature is specified. The product manager draws the data flow with an engineer, sorts the threats by expected loss, and writes the controls into the acceptance criteria next to the functional ones. Each role holds only the access it needs. A named person is on call for incidents, and the rehearsed timeline looks like Figure 4, because Indian law imposes clocks. CERT-In, the national computer emergency response team under MeitY, requires certain incidents to be reported within six hours of the organisation noticing them. Under the DPDP Rules, a personal-data breach must be notified to the Data Protection Board and to each affected person without delay, with a fuller report to the Board within 72 hours.

9. What Tanvi decided

On Wednesday 7 October, Tanvi took a recommendation to Girish and Gita. She proposed that the share-link launch would hold to Monday 19 October only if three conditions were met: random expiring tokens with an entitlement check, a second factor for staff, and a review of file-storage settings. If the storage review turned up the document types in the second pass, the launch would slip, and she would tell the distributor on Thursday rather than on the nineteenth. Her reasoning was the arithmetic of Exhibit 3: ₹10 lakh bought a 56.4 lakh reduction, against a penalty ceiling of ₹250 crore and a ₹90 lakh renewal that a breach would also have endangered.

The natural next topics are identity (authentication, single sign-on, roles and permissions), where Figure 3 would be built in earnest; compliance frameworks such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001; device security; and privacy-preserving architecture, which asks how to hold less data in the first place.

Two questions to sit with. First, in your own product, which decision did someone make by default that an attacker would call a gift, and who in your team owns reversing it? Second, if your most trusted vendor told you tomorrow that your customers' data had been exposed, who would decide what you say, to whom, and by what time?
case20v1-tech.security:
Hornbill Pay: The Invoice Flaw Before Diwali

1. Opening

On Thursday 22 October 2026, at 7:40 in the morning, Prasanth Aroor sat in the Indiranagar office of Hornbill Pay in Bengaluru with a printout he had not asked for. It listed 2,106 requests in which one merchant's account had asked the system for another merchant's invoice, and the system had answered each one.

Aroor was Hornbill's head of product. The festive release, a WhatsApp invoice-sharing feature on which the company had staked its Diwali quarter, was due to leave the engineering floor on Wednesday 28 October. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November. Parameswaran Ambalath, the chief executive, had asked for Aroor's recommendation by Monday 26 October: ship as planned, delay, or find some third way.

2. Company background

Hornbill Pay, founded in Kochi in 2017, sells UPI collection, GST invoicing and WhatsApp billing to small merchants: sweet shops, pharmacies, garment wholesalers and salons. By October 2026 it served 38,000 merchants, employed 310 people and had reported ₹96 crore of revenue for FY26. Its merchants paid a monthly plan, and a growing share paid for add-ons such as bulk reminders. Growth had come mostly from tier-two cities, through a network of resellers in Mumbai, Coimbatore and Jaipur who signed up shops in bulk and often wired Hornbill's interface into their own billing tools. The company held no formal security certification yet; a SOC 2 audit was pencilled in for the second half of 2027, and enterprise clients were beginning to ask about it.

The competition was crowded. PhonePe for Business and Paytm subsidised soundboxes and QR codes to the same shopkeepers, Razorpay served larger online sellers, and Zoho Invoice sat comfortably with accountants. Hornbill's edge was the invoice itself: a shopkeeper in Surat could raise a GST-compliant bill in under twenty seconds and send it to the customer. Money moved through a licensed bank partner; Hornbill held the invoices, and with them the names and phone numbers of its merchants' customers.

3. The situation

On Wednesday 14 October an independent researcher wrote to the company's security mailbox. She reported that any logged-in merchant could retrieve an invoice belonging to another merchant by changing the identifier in an ordinary request. In the vocabulary of the OWASP Top Ten this is broken access control: the system checked that the caller was a merchant, but not that the invoice was theirs. Pritika Arackal, vice-president of engineering in Pune, reproduced it within a day. A fix for that one endpoint was estimated at two days, plus regression testing that had not yet been scheduled.

What remained unknown was whether anyone else had noticed. Arackal's team searched ninety days of logs, covering 41.8 lakh invoice-view calls, and found 2,106 cross-merchant requests, about 0.05 per cent of the total. Exhibit 2 shows who made them. The researcher's 212 were explained, and she had attested in writing that she deleted what she saw. The reseller's 1,630 looked like a script replaying stale identifiers after a data migration, but the reseller had not yet confirmed it. That left the three accounts behind the remaining 264, two of which had been opened in September. Each call returned one invoice, so at most 2,106 customer records had been read, and for the three unexplained accounts at most 264.

The new feature complicated matters. Festive Bill Share would create public invoice links, multiplying the places where invoice identifiers travelled. Engineering had designed the links with a separate check, but nobody had yet tested the older endpoints against the same pattern. Exhibit 1 sets out the main dates.

Arackal's view was blunt: if one endpoint had been built without the check, others probably had, because the same small team wrote most of them under the same deadline pressure. The global team saw the problem differently. The Berlin designer, working three and a half hours behind Bengaluru until clocks changed on 25 October, warned that the sharing screen's promise of "private links" was now a claim the company had to be able to defend. The Toronto data scientist, nine and a half hours behind until 1 November, noted that the feature's ₹2.4 crore forecast came from only three weeks of pilot data. In Dubai, the largest enterprise client, a retail group with Indian outlets, had a security questionnaire due before it renewed.

4. The people

Prasanth Aroor (Bengaluru), head of product, owns the Diwali number and now the risk decision. Pritika Arackal (Pune), vice-president of engineering, wants the entire invoice surface audited and distrusts a one-endpoint fix. Parameswaran Ambalath (Kochi), chief executive, is raising a funding round in January and wants neither a missed quarter nor a headline. Prerana Aikara (Singapore), customer-success lead, speaks daily to the Dubai client and fears learning of a problem from a merchant rather than from Hornbill. Aroor himself leans toward shipping, since he promised the feature to the board in July, but he knows that a product manager who cannot say what the access check protects has not yet earned the right to a view. Ambalath has told him that he will back whichever recommendation comes with a clear account of the risk, the cost and the date by which each would be known to be right or wrong. The company's lawyer has said only that the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the CERT-In reporting directions of 2022 may apply, and that when the clock started is itself a question.

Exhibit 2. Cross-merchant invoice requests, 90 days to 21 October 2026
SourceAccountsRequestsStatus
Researcher's test accounts3212Explained; deletion attested
Mumbai reseller integration11,630Probable script bug, unconfirmed
Unexplained3264Under review
Total72,106

Total invoice-view calls in the same 90 days: 41.8 lakh. Each call returns one invoice. Share of calls that crossed merchants: 2,106 / 41,80,000 = 0.05 per cent.

5. The options

Option A: ship, patch later. Release on 28 October as planned and fix the flawed endpoint in the sprint ending 11 November, twenty days after today. The feature keeps its full forecast of ₹2.4 crore. The cost is that the weakness stays open through the busiest invoicing fortnight of the year, with a public-link feature on top, and any disclosure decision is deferred.

Option B: freeze and audit. Hold the release, and have Arackal's team test every invoice endpoint, finishing on 3 November. The feature moves to 16 November, after Diwali, and keeps only ₹0.6 crore of its forecast. The flaw is closed in twelve days and the team learns its full extent.

Option C: split the work. Ship the one-endpoint hotfix on 24 October. Release Festive Bill Share on 28 October to 20 per cent of merchants, widening only as the audit clears each endpoint by 3 November. Commission an outside review and write to the three unexplained accounts and to whichever authorities counsel advises. Exhibit 3 compares the three. Its costs are Arackal's estimates and its revenue figures come from the Toronto forecast, so the options differ in what they risk as well as in what they earn.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared
OptionKnown flaw closedFeature liveFestive revenue kept (₹ crore)Added cost (₹ lakh)
A. Ship, patch later11 Nov28 Oct, all merchants2.44
B. Freeze and audit3 Nov16 Nov0.66
C. Split the work24 Oct28 Oct, 20% then widening1.917

Revenue figures are Toronto's forecast of incremental plan upgrades, 28 October to 30 November. Option C cost: outside review ₹9 lakh, weekend engineering ₹3 lakh, merchant notification and support ₹5 lakh. 1 crore = 100 lakh.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using the OWASP vocabulary, what exactly went wrong, and which of the 2,106 requests should worry Aroor most?
  2. If you were threat-modelling Festive Bill Share, how would someone attack it, and what would stop them?
  3. What does each option assume about the 264 unexplained requests?
  4. Which option would you recommend by Monday, and what would make you change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

Security basics give a product manager one question: how would someone attack this, and what would stop them? The flaw is not exotic. It is the commonest category, a missing ownership check, and the principle it breaks is least privilege: a merchant's session should reach only that merchant's data. A manager need not write the fix, and need not have been the one to find it. The task is to ask the right questions of those who do, and to price the answers.

One defensible path is Option C. Compare it with the alternatives on the page's own numbers. Against Option B it keeps ₹1.9 crore instead of ₹0.6 crore, an extra ₹1.3 crore, which is 130 lakh of revenue, before margin, for 11 lakh more cost (17 less 6), while still closing the known flaw ten days sooner and auditing by the same date. Against Option A it gives up ₹0.5 crore of forecast, 50 lakh, and costs 13 lakh more (17 less 4), but closes the flaw in two days rather than twenty and stops adding a public-link surface on top of an unaudited one. The forecast itself rests on three weeks of data, so it deserves a wide margin.

The staged rollout is the key. It lets the feature ship while limiting how much unaudited surface it touches, and the audit gates its widening. Disclosure follows the same logic: the three unexplained accounts, at most 264 records, are a bounded group that can be contacted now, and the lawyer's question about when the clock started should be answered in writing before the board hears anything from a third party. Aikara should brief the Dubai client first, not last.

Option C is not free of risk. Twenty per cent of merchants is still 7,600 shops sending festive bills over a link, and the Mumbai reseller's 1,630 requests may prove less innocent than they look. Aroor should also name in advance what would change his mind: a fourth unexplained account, an audit finding in the payment path, or a reseller reply that contradicts the script explanation. The path is defensible because each risk has an owner, a date and a trigger for reversal, not because the risks are absent.
case40v1-tech.security:
Sampige Mobility Systems: What Left the Building

A case for discussion. Bengaluru, November 2026.

1. Sunday night, 22 November 2026

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, Devapriya Kaimal was still at her dining table in Jayanagar, Bengaluru, with three documents open and a fourth she had not written. The first was a draft security assessment from Spashta Labs, dated 2 October. The second was a capacity note from her vice-president of engineering, dated 16 November. The third was a note from counsel, two pages long, which concluded nothing.

The fourth document was the one Kaimal owed the board at nine the next morning: a single page saying what Sampige Mobility Systems would do about its partner gateway, and when, and whom it would tell. She was the vice-president of product.

The Spashta draft ran to thirty-one findings, four of them critical. Exhibit 3, prepared the previous day, listed two systems that hold no record of who has read them. The feature was called Fleet Command, and Shamal Haulage had written its go-live date into the master agreement. On 7 December, fifteen days away, the company was contracted to switch on a feature that would let a customer's dispatcher reach into a moving truck.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2019

Sampige was founded in Mangaluru in 2016 by Dayanidhi Karkera, who had spent nine years selling diesel-monitoring boxes to lorry owners in coastal Karnataka, and who named the company after the flower. Its first product was a tracking unit certified to AIS-140, the standard the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways had made mandatory for public service vehicles. By 2026 the device was the smaller half of the business. The larger half was software: trip reconstruction, driver-behaviour scoring from a cabin-facing camera, fuel analytics, and an application programming interface that let a customer's own transport management system read everything.

That interface — the partner gateway — was built in nine weeks in 2019 to close Sampige's first ten-thousand-vehicle customer. The customer's transport system could not rotate credentials, could not hold a secret for less than a year, and would not change. So the gateway issued one long-lived key per account, and the key carried the whole account's reach. Nobody wrote down that this was temporary. Seven years later, the partner directory held 312 integrations against that gateway, and the earliest of them had not changed a credential since it was issued.

By October 2026 Sampige employed 418 people — engineering split between Bengaluru and Pune, with a designer in Berlin, a data scientist in Toronto, a customer-success lead in Singapore and a sales head in New Jersey. Revenue for the year to 31 March 2026 was ₹118 crore. Annual recurring revenue at 31 October stood at ₹132 crore across 2,149 fleets and 1,33,000 vehicles (Exhibit 4).

3. The industry

Indian fleet telematics in 2026 was a market with a regulatory floor and no ceiling. AIS-140 had made a tracking box compulsory on buses and taxis, which turned hardware into a commodity and pushed every serious player upward into software. Connectivity came from Jio and Airtel IoT plans; the vehicles themselves were the familiar fleet of Tata and Mahindra light commercials; toll settlement rode FASTag and the NPCI rails. Sampige's customers were logistics companies, bus operators and distribution networks, and its competitors ranged from OEM-owned telematics arms to the device importers who undercut everyone on price and sold no software at all.

Two forces mattered more than competition. The first was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which had made a driver's location history and a cabin video clip something a company holds on terms, not something it owns. The second was procurement. A state road transport corporation's telematics tender, worth ₹46 crore over five years, required bidders to disclose any material security incident in the preceding twenty-four months.

Sampige's exposure was not only Indian. Its largest single contract was with Shamal Haulage FZE, a Dubai cold-chain operator running 6,400 vehicles across the Gulf, whose master agreement required notification of unauthorised access to its data within twenty-four hours. Dilsher Kidavu was running three fleet pilots in New Jersey and Ohio, with the first signature expected on 15 December.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The sequence is set out in Exhibit 1. On Monday 14 September Kaimal commissioned Spashta Labs, a Hyderabad assessment firm, to test the platform ahead of the ISO 27001 audit booked for 11 January 2027. Spashta's draft arrived on Friday 2 October: 31 findings, four of them critical (Exhibit 2). Two criticals sat in the partner gateway, where a partner's key could read trip and location data for fleets outside that partner's contract. One sat in the archive of cabin camera clips, which held about 4.7 crore clips from 58,000 camera-fitted vehicles since April 2024, unencrypted at rest and readable by a service account that had no business reading it. The fourth sat in the fleet admin console, where an operations support role carried permission to export any fleet's driver records.

On Tuesday 20 October, while scoping the fix, an engineer in Pune checked how far back the gateway's request logs went. The answer was thirty days. The company had told a customer questionnaire in November 2025, and the tender pre-qualification in September 2026, that gateway logs were retained for 180 days. Separately, the clip archive's access logging had never been switched on at all: there was no record, and no possibility of a record, of who had read what. Exhibit 3 sets out what evidence exists.

On Wednesday 28 October a researcher in Hyderabad wrote to the security mailbox to say that a Sampige partner credential was visible in a publicly distributed mobile application build belonging to Sarvatra Telematics Services, a Nagpur reseller. Dibakar Koshy, who had joined as head of security in August, logged it as a test credential on the strength of the partner's first reply. On Friday 6 November the reseller's own engineer confirmed it was live, issued in March 2021, and carried account-wide scope. In the thirty days to 21 November that key made 11,400 calls, all from two server addresses Sarvatra confirmed as its own. The key served 640 small fleets. It could reach all 2,149.

On Thursday 12 November, preparing the remediation plan, Dhruvika Kotian discovered that two legacy gateway endpoints, still serving seven partners, had been outside Spashta's scope and had never been tested. Counsel's note came the same day, and is summarised in Exhibit 7.

5. The people

Devapriya Kaimal (Bengaluru), vice-president of product, owns both the Fleet Command roadmap and, since July, the security backlog. She has not said that she rejected a scoped-token proposal in the 2024 planning round because it carried no customer-visible benefit. Dayanidhi Karkera (Mangaluru), co-founder and chief executive, wants the Series C term sheet expected in January and the transport tender in December. He has told two prospective investors that certification is on track. Dhruvika Kotian (Pune), vice-president of engineering, wants the gateway rebuilt properly and will not accept a patch she considers cosmetic. She also signed the November 2025 questionnaire answer that said 180 days.

Dibakar Koshy (Bengaluru), head of security, three months in post, wants broad notification now and says the company's position is indefensible. He has not said that his own detection query can only look at the fields the logs happen to carry. Deepthi Kalathil (Singapore), customer-success lead, speaks to Shamal Haulage weekly and answered its October questionnaire with "no known incidents". Dilsher Kidavu (New Jersey), sales head, ten and a half hours behind Bengaluru since 1 November, wants nothing disclosed before 15 December. Dipika Kajava (Toronto) built the detection query and the exposure estimate and has told Kaimal, twice, what the zeroes in Exhibit 3 do and do not mean. Daivik Kannampilly (Berlin), four and a half hours behind Bengaluru since 25 October, designed Fleet Command's confirmation screen and the driver-facing privacy notice, and has asked whose consent the notice is actually recording.

6. Exhibits

The exhibits below were assembled between 12 and 21 November by Kotian, Kajava and counsel, and were not written to be read together.

Exhibit 2. Assessment findings by area and severity

Engineering's triage of 13 October accepts 26 of the 31 and disputes 5 mediums as not exploitable in the production configuration. Of the 26 it accepts, it rates 2 critical, 9 high, 8 medium and 7 low, having re-rated two of Spashta's criticals downward. Spashta rates base severity without environmental context; the triage applies context. The two teams never agreed a rubric. Within the gateway, Spashta's scope covered the production endpoints only: the two legacy endpoints serving seven partners were never tested and appear nowhere above.

Prepared by Kajava on 21 November 2026. The last column counts records matching her detection query, which compares the fleet whose data a response carried against the fleet a caller's token was contracted to reach. It runs only where a log records both; it cannot run on the archive at all, and the legacy endpoints log failures but not successes. Earliest records are 21 November less the retention figure. The production gateway's retention was given as 180 days in the customer questionnaire of November 2025 and in the tender pre-qualification of September 2026.

Exhibit 4. Customers and contractual exposure, 31 October 2026

ARR as at 31 October 2026, a different measure from the ₹118 crore of revenue recognised in the year to 31 March 2026. Reseller agreements oblige the reseller, not Sampige, to notify the end fleet. The Sarvatra credential sits in the bottom row, serving 640 of the 1,940 reseller fleets, and its scope reaches all 2,149. Shamal Haulage FZE accounts for ₹11.2 crore of the top row. 1 crore = 100 lakh.

Exhibit 5. Remediation workstreams as planned on 16 November 2026

Kotian's plan. Elapsed weeks assume all four workstreams are staffed in parallel, which the capacity in Exhibit 6 does not allow. Criticals and highs are counted against Spashta's ratings, not the internal triage, which accepts two criticals. The 312 integrations are the count in the partner directory. Of these, 287 called the production gateway during the thirty days to 21 November, which is the only window its request log covers; the other 25 did not call within it and their status is unknown. Cost is loaded engineering at ₹1.30 lakh per engineer-week, ₹231.4 lakh in all, plus ₹10.6 lakh of tooling and storage: ₹242.0 lakh, or ₹2.42 crore.

Exhibit 7. Notification obligations as counsel reads them, 12 November 2026
