Counsel sets out four candidate start dates for every clock above, and declines to choose: 2 October, when the draft assessment was received; 20 October, when the retention gap made the question of access unanswerable; 6 November, when the Sarvatra key was confirmed live and account-wide; or no start at all, on the ground that no unauthorised access has been established. The note observes that the clip archive cannot be cleared by any amount of further log review.

7. Voices

From the incident channel, Friday 20 November, 11:52 IST. Kotian: "Thirty days. I signed one-eighty in that questionnaire because that was what the runbook said and the runbook was eighteen months stale. I am not going to pretend that is a small thing."

From the same channel, four minutes later. Koshy: "Then say that. Zero confirmed accesses is not zero accesses. It is zero rows returned by a query that cannot see before the twenty-first of October and cannot see the archive at all."

From a call at 19:30 IST on Thursday 19 November, which was 15:00 in Berlin, 09:00 in New Jersey and Toronto, 18:00 in Dubai and 22:00 in Singapore.

Kalathil: "I told Shamal in October that there were no known incidents. On the second of October that answer had already stopped being true, or it had not — that is the whole argument, and I was not in it."
Kannampilly: "The confirmation screen for Fleet Command says the command is authorised by the fleet. Authorised by the fleet's key, which is the same key that reads everything else."

From Karkera's pre-read to the board, circulated Saturday 21 November. "We commissioned an assessment before anyone asked us to, we are closing the findings, and we have no evidence of any customer data leaving our systems. I would like the discussion on Monday to be about sequencing, not about disclosure."

Kaimal's reply to Karkera, sent at 23:07 on Sunday and then deleted. "Four of these options are answers about the gateway. Ask me on Monday what we would have to have built to tell you, in one sentence, what left the building."

8. The options as Kaimal frames them

Option A — ship and remediate. Switch on Fleet Command for Shamal Haulage on 7 December as contracted. Run W1 and W2; defer W3 and W4 to the next financial year. Internal cost ₹86 lakh, no liquidated damages, the ₹46 crore bid filed on 18 December on the view that nothing material has been established. Engineer-weeks committed: 46 plus 18 plus 96 for Fleet Command plus 40 for the AIS-140 recertification, which is 200 — inside the 234.6 of Exhibit 6 and outside the 195.5.

Option B — rebuild the gateway. All four workstreams, ₹242 lakh, 178 engineer-weeks plus 40 for recertification: 218. Fleet Command leaves the window altogether and is rescheduled for 12 April 2027; liquidated damages of ₹35 lakh a commenced month reach their ₹1.4 crore cap in the fourth period, which begins on 7 March 2027.

Option C — stop and disclose. Pause Fleet Command. Run W1, W2 and W4 — ₹124 lakh, 130 engineer-weeks with recertification. File with CERT-In, intimate under the DPDP Act, notify all 42 clause-bearing contracts and the 1,940 reseller fleets, and disclose in the tender on 18 December. Liquidated damages reach the cap.

Option D — buy the fix. Contract Spashta's delivery arm for W1 and W2 at ₹1.62 crore against the ₹86 lakh of doing it inside, keeping 64 engineer-weeks for product. Internal demand falls to 136. Fleet Command ships on 5 January 2027 with remote commands cut to read-only, which commences one monthly period of ₹35 lakh.

9. The deadline, the constraints, and Sunday night

The board call is at 09:00 IST on Monday 23 November. The hard edges are these. Fleet Command is contracted for 7 December, with liquidated damages of ₹35 lakh for each commenced month of delay, capped at ₹1.4 crore. The tender bid closes on Friday 18 December. ISO 27001 Stage 1 is booked for 11 January 2027 and the SOC 2 observation window would need to open on 1 February. The AIS-140 recertification cannot move. Cash is ₹61 crore with a monthly net burn of ₹3.4 crore, and the Series C term sheet is expected in January. Four platform hires are approved and none can arrive before February. Shamal Haulage's clause runs in twenty-four hours from awareness, and awareness is the word nobody will define.

Kaimal closed the laptop at ten past midnight and opened it again. She pulled up Exhibit 3 and read the archive row, then the legacy-endpoint row, then the archive row once more. At twenty past one she wrote a single line on the fourth document, and then she looked at it for a long time without adding anything.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. In the vocabulary of the OWASP Top Ten, how would you label each of Spashta's four critical findings as section 4 describes them, and which would you close first on the evidence of Exhibits 2 and 5?
  2. Exhibit 3 reports zero unauthorised accesses in four of six rows. What does that zero measure, and what would have to be true for it to mean what Karkera's pre-read takes it to mean?
  3. Threat-model Fleet Command as a partner would see it: who holds which credential, what can each credential reach, and where would a narrower reach change the picture?
  4. Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 6 cannot both be satisfied. Whose number would you test first, and what test would settle it before Monday?
  5. Counsel offers four candidate start dates for the clocks in Exhibit 7. Argue for one. What would you put in writing, and to whom?
  6. What should Kaimal do on Monday morning — the first three decisions, in order — and what should she say to the board, including what she will not be able to tell them?
exp40v2-tech.debt.concepts:
Technical debt as a concept

Delivery & Technology › Technical Fluency — deliberate versus accidental debt, and the arithmetic of principal and interest

1. Two decisions, four days apart

On Thursday 12 March 2026, Manohar Chaubey, vice-president of product at Nivaran Robotics Industries in Coimbatore, opened a meeting he had postponed since January. Nivaran builds sortation robots for logistics warehouses: 2,400 machines at eighteen sites around Bhiwandi, Hosur and Luhari, four models in the field, a fifth promised for the October–December quarter. Nachiket Vaze, head of platform engineering, had priced it.

Nivaran ships one firmware image of model-specific branches, so every release is regression-tested across the matrix: four models by six scenarios by 1.5 engineer-days, or 36 engineer-days a release. Nine releases shipped in the year to March 2026: 324 engineer-days, ₹45,36,000 at ₹14,000 an engineer-day. Five models make it 45 engineer-days a release, 405 a year, ₹56,70,000 — ₹11,34,000 of extra testing for one product line. Vaze wanted a hardware abstraction layer putting model-specific behaviour in plug-ins: 14 engineer-months, ₹39,20,000, at an engineer-month of 20 engineer-days, ₹2,80,000. Oishani Guha, the finance director, asked what the return was and when. Nadia Kowalczyk, a reliability engineer in Kraków, added that two of the nine releases had needed a field rollback — 22.2 per cent — at seven site visits apiece, ₹85,000 a visit: ₹11,90,000.

Four days later, on Monday 16 March 2026, Namrata Sabharwal, chief product officer of Odhani Fashion Network in Bengaluru, faced the same idea in a different system. Odhani's app holds promotion logic in both the catalogue and the checkout service, so every pricing experiment needs coordinated deploys from two squads. In the thirteen weeks from 1 January to 31 March 2026 the team ran 31 experiments, 2.38 a week against a target of four, each costing 3.5 engineer-days of plumbing: 108.5 engineer-days, ₹12,47,750 at an engineer-day of ₹11,500. Nikhil Padhye, the engineering director, costed a unified promotions service at 9 engineer-months, ₹20,70,000, cutting plumbing to 0.8 engineer-days an experiment — 24.8 engineer-days, ₹2,85,200. Madhavi Rangarajan, who runs analytics, noted that 6 of the 31 produced a shippable win, a 19.4 per cent hit rate.

2. The idea, and the people who disagree about it

A working definition: technical debt is the gap between the design a system has and the design the work now being asked of it requires, expressed as two quantities — the principal, the one-time cost of closing the gap, and the interest, the recurring surcharge on every change until it is closed. A system can therefore carry a large principal and almost no interest, so not repaying is sometimes correct; and since the definition is relative to the work demanded, code becomes debt the day the roadmap turns towards it.

The metaphor is Ward Cunningham's, from a 1992 OOPSLA experience report on WyCash, a portfolio-management product: shipping first-time code is like going into debt, a little of which speeds development so long as it is repaid promptly; the danger is debt left unpaid, since every minute on not-quite-right code counts as interest. The problem it solved was translation: engineers called a design messy, and managers heard aesthetics. Cunningham then spent two decades objecting to how the word was used, and his objection is one of five live positions.

The accounting school — Cunningham via Steve McConnell's 2007 taxonomy and Martin Fowler's 2009 quadrant — signs that every material item has a principal and a rate, and that repayment is sequenced by rate; it will not sign that a static-analysis score measures debt, since scores count findings, not the cost of change. The purist school, sharpest in Robert C. Martin's remark that a mess is not a technical debt but merely a mess, signs that debt exists only where a team knew the better design and recorded choosing another; it will not sign "we took on debt" said of code nobody designed. The real-options school of Chris Matts and Olav Maassen signs that deferring a decision buys information worth more than the interest, and denies that the target design is knowable when the shortcut is taken. The architectural school — the Software Engineering Institute line of Kruchten, Nord and Ozkaya — signs that only debt crossing a service boundary compounds, not that tidying inside a component repays anything. The evolutionary school, from Manny Lehman's 1980 laws of software evolution, signs that systems lose fitness because the world moves, and denies any principal exists.

3. Mechanics: four quantities, worked through

Principal, which is not fixed

Vaze had quoted the layer three times: 8 engineer-months, ₹22,40,000, in January 2025 at three models; 11 engineer-months, ₹30,80,000, in January 2026 at four; and 14 engineer-months, ₹39,20,000, in March 2026 with provision for the fifth. The principal grew ₹16,80,000 over fourteen months of deferral — ₹1,20,000 a month, a 75 per cent increase — as each model added three engineer-months of branch logic. Financial principal does not grow while ignored; this does.

Interest, measured against a named alternative

Interest is the recurring cost of the present design minus that of the target design, over a stated window. Under the layer a release needs a core suite of six scenarios at 1.5 engineer-days, 9 in all, plus 1.5 engineer-days for each of the two models touched on average: 12 engineer-days a release, 108 a year. At five models the present design costs 405, so interest is 405 − 108 = 297 engineer-days, ₹41,58,000 — 106.1 per cent on the ₹39,20,000 principal. At three models it was 135 engineer-days, ₹18,90,000, on ₹22,40,000: 84.4 per cent. The rate rose because the numerator grew faster than the denominator.

Rate, and the sequencing it implies

Table 1. Nivaran debt register, 12 March 2026, in ₹ lakh. Rate is annual interest over principal; totals are exact row sums, and the blended rate is total interest over total principal.
ItemPrincipalAnnual interestRate
Model-specific firmware branches (no abstraction layer)39.2041.58106.1%
Telemetry schema shared with the warehouse console12.607.8462.2%
Hand-rolled update agent, no staged rollout8.4011.90141.7%
Spares-inventory service on a single-node database5.601.1220.0%
Calibration rig scripts outside version control2.803.36120.0%
Total / blended68.6065.8095.9%

A rate is only useful comparatively, and the register reordered the work: the update agent carries the highest rate, 141.7 per cent, on the third-smallest principal, ₹8,40,000, and lies behind Kowalczyk's ₹11,90,000 of rollback cost, while the spares service at 20 per cent is what aesthetics flag and finance ignores.

Horizon, and the discounting nobody does

Two engineers for seven months cost ₹5,60,000 a month, ₹39,20,000 in all, then save ₹3,46,500 a month (₹41,58,000 over twelve) from month eight. Undiscounted over 36 months: minus ₹39,20,000 plus 29 months of savings, ₹1,00,48,500, a net ₹61,28,500. At Guha's 18 per cent hurdle, a monthly 1.389 per cent, the outlay's present value is ₹37,10,997 and the savings' ₹74,68,020: net present value ₹37,57,023, simple payback 11.3 months.

The second-order effects

Capacity is not fungible. Those 297 engineer-days are 5.19 per cent of the 26-engineer platform group's 5,720 engineer-days a year at 220 days each, but 22.5 per cent of the six-engineer firmware team's 1,320. Odhani is identical: quarterly interest of 83.7 engineer-days (108.5 minus 24.8) annualises to 334.8, or 3.46 per cent of the organisation's 9,680 engineer-days and 21.7 per cent of the growth squad's 1,540. Interest also suppresses demand: Odhani runs six concurrent experiments read over two weeks, so a thirteen-week quarter has a ceiling of 39, and the team reached 31, or 79.5 per cent. The other 8, at the observed 19.4 per cent win rate, are an expected 1.55 wins at ₹18,00,000 each: ₹27,87,000 forgone, ₹3,48,000 per experiment not run. Resting on 6 observations it is the least defensible figure here, but omitting it values it at nothing.

4. When the concept applies, and when it misleads

Table 2. Five conditions for the debt framing to be useful, applied to both cases as at March 2026.
Testable conditionNivaran Robotics IndustriesOdhani Fashion Network
A target design can be named and costedYes: the abstraction layer, 14 engineer-monthsYes: a promotions service, 9 engineer-months
The area changes often enough for interest to existYes: nine firmware releases a yearYes: 31 experiments in thirteen weeks
The per-change surcharge is measurableYes: 45 versus 12 engineer-days a releaseYes: 3.5 versus 0.8 engineer-days an experiment
The principal ships in independent piecesYes: one model plug-in at a timePartly: app, web and seller tools cut over together
The product outlives the payback periodYes: a seven-year robot service lifeUncertain: the category was reshaped twice in four years

Where the framing misleads is worth stating as plainly. On code that will be deleted, repayment is waste. Where the target design is genuinely unknown the real-options school is right and the apparent loan is an option premium. Where the complaint is really a defect, the label buys an undeserved queue place. And where the area is frozen, as with the spares service, there is a principal with no interest.

5. Hard edge cases

Organisational seams. Nivaran's telemetry schema is shared between firmware and the warehouse console, two products with two roadmaps; three of the nine FY2026 firmware releases, 33.3 per cent, forced a console release in the same window. The ₹12,60,000 principal is in neither budget, and much of the ₹7,84,000 interest is paid in coordination no ledger records. Such debt has two owners and therefore none; mature companies move the seam, itself a principal.

Two-sided products. Odhani's promotions problem touches buyers and 4,100 sellers; changing promotion semantics changes what sellers were promised, so the migration is commercial and interest is paid in the slower side.

Regulated products. Where a regulator sets the pace of change, the team does not control its own interest: Oorja Grid Services, below, absorbed eleven tariff orders in fourteen months, each built into whatever design existed. Exogenous change frequency raises the value of early repayment.

Hardware plus software. Nivaran's hardest constraint is that 2,400 machines are built: the layer can reorganise firmware, but not the sensor placement that made model-specific calibration necessary. Part of hardware debt has no repayment until the fleet turns over, and an honest register marks it permanent.

AI-native products. Here interest is paid in a currency that is not engineer-days. Neerav Audio Labs, a speech-recognition company serving Indian-language contact centres, ran eleven retrains in FY2026, rebuilding the training set by hand each time: 6 engineer-days at ₹13,000, ₹78,000 a retrain, ₹8,58,000 a year. Three of the eleven — 27.3 per cent — shipped a model that scored lower on held-out data and was withdrawn, nobody being able to say which data had changed.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Only the rate orders the work. The competent practitioner ranks by how bad things look, which tracks principal; the expert ranks by rate. The tell-tale sign is a register sorted by size, its largest item perpetually top and unfunded. Nivaran's update agent, at 141.7 per cent on ₹8,40,000, returns capital in under nine months; the branches, at 106.1 per cent on ₹39,20,000, take eleven. Biggest-first is wrong because freed capacity funds the next repayment.

Interest exists only where you work. Change frequency multiplies every surcharge and varies hundredfold across a codebase; the sign is a team that can name the ugliest code but not how often it was edited. Ask not "how bad is this?" but "how often do we touch it, and how much slower is each touch?"

The principal inflates while you wait. Vaze's quotes of 8, 11 and 14 engineer-months are not estimation drift but ₹1,20,000 a month of accretion; the sign is a team that re-estimates the same refactor annually and finds the rise embarrassing rather than informative. Each new shortcut lands on the last one.

The surcharge is often paid in a non-monetary currency. At Odhani interest appeared as experiments not run, at Neerav as retrains withdrawn, at Nivaran as engineers flying to warehouses. The sign is an engineering leader saying the system slows the team down beside a product leader who cannot put a number on it. Converting is approximate; not converting values it at zero.

Partial repayment is usually the better trade. Neerav's full fix, a dataset registry of 6 engineer-months, ₹15,60,000, would cut reconstruction to ₹6,500 a retrain, ₹71,500 a year against ₹8,58,000: interest ₹7,86,500, rate 50.4 per cent, payback 23.8 months. The company declined, spending ₹2,86,000 on lineage logging alone: reconstruction untouched, withdrawal mode gone. Expertise shows as items marked part-paid, with a reason.

A rewrite is not a repayment unless it ships in pieces. Repayment that cannot be delivered incrementally is a second bet taken while servicing the first; the sign is one go-live date more than two quarters out. The obvious reading, that the clean design must be finished before use, destroys these projects, because the old system keeps changing meanwhile.

Deliberate debt becomes accidental debt in two quarters unless a trigger is written down. The distinction lives in the record, not the code: six months on, the deciders have moved teams and a priced loan is indistinguishable from neglect. An expert writes the trigger as a condition: at Nivaran, start before the fifth model's branch is cut, since afterwards the principal is three engineer-months higher.

There is no lender, so nothing forecloses. A bank sends notices; a codebase just gets slower, and the slowdown is blamed on scope or morale. The sign is a team whose lead time has tripled over two years with no quarter in which anything went wrong. The discipline a lender imposes from outside has to be manufactured internally.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The four quantities are identical everywhere; what changes is the currency of the interest and the constraints on repayment. In consumer products interest appears as experiment throughput, as at Odhani, and repayment is easier because nobody external is migrated. In B2B and enterprise products it appears as per-customer forks and migration windows the customer controls; Oorja's three customers each had a branch. In platform and marketplace products it compounds through a contract's consumers, so the principal includes a deprecation programme. In hardware part of the principal is unrepayable, and in AI products the debt sits in data and evaluation and is paid in model quality.

Where the difference is less real than claimed: the arithmetic does not change across these types, nor does the sequencing rule. Teams insisting their domain is special usually mean their change frequency is unusual. Stage matters more. A company with nine months of cash should borrow aggressively, since most of its code will be discarded; the dangerous stage is the one both protagonists occupy, with real customers and first-generation code carrying a lengthening roadmap. At scale interest compounds through dependencies and coordination binds.

8. Three worked examples

Mithaas Foods Group: a loan that paid

Mithaas runs an order platform for 1,100 sweet-shop retailers in Maharashtra and Gujarat. In 2025 it ran festival reports against the live order database rather than a separate store: 5 engineer-weeks at ₹72,000 each, ₹3,60,000, against 13 engineer-weeks, ₹9,36,000 — a principal of ₹5,76,000. It shipped on Monday 8 September 2025 rather than Monday 3 November 2025, eight weeks earlier, each worth ₹2,15,000 of festival margin: ₹17,20,000.

Table 3. Mithaas Foods Group: the shortcut path through to full repayment on Monday 4 May 2026. Exact figures in ₹; the total is the sum of the four rows.
ItemAmount (₹)
Shortcut build, 5 engineer-weeks3,60,000
Interest: one engineer-day a week of query scheduling for 34 weeks, at ₹14,4004,89,600
Interest: 70-minute checkout outage, 4 November 2025 — ₹6,30,000 of orders at an 11 per cent margin69,300
Repayment, 11 engineer-weeks rather than 8, three reports having been built on it7,92,000
Total cost of the shortcut path17,10,900

The proper path would have cost ₹9,36,000 and nothing more, so the shortcut cost ₹7,74,900 extra for ₹17,20,000 of margin: a net gain of ₹9,45,100. Repayment came in 37.5 per cent above the original principal, the inflation effect at work; the outage nobody forecast was 4.1 per cent of the total, the weekly surcharge seven times larger.

Neerav Audio Labs: accidental debt, correctly left standing

Neerav's figures are above: ₹8,58,000 of annual reconstruction effort, a ₹15,60,000 principal, interest of ₹7,86,500, a 50.4 per cent rate, a 23.8-month payback. Nivedita Shirke, the head of engineering, held that 50 per cent was affordable at Neerav's stage and the ₹15,60,000 better spent on acoustic models. She was right about the loan and wrong about its shape: three withdrawn retrains in eleven is a cycle-time cost no engineer-day figure holds. The ₹2,86,000 lineage fix cuts interest without cutting principal — the most instructive move on this page.

Oorja Grid Services: the rewrite that failed, and the recovery

Oorja sells billing software to state electricity distribution companies. Its billing engine was nine years old by late 2024, with 412 configuration flags and a fork per customer. In January 2025 Nitin Bhide, the chief technology officer, won approval for a rewrite estimated at 22 engineer-months, ₹68,20,000 at ₹3,10,000 an engineer-month. It was abandoned fourteen months later, in March 2026, having consumed 61 engineer-months, ₹1,89,10,000, or 2.8 times the estimate, and covering two of three customers' tariff rules. Neither cause was estimation error. The target moved: eleven tariff orders landed in those fourteen months, each built twice, an extra 0.9 engineer-months apiece, 9.9 engineer-months or ₹30,69,000 of the overrun. And with no incremental cutover, none of the 61 engineer-months had returned a rupee when it stopped.

The recovery, from 1 April 2026, was a change of unit rather than a new plan: four seams, replaced one at a time behind existing interfaces. The first, meter-reading ingestion, took 3.5 engineer-months, ₹10,85,000, and went live for one customer on Wednesday 15 July 2026, cutting its monthly reconciliation from 16 engineer-days to 4. At ₹15,500 an engineer-day the 12 saved are ₹1,86,000 a month, a payback of 5.8 months, with ₹4,65,000 returned by 30 September 2026 — the same engineering, decomposed so each piece paid before the next began.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Table 4. Five failure modes, the earliest observable sign, the question that catches it, and what late detection costs.
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
No register: items accidental by neglectNobody can date a decision or name its ownerShow me the list, with principal and ownerNivaran's principal grew ₹1,20,000 a month for fourteen months
Counting principal, ignoring interestProposals quote only a rebuild costHow often does this change, and how much slower is each?The ₹8,40,000 update agent charged ₹11,90,000 in a year
Sequencing by size rather than rateThe register is sorted largest firstWhich item returns capacity soonest?A quarter on a 20 per cent item while a 141.7 per cent item runs
Repayment scheduled as “when we have time”The same item on four consecutive plansWhat condition, not what date, triggers this?Deliberate debt reclassifies itself as accidental
Rewrite instead of decompositionOne go-live date more than two quarters outWhat ships first alone, and what does it save?Oorja: ₹1,89,10,000 and fourteen months, nothing live

In all five the early warning is organisational and the late cost financial: none shows in a metric, each in a missing artefact.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether debt can be quantified at all. The accounting school's evidence is cases like Nivaran's, where interest is observable as regression engineer-days and the counterfactual design is concrete. Opponents reply that this is the easy case: that design existed and was costed. For most debt the counterfactual is imaginary, and a rate computed against it has the authority of arithmetic and the content of an opinion. The school is wrong only if such registers fail to beat intuition.

Whether the metaphor does net harm. The purist position rests on behaviour: teams that adopt the vocabulary use it to pre-authorise shortcuts, and "we'll take on some debt" ends discussions rather than starting them. The defence is that craft and quality lose the funding argument. The purists are right only if the licensed sloppiness costs more than the repayment the word funds.

Whether deferring design is a loan or an option. The real-options school's strongest evidence is how often designed abstractions are discarded: Odhani's catalogue service was built for a wholesale business exited in 2023. If the proper design is frequently wrong, paying early is waste. Nivaran shows the limit: after four models the right design was no longer uncertain, and the option had stopped buying information.

Whether only architectural debt matters. The Software Engineering Institute points to registers like Nivaran's, where the two structural items are ₹51,80,000 of the ₹68,60,000 principal, 75.5 per cent. Neerav is the counter-case: a missing data practice. The school describes mature systems and understates data debt in newer ones.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with the word debt and a plea. Someone who has internalised it arrives with four numbers and a trigger, willing to lose on the numbers. Three differences are reliable: the expert quotes change frequency before code quality, because the first is the multiplier; proposes partial repayments and says which part of the interest each removes; and writes the repayment condition down when borrowing. A rarer mark is recording an item as permanent, like the calibration Nivaran can never undo, and charging it annually rather than calling it a loan.

12. The decisions, and questions for discussion

Chaubey funded the abstraction layer, but not first. Nivaran began with the update agent, ₹8,40,000 at 141.7 per cent, because it returned capital fastest and removed the rollback exposure Kowalczyk had quantified at ₹11,90,000. The layer started on 1 April 2026 with two engineers; by 30 September 2026, 12 of its 14 engineer-months were spent, 85.7 per cent complete, and the condition in the plan had been met. The telemetry schema was deferred: it needs a team-boundary decision before engineers.

Sabharwal did not fund the promotions service, citing the fourth and fifth rows of Table 2. Odhani instead spent ₹4,60,000 on a shared experiment-configuration library that cut plumbing from 3.5 to 1.9 engineer-days without unifying anything: a partial repayment which, on the same 31-experiment quarter, cuts quarterly interest from ₹9,62,550 to ₹3,92,150, since 31 experiments at a 1.1 engineer-day surcharge are 34.1 engineer-days. She agreed to revisit the full service if the app held the 39-experiment ceiling for two quarters.

Three questions. First, Nivaran prices the telemetry schema at 62.2 per cent, but it sits between two teams: if moving the boundary eliminated the interest without repaying any principal, is it debt, and whose budget carries it? Second, Sabharwal's ₹27,87,000 of forgone upside rests on a 19.4 per cent win rate from 6 observations — what would move that by half, and would it change her decision? Third, which of the five failure modes in Table 4 would have caught Oorja's rewrite in its first quarter, and what would Bhide have had to give up to run it honestly?

13. Going deeper

Reading an architecture diagram is the prerequisite in reverse: debt is architecture that no longer fits, so you must see the fit. Working with legacy systems applies this where no register exists and the borrowers have left; Oorja's seam method is its technique. How web and mobile apps work explains why Odhani's surfaces could not cut over separately. APIs and integration basics is where platform debt lives, since a published contract makes every consumer a creditor. Data modelling for PMs is the discipline whose absence produced Neerav's reconstruction cost. Databases, storage and caching explains Mithaas's outage: reports and order writes on one engine. Cloud infrastructure basics sets what a staged rollout costs, and so the update agent's rate. Scalability and performance supplies the measurements that turn a suspicion into a register entry.

Sutradhaar Technologies: the Fork and the Filing

A lending-platform company in Bengaluru has five ways of disbursing a loan where it meant to have one. Two estimates say what the fix costs, and they disagree by twenty-one crore. The pack is due in seven hours.

1 · The night before

At twenty to midnight on Sunday 15 November 2026, with the rain over Koramangala settled into the steady kind Bengaluru gets after Deepavali, Diksha Khajuria had three documents open on a kitchen table not meant for work. The first was the board pack due in the Sutradhaar Technologies shared drive by seven next morning. The second, a spreadsheet from Pune, said the company's disbursal layer needed ₹52.70 crore and six quarters of rebuilding. The third, a note from her chief executive, said ₹31.68 crore and four.

Khajuria had been chief product officer for nineteen months. She had joined on the understanding that the platform was, per the recruiter, "ninety per cent built" — true in a way nobody intended: ninety per cent of it existed five times over.

What made the night difficult was not the gap between the figures but that they answered different questions, that she was not sure either was the right question, and that a third number — the ₹7.04 crore of uncommitted FY27 platform budget she actually controlled — was smaller than either figure in front of her. At 11:52 pm a message came from Durriya Kuthiala in Singapore, where it was already past two. The Dubai client's chief operating officer had asked that afternoon whether Sutradhaar could produce a day-end co-lending position without a human in the loop. Kuthiala had said yes. She was writing to ask whether that was true.

2 · The company, and one decision in August 2021

Sutradhaar was founded in Bengaluru in June 2017 by Dalbir Kochhar and two colleagues from a core-banking practice. Its first product was a loan-origination system for NBFCs too small to buy Infosys Finacle or TCS BaNCS and too regulated for spreadsheets. Ledger Core, the platform that still carries the company, went live in January 2019: one PostgreSQL schema, one rules engine written by Kochhar himself, one disbursal path. FY26 revenue was ₹268 crore, up 34.0 per cent on FY25's ₹200 crore, with EBITDA of ₹11.2 crore — 4.2 per cent of revenue. In November 2024 Saptarishi Growth Capital put in ₹340 crore at ₹2,600 crore post-money, 13.0 times FY25 revenue, and took a board seat.

The decision that shapes everything else was taken, on Kochhar's account, in August 2021. A Chennai-headquartered vehicle-finance NBFC — today Sutradhaar's largest client, ₹26.75 crore of annual contract value on ₹21,900 crore of disbursals, a take rate of 0.122 per cent — would sign only if its co-lending waterfall went live in eleven weeks. Generalising the schema for two lenders per loan was scoped at nine months. Kochhar authorised a copy of the disbursal module instead, to be reconciled with the trunk inside two quarters at a cost put then at 310 engineer-weeks, roughly ₹1.61 crore at the 2021 blended rate of ₹0.52 lakh a week. It was never funded; the copy was copied three more times. Figure A sets out the sequence.

3 · The industry

Sutradhaar sells into a market the Reserve Bank of India has been steadily formalising. The Digital Lending Directions of 2025 tightened what a lending service provider may hold and for how long; the Account Aggregator framework moved statement analysis onto consented rails; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 attached a purpose tag to every borrower field; UPI and the NPCI rails made disbursal instantaneous and unforgiving.

Against the incumbent cores from Infosys and TCS it competes on configurability: it says yes to the variant a client's credit committee invented last quarter. Against the Indian software firms investors benchmark it to — Zoho, Freshworks, Postman — it looks expensive, spending ₹84.96 crore of ₹268 crore on platform engineering, 31.7 per cent of revenue. Its Gulf exposure runs through Saqr Capital Partners of Dubai, which lends in dirhams, reports to another regulator, and renews or does not on 31 January 2027.

Figure A — Disbursal paths and the filing deadline

Scale: a point dated month M of year Y sits at x = 80 + ((Y − 2017) + (M − 1)/12) × 76, so year gridlines fall 76 units apart. Numerals key to the list beneath and sit on two rows, odd above even, for clearance; the dashed rule is the board meeting. Source: Sutradhaar's release register, which records the Aug 2021 fork branch's merge date but not when Kochhar authorised it.

4 · What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Fork B followed in July 2022 for three gold-loan lenders wanting a shared appraisal step, Fork C in March 2023 for Saqr Capital Partners with dirham settlement and a second day-end cut-off, Fork D in March 2024 for two co-lending partnerships. Each was signed off on the first's reasoning and believed isolated: a copy of the disbursal module, touching nothing else.

Four of those beliefs have since failed. First, the forks are not isolated: four of the eight fields the revised co-lending return requires come from shared code each fork overrides, so a change in the trunk now has five behaviours. Second, the reconciliation is not a two-quarter job. Kirpal's October 2026 estimate puts it at 5,925 engineer-weeks — 19.1 times the 310 the company told itself in 2021, and ₹42.66 crore of internal engineering against ₹1.61 crore then, at different price levels and not directly comparable.

Third, the January 2026 incident was not a one-off. Between Thursday 15 and Friday 23 January 2026 a day-end position across the three Fork B lenders diverged from their own books by ₹41.60 crore gross, netting to ₹2.90 crore. A client's auditor found it, not Sutradhaar. Reconciliation took seven working days and about 33 engineers — 46 engineer-weeks — and ₹1.85 crore of service credits followed. The event is one of the 257 P1 and P2 incidents Exhibit 3 records for FY26.

Fourth, the company does not reliably know what the forks cost. Exhibit 1, the FY26 effort ledger, is not disputed. Exhibit 2 is Kirpal's attribution of part of that effort to the forks — 3,717 of the 11,800 engineer-weeks the platform had, or 31.5 per cent of capacity — and has never been audited. Exhibit 4 rests on it.

5 · The people

Diksha Khajuria, chief product officer, Bengaluru, owns the board recommendation and an FY27 roadmap already shown to clients. Unsaid: she has had the fork list for nineteen months and never asked what each one touches.

Dalbir Kochhar, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wrote Ledger Core's disbursal module and authorised the 2021 fork. He sponsors Estimate B, built with a Pune systems-integration partner, and says Sutradhaar cannot stop selling for six quarters. Unsaid: a rebuild replaces the last of his own code in production.

Dipanita Kirpal, acting head of platform engineering, Pune, has run it since the chief technology officer left in July 2026 and wants the job confirmed. She authored Exhibit 2 and Estimate A. Unsaid: 164 of her 236 platform engineers sit in Pune, 31 have never worked on anything but a fork, and her attribution has no audit behind it.

Dilbagh Kalsotra, chief financial officer, Bengaluru, is preparing a Series D for the first half of FY28 and needs a clean capitalisation story. He treats remediation as capital expenditure where accounting allows. Unsaid: which part of ₹52.70 crore he thinks qualifies.

Damanjit Kahlon, sales head for the Americas and the Gulf, in Edison, New Jersey, carries a ₹41.30 crore late-stage pipeline of which ₹16.90 crore — 40.9 per cent — needs a variant no path supports. He is paid on bookings. Unsaid: two of those deals were qualified on a configurability claim assuming a fifth fork.

Durriya Kuthiala, customer-success head, Singapore, holds the Saqr relationship and the 31 January renewal. She reports that Saqr's operations team produces its day-end position in a spreadsheet. Unsaid: she told Saqr's chief operating officer the platform could do it unaided.

Darsheel Katyal, principal designer, Berlin, asked for one onboarding flow, has shipped five, one per path. He wants the rebuild. Unsaid: his consolidated flow assumes a field Fork A does not emit.

Dibyendu Kainth, lead data scientist, Toronto, built the telemetry behind Exhibit 3 and reads it differently from everyone else. His models need one event schema. Unsaid: the telemetry does not cover all five paths equally — Fork C was instrumented only in May 2025.

Solid lines mark sites inside one delivery organisation; the dashed line marks a client site, not a reporting line. At November 2026 offsets — Berlin went to IST −4:30 on 25 October, Toronto and New Jersey to −10:30 on 1 November — the weekly 19:30 IST platform call reaches Berlin at 15:00, Toronto and Edison at 09:00, Singapore at 22:00 and Dubai at 18:00. "That is a three-year cumulative total against a one-off. Like for like is FY26 adaptation alone, ₹23.21 crore a year, against a ₹42.66 crore principal — 1.84 years of adaptation spend. And only part of that adaptation would disappear."Kalsotra, reply, 12 November

7 · The options as Khajuria sees them

A — rebuild to one path. Fund Estimate A: ₹52.70 crore over six quarters from 1 January 2027, a standing team of 79, one disbursal path by 30 June 2028. Kirpal argues the eight return fields can be sequenced into the first three quarters. Nobody has written the sequence down.

B — rebuild with the partner. Fund Estimate B: ₹31.68 crore over four quarters, 58 internal engineers and 20 from the Pune firm, finishing 31 December 2027. The number is lower partly on scope — Exhibit 4A shows two lines B does not estimate — and partly on engineer-weeks. Kalsotra likes the headline and will not say whether the omitted lines are free.

C — comply and leave the forks alone. A reporting layer that reads all five paths and produces the eight fields: 32 engineers for three quarters, 1,200 engineer-weeks, ₹8.64 crore, live 1 October 2027. It is the only plan that meets the filing date on its own schedule, and it adds a sixth thing to maintain.

D — stop forking and reprice. No capital. Refuse the next variant, charge adaptation as a professional-services line, let the carrying cost sit. Kahlon says ₹16.90 crore of pipeline dies the day it is announced.

Around one in the morning Khajuria had all four on a single page, in her own handwriting, and read them again from the top.

8 · The deadline and the hard constraints

The revised return must be filed for the quarter ending 31 December 2027, by 15 January 2028, and requires a full quarter of captured data, so systems must be live by 1 October 2027. The FY27 platform-engineering budget the board approved is ₹92.00 crore on Exhibit 1's basis, excluding the same 54 data, SRE and security engineers, against an FY26 run rate of ₹84.96 crore: ₹7.04 crore uncommitted, with FY28's budget not yet set. Options A, B and C each begin on 1 January 2027, the last quarter of FY27, and A's team of 79 costs ₹7.11 crore in it, breaching the uncommitted figure by ₹0.07 crore; B's 58 internal plus 20 partner engineers cost ₹7.92 crore, breaching it by ₹0.88 crore; C's 32 engineers cost ₹2.88 crore. Kalsotra scores it differently, a redeployed team being already inside the ₹84.96 crore, so that on his reading only B's ₹2.70 crore of partner fees is new money. Headcount is frozen at 290 until the second quarter of FY28, so any standing team must come out of the existing 236. Saqr's renewal notice falls due 31 January 2027, and Saqr's ₹18.40 crore of annual contract value plus the Fork A client's ₹26.75 crore are ₹45.15 crore, 16.8 per cent of revenue.

At 1:20 am Khajuria opened the pre-read again and read her own first sentence, which said the company had taken on debt deliberately and should now repay it. She deleted the word deliberately, looked at the sentence, and typed it back in. Outside, the rain had stopped.

9 · Questions for discussion

  1. Separate what Sutradhaar owes from what it pays to carry. Which figures in Exhibits 2 and 4A are principal, which interest, and on what basis is each measured?
  2. Exhibit 3 ranks the five paths. On which measure, and what happens when the denominator changes? Which denominator would you put before the board?
  3. Which parts of the August 2021 fork were deliberate and which accidental? Does the answer change what Sutradhaar should do in 2027, or only how the board feels about 2021?
  4. Ten of the forty cells in Exhibit 5 are blank. What would you do about them before Monday, and what would you tell the board you do not know?
  5. Exhibit 2 has never been audited. If the attributed share were 30 per cent rather than 53.3, which option survives and which collapses? What would it cost to find out?
  6. What should Khajuria do on Monday morning, in what order — and what should she say to Kochhar, Kalsotra and the Saptarishi nominee about the ₹7.04 crore she controls, the 1 October 2027 date and the 31 January 2027 renewal?
exp20v2-tech.debt.concepts:
Technical debt as a concept

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 5 October 2026, Esha Venkataraman, head of product at Dastkar Freight Systems, sat down with two colleagues to settle a question that would shape the company's next twelve months. Dastkar runs a payments and billing platform for small trucking operators in Pune, Nagpur and Surat. Its newest feature, Dastkar Advance, lets an operator draw cash against a freight bill the moment the consignee confirms delivery, funded by two partner lending companies instead of waiting thirty to forty-five days for payment. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, the heaviest freight fortnight of the year.

Devendra Shetty, the engineering lead, offered two ways to build it. The first was a proper rules service: a separate component in which each lender's eligibility rules (maximum advance, permitted routes, cooling-off periods) live as configuration. It would take nine engineer-weeks and ship on Monday 16 November, eight days after Diwali. The second wrote the lenders' rules directly into the existing payments code. It would take four engineer-weeks and ship on Monday 19 October. Falguni Rathod, the finance manager, had costed an engineer-week at ₹60,000 and estimated the advance fee would earn about ₹1,10,000 of margin a week once live.

Shetty was candid about the catch. The lenders revised their rules often, partly in response to the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions, and every revision to a hard-wired rule meant touching code that also handled settlements. Emre Aksoy, a reliability engineer in Istanbul, had flagged the payments module as "the one place we all hesitate to edit." Her problem was not whether to take a shortcut but whether she could say, in numbers, what it would cost and when it would be repaid.

2. The idea

Technical debt is the future cost of rework created when software is built in a way that is faster now but harder to change later. The word debt is deliberate and exact. Like financial debt, it gives you something today (speed), charges you for as long as it stands (the extra effort on every later change), and can be cleared by paying down a fixed amount (rebuilding the work properly).

The metaphor comes from Ward Cunningham, a programmer who in 1992 described the development of a financial portfolio system at an object-programming conference. Shipping first-time code, he said, is like going into debt: a little speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite. The danger is the debt left unpaid, because every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest. The problem it solved was a communication failure: engineers said a shortcut would "make things messy," and managers heard an aesthetic complaint rather than a cost.

The sentence Venkataraman could repeat in a meeting: "This shortcut lets us ship four weeks sooner, it carries a known repayment and a known running charge, and I would like us to decide it as a loan, not as a favour."

Figure 1 matters because the correspondence is not decorative. Each term on the left has a counterpart on the right that can be measured in engineer-weeks, and the sections below do exactly that for Dastkar.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have four steps, and practitioners usually say only the first aloud. Step one is the shortcut: the team picks a cheaper design than the one it believes is right. Here, rules go into the payments code rather than into a separate service.

Step two, usually left implicit, is naming the principal: the work you have chosen not to do. It is the difference between the proper build and the shortcut build, nine engineer-weeks less four, or five engineer-weeks. At ₹60,000 each, that is ₹3,00,000. Without this number the loan has no size, and a loan without a size cannot be compared with anything.

Step three is the interest: the extra effort every future change costs because the shortcut exists. Interest is paid when someone touches the area, not on a calendar. Step four is repayment: spending the principal, in a later period, to restore the proper design.

Note what the diagram implies: the later the repayment, the longer step three lasts, and the more code accumulates on top of the shortcut, so step four itself tends to grow. Financial principal does not usually increase while you ignore it; software principal sometimes does.

4. A worked example

Falguni Rathod's inputs are these. Proper build: nine engineer-weeks, ₹5,40,000. Shortcut build: four engineer-weeks, ₹2,40,000. Lender rules change six times a year. Under the proper design a change costs half an engineer-week (₹30,000); under the shortcut it costs one and a half (₹90,000), so the interest is one extra engineer-week, ₹60,000, per change. The shortcut ships four weeks earlier, and each live week earns ₹1,10,000 of margin, so the speed is worth four times ₹1,10,000, or ₹4,40,000. Assume repayment happens at month twelve, at the original five engineer-weeks.

Twelve-month cost, first pass (six rule changes; exact figures, ₹)
ItemProper rules serviceShortcut
Initial build5,40,0002,40,000
Six rule changes1,80,0005,40,000
Repayment at month 1203,00,000
Total cost7,20,00010,80,000

The shortcut costs ₹3,60,000 more over the year, which is exactly six changes at ₹60,000: the principal is repaid in full, so what remains is interest. Against that sits ₹4,40,000 of earlier margin. The shortcut wins by ₹80,000 (4,40,000 minus 3,60,000). Expressed as a rate, ₹3,60,000 of interest on a ₹3,00,000 principal is 120 per cent a year, or 10 per cent a month: an expensive loan, worth taking only because four weeks over Diwali are worth more.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the lenders revise rules twelve times a year, not six. Interest becomes twelve times ₹60,000, or ₹7,20,000. The shortcut's changes now cost 12 × 90,000 = ₹10,80,000 and the proper service's cost 12 × 30,000 = ₹3,60,000. The shortcut's net result is ₹4,40,000 minus ₹7,20,000, a loss of ₹2,80,000. The break-even is the number of changes at which interest equals the speed benefit: 4,40,000 divided by 60,000 is 7.33 changes a year. Below about seven the shortcut wins; above about eight it loses.

A third variation shows why repayment timing matters. If the team repays after month six, when three changes have occurred at the six-a-year pace, interest is 3 × 60,000 = ₹1,80,000 and the net gain rises to ₹2,60,000 (4,40,000 minus 1,80,000). Early repayment turns the same loan from marginal to comfortable.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Deliberate versus accidental debt

Dastkar's decision is deliberate: the team knows the shortcut exists and has sized it. Accidental debt arises when a team builds what it believes is a sound design and learns later, as the product evolves, that it was not. Martin Fowler's 2009 quadrant adds a second axis, prudent versus reckless. Deliberate and prudent ("ship now, and handle the consequences") is the legitimate loan. Deliberate and reckless ("we have no time for design") is not.

Principal and interest are different quantities

Principal is a one-time cost to remove the problem; interest is a recurring cost of living with it. A team can have a large principal and negligible interest, such as an ugly report generator no one edits, and rationally never repay it.

Interest only exists where you work

The payments module carries interest because it changes frequently. An equally untidy archive process, touched once a year, costs almost nothing. Ask not "how bad is the code?" but "how often do we touch it, and how much slower is each touch?"

It is not the same as bugs

A defect is wrong behaviour today. Debt is a structure that makes future change expensive while behaviour may be perfectly correct.

Not all "legacy" is debt

Old code that works, changes rarely and is understood by the team is an asset with a long life. Debt is defined by the cost of change, not by age. Debt is architecture that no longer fits the work being asked of it.

The estimates are soft

The ₹60,000 per change figure is an estimate by Shetty's team. A forecast of six lender revisions a year can be wrong by a factor of two, as the second pass showed. The model cannot tell you the true change frequency; it tells you how sensitive the answer is to it.

What it cannot tell you

The arithmetic cannot say whether four weeks over Diwali is truly worth ₹4,40,000. Festive weeks may earn more than average, or operators may not adopt a new feature that quickly. It converts an argument about taste into one about inputs.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products, and company stage

In consumer products, debt interest is paid mostly in experimentation speed: a growth team that runs one test a week against a tangled codebase runs half as many as it should. In B2B products such as Dastkar's, interest is paid in custom rules for particular customers and in integration fragility, and the repayment is harder to schedule because enterprise customers resist downtime. In marketplaces, debt concentrates around matching, pricing and payments, where two sides are affected at once, so a failure from debt can hurt supply and demand together.

Stage changes the calculation more than product type. An early-stage company with nine months of cash should borrow heavily, because survival depends on learning whether anyone wants the product, and most early code will be discarded anyway; repaying debt on code that is deleted is waste. A large company has the opposite problem: many teams, long-lived systems and slow interest compounding through dependencies. There, debt left unmanaged can consume most engineering capacity.

7. Common mistakes

Treating all debt as bad

Symptom: a team refuses every shortcut, and ships a month behind rivals. Misunderstanding: that debt is a moral failing rather than a financing choice. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what the delay itself costs per week. At Dastkar the answer was ₹1,10,000, which made four weeks worth ₹4,40,000.

Never recording the loan

Symptom: no one can say what was borrowed last quarter, and surprises arrive as "the module is unfixable." Misunderstanding: that a verbal agreement to fix it later counts as repayment. Cheapest diagnostic: ask for the debt register, a short list with each item's principal, interest and owner. If none exists, the debt is accidental by neglect.

Counting only principal

Symptom: a shortcut approved because "it is only five weeks of rework." Misunderstanding: interest is ignored. Cheapest diagnostic: ask how often the area changes. At twelve changes a year, five weeks of principal sat beside 12 weeks of interest.

Scheduling repayment as "when we have time"

Symptom: the same item appears on every quarterly plan. Misunderstanding: treating repayment as discretionary, when interest is compulsory. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether a date and a trigger (for example, "after the fourth rule change") were written down at the time of borrowing.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Venkataraman's decision looks like this. The proposal arrives as one page: principal ₹3,00,000, interest ₹60,000 per change, benefit ₹4,40,000, break-even at 7.33 changes a year. The team states its own forecast of change frequency, with a range of four to ten, and notes that the answer flips inside it. A guardrail keeps the lender rules in one marked file, so later extraction is a move, not an excavation. A trigger and an owner are agreed: after the third rule change, or by 15 January 2027, whichever comes first, Shetty's team repays. The loan is entered in the debt register. The decision is explicit and dated.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Venkataraman chose the shortcut. Her reasoning followed the arithmetic: at the forecast of six changes the shortcut gains ₹80,000 over a year, and repaying after three changes lifts the gain to ₹2,60,000. The deciding factor was that repayment was in her control, whereas a missed Diwali was not. She wrote the repayment trigger into the sprint plan, asked Aksoy to monitor change frequency monthly, and agreed with Shetty that a fifth rule change in any six-month period would force the repayment forward. Dastkar Advance went live on 19 October.

The natural next step is working with legacy systems, where the loans were taken long ago, by people who have left, and the register does not exist. The skill there is the one you have just practised, applied in reverse.

Two questions to sit with. First, where in a product you know is interest being paid today without anyone calling it that, and what would you measure to prove it? Second, Venkataraman's ₹4,40,000 benefit assumed an average week; if Diwali weeks earned double, how would you decide whether a number you cannot verify is good enough to borrow against?
case20v1-tech.debt.concepts:
Rangsaaz and the Sixth Copy

A decision about borrowing against the future

1. Opening

At eight on Thursday evening, 22 October 2026, Charanpreet Jamwal sat alone in Rangsaaz Technologies' Koramangala office in Bengaluru, with a whiteboard still showing the day's argument. As chief product officer, she owed a Dubai distribution group an answer by four o'clock Gulf time the next afternoon (5.30 pm in Bengaluru): could Rangsaaz give its 310 Indian dealers one invoicing system, live before the year ended? The group would sign a contract worth ₹2.4 crore a year if the answer was yes. Her head of engineering had told her, politely and firmly, that the quickest way to say yes would make the company's real problem worse.

2. Company background

Rangsaaz sells GST billing and accounting software to small businesses. Two founders from Ludhiana's hosiery trade started it in 2016, and it grew by selling to traders who had never used software beyond Tally and a spreadsheet. Today 42,000 paying merchants average ₹18,000 a year, giving annual recurring revenue of about ₹75.6 crore. Most merchants collect payments by UPI through Razorpay, file returns on the GST portal, and open the product hardest during the Diwali and wedding-season rush, when they expect it to work. Its engineers number 38: 24 in Bengaluru and 14 in Pune. It competes with Zoho Books, Tally and Vyapar for the small trader, and with the billing modules inside Razorpay and Paytm for those who want payments bundled in.

Rangsaaz's growth began with a deliberate shortcut. When GST launched on 1 July 2017, the company shipped compliant invoicing in eight weeks by writing the tax-rate rules directly inside the invoice module. Everyone knew it was a shortcut, and it won the company its first 9,000 customers. In the language of this topic, it was deliberate debt, taken to buy speed in a market that would not wait.

3. The situation

The shortcut was never repaid. As the product grew, each new module needed the same tax rules and, under deadline, copied them. By 2024 the rules lived in five places (Exhibit 2). When the GST Council's rate rationalisation took effect on 22 September 2025, engineers updated the five copies over three weeks, and the point-of-sale copy lagged by nine days. Nobody chose that outcome; it accumulated. Jamwal read the post-mortem twice. The engineers had acted quickly and in good faith, and the design had left them no better option.

The Toronto data scientist, who tracks engineering time, measured the cost. Exhibit 1 shows the share of capacity spent servicing the old design (workarounds, hotfixes, manual reconciliation) rising from 22 per cent to 40 per cent in four quarters, while feature work fell from 230 to 164 engineer-weeks. At a loaded cost of ₹75,000 per engineer-week, the 160 weeks in the latest quarter cost ₹1.2 crore.

The team sees the choice differently from each city. Pune argues for repair. In Berlin, the designer says the dealer screens look different from every other invoice screen precisely because they cannot share logic. In Singapore, the customer-success lead says merchants judge Rangsaaz by whether the tax is right, not by its features. New Jersey wants the Dubai contract, and its head points out that the group's finance director has asked for a written date, with a competing vendor's demo scheduled for the following Monday. Jamwal knows the Dubai dealers need invoices that handle both GST and the group's own multi-entity rules, which no existing module does. She also knows the engineers are split: Pune wants repair, while Bengaluru, newer to the code, doubts that repair can be funded.

4. The people

Charanpreet Jamwal, chief product officer, Bengaluru, owns the answer. She wants a decision she can defend in a board meeting a year from now.

Chandrahas Jasrotia, head of engineering, Pune, wants to stop the work and rebuild the billing core. He has watched his best engineers spend Fridays reconciling tax mismatches, and he fears a sixth copy will make the next rate change unmanageable. He does not oppose the Dubai deal; he opposes taking it without a plan to pay.

Chakshu Jhanji, head of sales, New Jersey, wants the Dubai contract signed. It is Rangsaaz's first enterprise-scale deal outside India, and he believes a refusal will send the group to a competitor.

Chahat Jolly, customer-success lead, Singapore, wants no new surprises for existing merchants. Her team fields every tax complaint first, and in a rate-change week she has seen ticket queues double.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the ledger of interest Rangsaaz is already paying. Exhibit 2 shows where the debt sits, and Exhibit 3, discussed with the options, prices the choices. Read Exhibit 1 for direction before magnitude: the debt-service share rose by six percentage points in every quarter while total capacity stayed flat. The team is not shrinking; the debt is eating a larger share of the same team.

6. The options

Option A: ship the quick version. Twenty engineers would copy the rules once more into a dealer module, taking seven weeks and 140 engineer-weeks, and going live on 14 December. Sales is delighted, and the group signs. But each further copy adds interest: Jasrotia's estimate is 24 engineer-weeks a quarter, or 15 per cent on top of the 160 already being paid.

Option B: rebuild first. Twenty engineers would replace the billing core in 26 weeks, 520 engineer-weeks, finishing on 26 April 2027. Jasrotia estimates this would clear about 100 of the 160 weeks of quarterly interest. The Dubai group has said it will choose another product without a date by 31 December, and the ₹2.4 crore a year would go elsewhere.

Option C: borrow on purpose, with a repayment date. Twenty engineers would spend nine weeks, 180 engineer-weeks, building the dealer module on a single shared tax-rules service rather than a sixth copy. Go-live is Tuesday 29 December, inside the group's 31 December limit but after its preferred 15 December. In January to March 2027, 120 engineer-weeks would move the five old copies behind the same service, which Jasrotia expects to clear about 40 weeks of quarterly interest. The risk is discipline: the repayment must survive the first sales request after launch.

Interest cleared counts only full quarters after completion: B 100 x 6 = 600 (from July 2027), C 40 x 7 = 280 (from April 2027). Both rates are Jasrotia's estimates. Net = gross less cleared, at ₹75,000 per engineer-week. Build weeks displace feature work. The ₹2.4 crore a year contract is outside every column.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Which parts of Rangsaaz's debt were deliberate and prudent, and which were accidental? What does Exhibit 1 say is the current interest?
  2. In Exhibit 3, why does Option A's gross cost exceed Option C's although A's build is 40 weeks cheaper?
  3. How should Jamwal weigh Jasrotia's unverified estimates of interest cleared (₹3.0 crore a year for B, ₹1.2 crore for C) against a ₹2.4 crore-a-year contract that is contracted only if the date is met?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what must be written down tonight to make it a decision rather than a drift?

8. A note for the learner

Technical debt is a design that no longer fits what the business needs. The borrowing metaphor is useful because it separates two things: the principal, the work to fix the design, and the interest, the extra work every change now costs. Debt is not itself a mistake. The 2017 shortcut was a good loan, taken knowingly, for a market that would not wait. The error was not repaying it. The four later copies were deadline-driven debt, never weighed against repayment, whose interest surfaced only in September 2025. The distinction matters because the cures differ: a deliberate loan needs a repayment plan, an unexamined one needs a conversation about why it was invisible.

A defensible answer is Option C, once the netting is honest. On engineering cost alone, Option B wins: net minus 80 weeks against C's 24 and A's 332, a gap of 104 weeks, or ₹0.78 crore. B loses on the contract. The ₹2.4 crore a year, up to ₹4.8 crore over the same eight quarters, is contracted only if the date is met, and B misses it. Every cleared-interest figure is an estimate, C's as much as B's. Option A is the bad loan: no repayment date, and interest of 192 weeks, more than its own 140-week build. Option C borrows deliberately, stops the sixth copy, and attaches a dated, ring-fenced repayment of 120 weeks, which pays back in three quarters if the 40-week estimate holds. It also leaves B's rebuild available as the next step.

Jamwal should accept the 29 December date with Jhanji, tell Dubai the reason, and commit the January to March repayment in writing, with Jolly's team named as the first to feel the benefit. If the repayment slips, Option C is simply Option A with extra steps.
exp40v2-tech.mobile:
Mobile Platform Constraints

Admission, capability, delivery and consent — and the horizon over which each is a fact.

1. Two rooms, four days apart

On Monday 5 October 2026, in Pune, Chhavi Nalawade left one slide up for the whole meeting. She is vice-president of product at Nishtha Field Services, which sells an Android order-capture app to pharmaceutical distributors; 9,200 field staff at 214 customers open it daily. The slide read go-live Monday 1 February 2027 — the date a distributor group had written into a contract worth ₹2.4 crore a year, seventeen weeks away.

The feature was an order line carrying scheme-wise tax fields for e-invoicing. Nehal Chitale, who runs engineering, had shown it could not be done on the server alone: three older response shapes in the sync service would have to be rewritten. The cheap path was a minimum supported version of 7.2, stranding 1,104 of the 9,200 devices, 12.0 per cent. Chandrakant Naik, in customer operations, added that 784 of the 1,104, 71 per cent, sat in nine accounts whose IT departments push updates once a quarter. "Play will let us ship on Thursday," Chhavi said. "The question is who owns the last mile."

Four days earlier, on Thursday 1 October 2026, a mirror-image conversation ran in Bengaluru. Chakori Sleep Labs makes a sleep-and-heart-rhythm band and an app that scores the night: 2,40,000 bands active, 1,42,000 on Android and 98,000 on iOS, and 48,000 owners paying ₹249 a month for the premium score. Nandini Chhabra, head of product, had a third-generation band launching Monday 16 November 2026 with 14,000 pre-orders, of which 11,000, 78.6 per cent, came from existing owners. Chirayu Nandedkar's firmware and Charu Nimkar's iOS build were ready, and Chiara Novelli in Milan had a better scoring model. But in March one release had raised the minimum operating-system version and gated a firmware update behind it. Nandini's question was Chhavi's inverted: "which of these things will still be true for a user on 16 November, and which am I assuming?"

2. The idea, and four schools that disagree

Mobile platform constraints are the decisions about a mobile product made by someone other than its team. Admission: whether a store will publish a binary and listing, and when. Capability: what the operating system permits a process to do, especially outside the foreground. Delivery: how code, configuration and messages reach devices, and how long that takes. Consent: what the user must grant, can revoke, and in practice never revisits.

The 2007 iPhone had no third-party native apps; the official answer was the web. The App Store arrived in July 2008 and Android Market that October. The capability rules came from physics rather than policy: a phone has one battery, and an app that spins the radio spends a resource the user blames the handset for. Apple's 2010 answer was a short list of permitted background modes; Android's, from Doze in 2015 to the background-execution limits of 2017, was to ration wake-ups centrally. Then came the regulatory layer: Digital Markets Act obligations in Europe, user-choice billing in India, and scrutiny of store terms by the Competition Commission of India.

A platform constraint is a fact over a quarter, a design choice over a year, and a contested contract over three years.

The platform-citizen school holds that the rules encode a quality contract and that most constraint pain is a design smell: an app that cannot live inside the battery budget has a bad sync design. The escape-the-landlord school builds for the web and for payment outside store billing; it signs "a capability you cannot replace is a single point of failure in the business model". The release-engineering school treats the subject as scheduling — the binary is a long-lived shell, value ships as configuration — and signs "ship early and dark". The structural school reads the rules as an output of market power, assumes they will move, and will not sign "treat the guidelines as physics".

3. Mechanics, including the parts left implicit

Treat review as a distribution, not a duration. Chakori submitted twelve iOS builds between Tuesday 6 January and Tuesday 22 September 2026. Hours from submission to first decision, in order: 14, 19, 22, 26, 31, 33, 38, 41, 47, 62, 88 and 149. The mean is 47.5 hours and the median 35.5 — the mean sits 34 per cent above the median because the tail is long. Two of the twelve, 17 per cent, were rejected on first pass.

Table 1. Chakori Sleep Labs, time from submission to first review decision, twelve iOS submissions, 6 January to 22 September 2026.

Hours to first decisionSubmissionsShare of the twelve

Total12100.0%

Shares are of the twelve submissions in that window, rounded to one decimal; they sum to 100.0 exactly.

A schedule built on 47.5 hours is wrong twice: it uses a mean inflated by a tail, and the tail is not random. Experts plan against roughly the ninetieth percentile, here the eleventh of twelve at 88 hours, and note the worst observed case of 149 hours, 4.2 times the median.

Capability is the second family, and its implicit step is measurement. Once an app is backgrounded, the operating system decides when it runs. Chakori cannot wake its app at six in the morning; it sends a silent push. Over the thirty days to 30 September 2026 it sent 72,00,000 such pushes — one per active band per day across 2,40,000 bands — and the app woke and completed a sync for 58 per cent of them, 41,76,000 completions in that same window. Only completions become a sleep score.

A night of raw samples is about 2,400 kilobytes, which at a realistic Bluetooth Low Energy throughput of 30 kilobytes per second is 80 seconds of radio time — cheap. What is expensive is waking the processor often, as Chiara Novelli's instrumentation on a 4,000 milliamp-hour handset showed.

Table 2. Measured cost of three sync designs over a 24-hour window on a 4,000 mAh reference handset.

Sync designWake-ups per 24 hRadio seconds per 24 hCPU seconds per 24 hmAh per 24 hShare of battery
A. Poll every five minutes288480720962.40%
B. Sync when unlocked or charging1211060140.35%
C. One push-triggered morning sync39040110.28%

Each row is a measured 24-hour average, not a sum; the share column is that row’s mAh divided by 4,000.

This is what makes battery a product variable rather than an engineering one. The operating system attributes battery use to named apps, and several Android manufacturers add power managers that suspend apps with a record of background activity. In one representative week, 11.3 per cent of Android devices on design A had a gap of 24 hours or more between syncs, against 3.1 per cent on design B. The team thought it had a Bluetooth problem; it had a battery-reputation problem.

Delivery is where teams most often use a model that is quietly wrong. The usual model is geometric: a constant fraction r of not-yet-updated devices updates each day, so the updated share after t days is 1 − (1 − r)t. Chakori's blended daily rate is 0.1668, which that formula turns into 92.2 per cent by day 14 and 99.6 per cent by day 30. But the population is not one population. Measurement found 72 per cent of devices — 1,72,800 of the 2,40,000 — with automatic updates on, updating at about 0.22 a day, and 28 per cent, 67,200 devices, with them off, at about 0.03 a day. Blend the segments and the same base reaches 79.5 per cent by day 14 and 88.7 per cent by day 30.
