Estimating from the happy pathOne number, no tableWhich of Figure 1’s six bars did you size?A ten-week promise vs 615 days
Limits found at launchNobody can state the capOur busiest minute, and the cap?Patang stalls at 654 against 400
Trusting webhooks aloneNo nightly count comparisonWhat would we see if deliveries stopped?Silent loss, found by a customer
No idempotencyDuplicates “not seen in testing”What identifier do we deduplicate on?₹8.36 lakh a day of double postings
Deprecation notice unownedPartner mail to a shared inboxWho owns this interface?Rath: ₹38.42 lakh against ₹3.08 lakh
Mapping deferredOnly sandbox data seenWhen did we last read a real record?Rework of the data layer post-launch

Every warning sign above is an absence — of a table, a number, a name — which is why these failures are visible to a product manager before an engineer sees them. The diagnostic column is this page’s practical content: six questions, none needing technical knowledge to ask, all needing it to answer.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Build direct, or route through a shared rail? The direct camp argues a point-to-point integration is fully under your control: you can fix it at 2 a.m., and no third party can price you. Its evidence is every team that waited on an aggregator’s roadmap for a field it needed. The rail camp argues Table 3 settles it at scale, and that the direct camp underweights upkeep because upkeep is invisible in year one. For the direct camp to be wrong, coverage must stay high and the fee low; for the rail camp, one critical field missing from the standard is enough — which happened to Shalini with diagnosis codes.

Events first, or request-and-response first? The event camp points at Table 2: two orders of magnitude fewer messages and far better freshness. The request camp replies that a system you can query is one you can debug, and that events move complexity from the network into the receiver — idempotency store, ordering, replay tooling. Both are right about the other’s weakness, which is why dominant practice is a hybrid nobody writes up: events for freshness, a query for truth.

Is a public API a moat or a tax? The moat argument is that an interface makes you the system of record and raises switching cost with every partner who builds on you. The tax argument is that a public interface is permanent, every field becomes a support obligation, and those engineers could have shipped features. It depends on whether your API serves customers who would otherwise leave or ones who would never have come — which most companies never measure.

How much should a product manager know? One school holds that a PM should read a specification and compute a request budget unaided; the other that this invites the PM to design the system badly, and that the skill to cultivate is asking Section 9’s six questions well. The split is visible in curricula and is not resolving.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks whether the partner has an API. Someone who has internalised it asks four things in the first meeting: the cap and its window, the identifier on each webhook, the deprecation policy, and the named person. They ask for estimates as tables, treat a single number as proof that only Figure 1’s first bar was sized, insist a real customer’s data is read in week one, and defend the reconciliation sweep everyone else cuts. When sales says “we’ll just integrate with it”, they ask for the customer list and the date, and return with Table 1.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 24 February 2026 Shalini committed to the hybrid: the exchange for its 157 hospitals, direct work for Sankalan’s 16, and Rudraksh’s 7 deferred past 31 March 2027 — accepting 173 against 180 rather than spending 150 person-days on the smallest vendor. She took webhooks plus a nightly reconciliation sweep, funded the idempotency store, and wrote the ₹11.76 lakh annual upkeep into the plan before building began. Pritha, on 2 March, held the coach at a 25 per cent opt-in ceiling until queueing was built, published a read-only API with four fields and a one-year version guarantee, and moved deprecation notices into a named owner’s calendar.

Three questions. First: the hybrid saves 31.7 per cent of build cost but 16.4 per cent over three years; if the exchange raised its fee from ₹1.20 to ₹3.00 a claim in year two, was Shalini’s decision wrong, or merely expensive? Second: Pritha’s coach has an 89.2 per cent gross margin and a hard ceiling on its busiest minute — which should govern the launch date, and who decides? Third: if Rath’s notice arrived at Sopaan tomorrow, what in Shalini’s plan would catch it, and on what day?

13. Going deeper

How web and mobile apps work is the floor: until the client-server split is concrete, a rate limit is an abstraction. Reading an architecture diagram shows where an integration sits and what fails with it; Security basics for PMs matters because every token is a key, deepened by Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions. Specifying APIs and data contracts shrinks the 196-day mapping bar; Integration patterns: sync, async, events, webhooks turns Table 2 into a deliberate choice; Integrations and ecosystem makes it a portfolio question; Developer experience is the mirror image. Data modelling for PMs attacks meaning at its root, Databases, storage and caching explains pagination and idempotency stores, Scalability and performance and Cloud infrastructure basics cover a webhook flood, and CI/CD, environments and deployment explains why a sandbox is not production.
case20v1-tech.apis:
Ekatra Books and the Two-Week Integration

Delivery & Technology: APIs and integration basics

1. Opening

On Monday 2 November 2026, Mitesh Vaghela, head of product at Ekatra Books, opened a message from Meghna Virani, the engineering lead in Pune. It read, in full: "Sahra integration: two weeks, one engineer. Can start after Diwali." Mitesh had until Friday 6 November to tell Sahra Trading Group in Dubai whether Ekatra would deliver a live invoice feed into its ERP by Friday 15 January 2027. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, Ahmedabad would close for the week, and Mitesh suspected that two weeks described only the first stage of the work.

2. Company background

Ekatra Books, founded in Ahmedabad in 2017, sells GST billing and ledger software to small traders and wholesalers in textiles, chemicals and hardware. It had 9,200 paying firms and annual recurring revenue of ₹24 crore. Thirty-one engineers worked in Pune and Bengaluru. Its rivals were Zoho Books, Vyapar, Tally Prime, Marg ERP and ClearTax.

Ekatra already lived on other people's APIs. Every qualifying invoice went to the government's e-invoice portal, the Invoice Registration Portal run under GSTN, and its payment links ran on Razorpay, which told Ekatra by webhook, a message sent to Ekatra the moment a payment succeeded, rather than waiting to be asked. Both had taught the team that when a service Ekatra does not control slows down, Ekatra's customers blame Ekatra.

3. The situation

Sahra Trading Group imports building materials into Dubai and buys from 410 Indian suppliers, of whom 120 used Ekatra. Sahra wanted every invoice those 120 firms raised to appear in its SAP system within minutes, not at month-end. It offered ₹42 lakh a year, the largest contract Ekatra had been offered. Its finance controller, Mrugesh Vachhani, explained the terms: Sahra's interface used OAuth 2.0 for authentication and accepted 60 calls a minute per integration. Ekatra would have one integration.

Meghna's two weeks covered one task, mapping Ekatra's invoice fields onto Sahra's. At Mitesh's request she listed everything else, and Exhibit 1 is the result: 14 person-weeks. Her loaded cost is ₹1.0 lakh per person-week, so the build alone is ₹14 lakh. The rate limit was the item she worried about most. On 31 March 2026, the busiest day of the year, the 120 suppliers raised 9,000 invoices, to buyers of every kind and not only Sahra, in the busiest two hours. Sending one call per invoice means 75 calls a minute against a limit of 60. Sahra's system would reject the surplus unless Ekatra queued it, and the queue would hold 1,800 invoices at the peak and, if arrivals then stopped, take another half hour to clear.

The view from Singapore was different. Minal Vijayvargiya, who led customer success, reminded the Monday call (10:30 in Ahmedabad, 9:00 in Dubai, 13:00 in Singapore) that the October e-invoice portal outage had produced 19 support tickets in a single week. A feed into Sahra's ERP would add a second thing that could fail without Ekatra being at fault, and Ekatra would again be the one phoned. Manav Vadodaria, who sold to Gulf-linked trading groups from Dubai, had learned that Sahra's procurement director meant to name the integration in a board paper. Invoices carry buyers' names and GSTINs, so sending them abroad would need data-processing terms under the DPDP Act.

The product team had also kept a log of integration requests. Exhibit 3 shows eleven in the six months to 30 September, only one of them Sahra's.

4. The people

Mitesh Vaghela, Ahmedabad, owns the decision and answers to the founder-CEO. He wants the contract without a commitment that will consume the roadmap.

Meghna Virani, Pune, runs engineering. She will build whatever is chosen,; she wants an estimate that survives January.

Manav Vadodaria, Dubai, wants a yes. He has promised Sahra a conversation, not a date.

Minal Vijayvargiya, Singapore, wants any new integration to arrive with monitoring and a runbook, since her team will answer the phones.

Mrugesh Vachhani, Dubai, represents the client. Sahra's board expects live invoices, but he said privately that a reliable nightly file beats an unreliable live one.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: build to Sahra's specification. This is the quickest route to a live feed: 4 January, 11 days ahead of Sahra's deadline. The year-one cost is ₹27 lakh against ₹42 lakh of revenue. The cost is that the code serves one customer. Any change to Sahra's SAP settings, such as a new token lifetime or a lower rate limit, becomes Ekatra's emergency, and the next customer who wants a feed starts from zero.

Option B: publish Ekatra's own API. Ekatra would offer versioned REST endpoints, webhooks announcing "invoice created" and "invoice updated", token-based authentication, per-customer rate limits, a sandbox and documentation. Sahra's IT partner would receive the events and handle SAP's 60-call limit on its side. That work is uncosted here and sits outside the four days of slack. Exhibit 3 suggests this serves six of the other ten requests from five accounts, but not Tally's four. It costs ₹40 lakh in year one, leaves ₹2 lakh of Sahra's contract and goes live on 11 January with four days of slack.

Option C: a nightly file. A spreadsheet-format export is dropped on a secure server each night. It costs ₹7 lakh and arrives in December, but Sahra would see invoices up to a day late. Mrugesh might accept it; the board might not.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Which items in Exhibit 1 would a product manager not think of when told "we'll integrate"? Which two would hurt most if skipped?
  2. Why does 75 calls a minute against a limit of 60 matter even though the day's average is far below 60? What does the queue protect, and what does it cost?
  3. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, if API access were priced at ₹4 lakh a year, how many other accounts must buy before Option B costs Ekatra no more than Option A?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what would you tell Sahra on 6 November?

8. A note for the learner

The topic frames the decision through one question: what does "we'll just integrate" cost? The answer has three parts. There is the build (authentication, rate limits, retries, testing). There is the running (monitoring, support, and every upgrade of the other party's system). And there is the reuse, meaning whether the work serves anyone beyond the first requester. A good answer prices all three and does not accept the two-week figure as the whole.

One defensible path is Option B with Option C as a bridge. Option A is the cheapest live build this year, but Exhibit 3 says Sahra is one of ten requesters. If each of the five other accounts an API could reach also took the full 14 weeks (an assumption), six point-to-point builds would cost up to 84 person-weeks, or ₹84 lakh, against Option B's 22. B costs ₹13 lakh more than A in year one (₹40 lakh against ₹27 lakh). At ₹4 lakh a year for API access, four of the five other accounts must buy to cover that gap: four pay ₹16 lakh, while three pay only ₹12 lakh. Adding the C bridge makes the total ₹47 lakh, ₹5 lakh more than Sahra's ₹42 lakh. Against that path the gap to A is ₹20 lakh, so all five must buy at ₹4 lakh. That is uncertain, so the argument for B rests on reuse more than on year one, and the bridge should be built only if the January date starts to slip.

The four days of slack are thin. Mitesh should tell Sahra on 6 November that live feeds arrive by 15 January through an API, and offer a nightly file from 7 December as insurance. He should ask Mrugesh to confirm Sahra's rate limit in writing, agree the DPDP data-processing terms before the build starts,. The price of "we'll integrate" was never two weeks; it was ₹40 lakh, or ₹47 lakh with the bridge, and a promise to keep it working.
exp20v2-tech.apis:
APIs and Integration Basics

What does “we’ll just integrate with it” really cost?

1. The sentence in the sales meeting

On Monday 8 June 2026, Girija Mehendale, the product manager for invoice financing at Hastakshar Exchange, a Pune-based marketplace that lets small manufacturers sell their unpaid invoices to lenders, sat through a sales review that ended with a sentence she had learned to dread. Forty of the company’s anchor customers kept their books in Indrayani Books, a cloud accounting package. Hastakshar’s head of sales, Hemlata Gokhale, reported that every one of them had asked the same question: could invoices flow from Indrayani Books into Hastakshar automatically, so nobody had to export a spreadsheet each evening? Together the forty accounted for a pipeline worth ₹2.4 crore in annual revenue. “We’ll just integrate with it,” Hemlata said, and promised a date of Friday 4 September.

Girija turned to Gaurav Tilak, the engineering lead, who had read Indrayani’s developer documentation over the weekend. His estimate was two weeks, one engineer. She had until Friday 12 June to tell the customers whether 4 September was a commitment, twelve weeks away. If she promised too much, forty customers would be waiting on a date the team could not keep, and lenders would be offered stale invoices. If she promised too little, the pipeline would go to a competitor that already advertised the connection.

The argument of this page is a single one: an API is a small, precise thing, but an integration is a relationship with another company’s system, and the cost lives in the relationship.

2. The idea

An API, short for application programming interface, is a published set of requests that one piece of software may make of another, together with a promise about what each request returns. The word integration means the working connection built on top of such an interface: the code, the credentials, the data mapping and the operating routine that make two systems behave as one for a customer.

The problem APIs were invented to solve is older than the web. Programs written by different teams needed to cooperate without either team reading the other’s source code. The modern form took shape around 2000, when Roy Fielding, then a doctoral student at the University of California, Irvine, described REST (representational state transfer) in his dissertation: an approach in which every thing a system holds, such as an invoice, has an address, and a small set of standard verbs acts on it. The pattern then spread to payments, maps, messaging and accounting.

The sentence Girija could repeat without sounding glib was this: the interface is the easy part; what we are buying is a dependency on someone else’s roadmap, limits and uptime.

3. How it actually works

Consider one evening’s task: Hastakshar wants the unpaid invoices of one customer. Figure 1 shows the exchange. The steps are as follows.

Steps 1 and 2 are authentication: proving who is calling. Here Hastakshar presents an application credential and receives a short-lived token, a string that stands in for permission. In practice Indrayani uses OAuth 2.0, a standard in which the customer approves access once on a consent screen, so the token carries the customer’s authority and not merely Hastakshar’s. Step 3 is the request: a verb (GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH changes, DELETE removes), an address, and parameters. Step 4 is the response: a status code (200 means success; the 400s mean the caller erred; the 500s mean the server erred) and a body, usually in JSON, a plain-text format of labelled values.

Three steps are routinely left implicit. First, pagination: servers will not return 18,000 invoices at once, so they return pages of 50 and a link to the next. Second, rate limiting: the server caps how many requests a caller may make in a minute so one noisy client cannot starve the rest, and step 5 is what that cap feels like. Third, the reverse direction in step 6: a webhook is a request the server makes to you when something changes, so you need not keep asking. It means Hastakshar must itself run a public address that is always available to receive them.

4. A worked example

Gaurav’s two weeks covered steps 1 to 4. Girija asked him to list everything else. Table 1 is the result, in person-days, costed at a loaded ₹12,000 per engineer-day (₹0.12 lakh).

Work itemPerson-daysCost (₹ lakh)
OAuth consent, token storage and refresh60.72
Initial sync with pagination80.96
Rate-limit handling and retries50.60
Webhook receiver and signature checks60.72
Field mapping (invoice, buyer, GST fields)121.44
Error handling and nightly reconciliation101.20
Sandbox testing and partner certification91.08
Monitoring and alerts40.48
Total build607.20

The build is 60 person-days, six times the original ten (two weeks of one engineer), and ₹7.2 lakh, which is 3 per cent of the ₹2.4 crore pipeline (₹240 lakh). The first year adds upkeep: partners change their interfaces, so Gaurav budgeted 15 person-days (₹1.8 lakh). Year one therefore costs 75 person-days and ₹9 lakh, or 3.75 per cent of the pipeline. The calendar, not the money, is the problem. One engineer working 60 days fills exactly the twelve weeks to 4 September, with no allowance for leave, illness or a fortnight lost waiting for the partner’s certification team.

Now the arithmetic of the first synchronisation. An average customer holds 18,000 invoices. At 50 per page, listing them takes 18,000 ÷ 50 = 360 requests. Indrayani’s list, however, omits line items, so each invoice needs its own detail call: another 18,000. That is 18,360 requests per customer. The limit is 60 requests a minute per customer token, so one sync takes 18,360 ÷ 60 = 306 minutes, or 5.1 hours. There is also a global cap of 1,200 requests a minute across all of Hastakshar’s customers. If all 40 are connected on launch day, the total is 40 × 18,360 = 7,34,400 requests, and 7,34,400 ÷ 1,200 = 612 minutes, or 10.2 hours. The global cap, not the per-customer cap, is what binds.

The second pass changes one input. Reading the documentation again, Gaurav found that the list call accepts an option to include line items. The detail calls disappear, and each customer needs only 360 requests; for all 40, 40 × 360 = 14,400 requests, and 14,400 ÷ 1,200 = 12 minutes. One sentence in the documentation moved launch-day load from 10.2 hours to 12 minutes, a fifty-one-fold reduction (612 ÷ 12 = 51). The cost of an integration depends on how you call the interface.

Steady state tells a similar story. Polling every five minutes means 288 requests a day per customer (24 × 60 ÷ 5), or 11,520 for forty. If each customer changes 150 invoices a day, webhooks deliver 40 × 150 = 6,000 messages, about 52 per cent of the polling volume, and they arrive within seconds instead of after an average delay of two and a half minutes.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

An API is not an integration

An API is an offer; an integration is a commitment. The first can be evaluated from the documentation in an afternoon. The second takes weeks, and keeps taking time after launch. “It has an API” answers a feasibility question, not a cost question.

Authentication is not authorisation

Authentication establishes who is calling; authorisation establishes what that caller may do. A token that proves Hastakshar’s identity may still be limited to reading invoices and forbidden from reading bank details. Ask early which scopes (named permissions) exist; a missing one can be a commercial negotiation.

Rate limits are a product constraint

Ask whether a cap is per customer, per application or per endpoint, whether it resets each minute or each day, and whether it can be raised by contract, because it bounds how fast you can onboard.

Webhooks are promises with fine print

Most senders deliver a webhook at least once, meaning duplicates occur, and a message may arrive late or out of order. Suppose 0.5 per cent of the 6,000 daily deliveries repeat: that is 30 duplicates a day, each of which can create a double entry unless the receiver is idempotent, meaning that processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once. A webhook that never arrives leaves no trace, so teams reconcile nightly.

Versions and deprecation

Interfaces change, and retirement notice may be ninety days. The 15 upkeep days budgeted outside Table 1 exist for this reason. Ask for the deprecation policy before you commit.

The sandbox is not production

A sandbox is a test copy of the partner’s system. It holds a few tidy records, while a real customer’s books hold thousands of messy ones. Test against one real customer early.

Data meaning is not data format

An API guarantees the shape of the data, not its meaning. When Indrayani says an invoice is “open”, does that include invoices already disputed? The twelve days of field mapping in Table 1 are mostly spent on this question, which no schema answers.

What an API cannot tell you

It cannot tell you the partner’s reliability, their appetite to help, or whether they will one day compete with you.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In consumer products, integrations are mostly with large platforms, such as payment gateways, whose terms are not negotiable; the cost is compliance and dependence. In B2B products such as Hastakshar’s, the integration is often the product. Forty customers on one package justify the work, but a long tail on ten packages demands another strategy, such as an aggregator interface. In marketplaces both sides integrate, and a failure on one side shows up as a bad experience on the other.

Size changes the answer too. An early-stage company has one engineer who knows the partner’s quirks and no monitoring, so it should integrate narrowly and expect to babysit. A large company has a platform team and a partnerships function that can negotiate limits; its risk is the opposite, a quarter of coordination before a line of code is written.

7. Common mistakes

Estimating from the happy path. The symptom is a two-week estimate that becomes eight weeks. The misunderstanding is treating the documentation’s first page as the whole task. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask the engineer to list every item beyond steps 1 to 4, as Girija did.

Ignoring limits until launch. The symptom is a sync that stalls on the first day with many customers. The misunderstanding is that limits belong to operations. The diagnostic is a two-line calculation of requests per customer against the cap, like the one above.

Trusting webhooks alone. The symptom is a customer reporting that a payment was missing three days ago. The misunderstanding is that “push” implies “delivered”. The diagnostic is a nightly count comparing both systems.

Treating the partner as a utility. The symptom is surprise at a deprecation notice. The misunderstanding is that the interface is stable like electricity. The diagnostic is to ask who at the partner you would call, and to find out whether you know their name.

8. What good looks like

In a well-handled week the estimate arrives as a table, not a number. The team has read the rate-limit page and the options on every list call. One real customer’s data has been pulled by Wednesday. The date given to customers is a pilot first. And someone has been named to own the integration after launch, with the 15 upkeep days already in the plan.

9. What Girija decided

On Friday 12 June, Girija told Hemlata that 4 September was achievable for a pilot with six customers, and that general availability for the other thirty-four would follow once the partner’s certification was complete. She assigned two engineers rather than one: 60 person-days over two people is 30 days each, six weeks of focused work, which leaves the other six weeks of the twelve as slack for certification and surprises. She asked Gaurav to adopt the include-lines option from the start, to receive webhooks but reconcile nightly, and to request a higher global cap from Indrayani’s partner team before launch. The ₹9 lakh year-one figure went to finance as a line item.

To go further, study how to read an architecture diagram,, and the integration patterns of synchronous calls, queues and events. Security basics for product managers follows naturally, since every token is a key. Two questions to sit with: if Indrayani raised its prices or closed its interface next year, which of the 60 person-days would be wasted, and which would remain useful? And what would you need to know about a partner before you were willing to put forty customers’ trust on its uptime?
case40v1-tech.ai.build:
Delivery & Technology · Technical Fluency

Bunyaad Systems: Sixty-One Apps Nobody Ordered

Pune, Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore, Edison and Dubai, October 2026.

1. Baner, Pune — Sunday night, 11 October 2026

The office in Baner was empty except for the security desk. Jhelum Randeria, chief product officer of Bunyaad Systems, had the board pack open on one screen and, on the other, a spreadsheet her own team had built and no longer trusted. The board met at four on Monday 12 October, and item four read: Edge applications programme — scale, pause or absorb.

Nine months earlier Bunyaad's solution consultants had been given licences to a set of AI build tools. They had since shipped sixty-one small applications around the platform: a photo-upload queue for warranty claims, a GST reconciliation viewer. Jhelum signed the first six licences herself in December 2025, without the architecture council.

Four questions sat in front of her wearing one coat. Was the programme cheap, as her services organisation read Exhibit 3? Expensive, as her platform team read Exhibit 4? Was it why win rates had risen, which Exhibit 5 could neither prove nor refute? And had it endangered the largest contract on the books, whose renewal notice fell due on 30 November 2026?

2. How Bunyaad got here

Bunyaad was founded in Pune in 2016 by Jinesh Rawal, on the observation that India's mid-market manufacturers ran their dealer networks on paper, WhatsApp and a clerk's memory. Bunyaad Flow handled dealer onboarding, warranty claims, field-service scheduling and secondary-sales reporting for paint, cement and auto-component distributors, and grew on implementation revenue (Exhibit 1) behind Zoho and Freshworks.

The decision that constrains 2026 was taken in 2022. Rather than fork its codebase per client, Bunyaad built Khaka: a layer in which a client's forms, approval chains and reports were data, not code. Khaka worked. It also meant anything Khaka could not express had nowhere to live: no plugin runtime, no extension point, no way to add a screen. For three years the answer to “can we just add this?” was a nine-month queue.

The second constraint was commercial. In July 2023 Bunyaad signed Bahri Building Materials, a Dubai distribution group, on terms it would not accept today: the client's own cloud tenant, source in escrow, and quarterly external review of every artefact touching client data, with twenty working days' notice before go-live (Exhibit 6).

3. The industry around the decision

By 2026 the Indian mid-market had stopped asking whether to buy software. GST e-invoicing pushed invoice-level discipline down to distributors who had never kept a ledger in software. UPI and the rails NPCI built around it made dealer payments traceable, dealer credit scoreable, and every manufacturer want a dealer app. ONDC made a certain kind of distributor nervous enough to spend. The DPDP Act, 2023 made every Bunyaad client a data fiduciary that expected its vendor to carry the obligation.

Competition came from three directions. Zoho Creator and Microsoft Power Apps promised a client's own IT team could build what it needed; Salesforce and the large Indian integrators promised someone else would. From late 2024 AI build tools made a third promise, to whoever sat closest to the problem. Exhibit 2 is Bunyaad's attempt to say what each was for, first written in August 2026 and updated to 30 September by an engineer who had used three of them.

4. The situation in detail

On Monday 12 January 2026 Bunyaad began what services called the Khaka Sprint: consultants already wrote Khaka configuration, so let them build the screens it could not express. Figure 1 traces what followed.

By 31 March 2026 fourteen apps were live; by 30 June, thirty-three; by 30 September, sixty-one, across thirty-eight of Bunyaad's 184 paying clients. Jaswandi Raniwala's team reported a mean first-build time of 13.9 hours; Jairaj Rungta's began demonstrating them in pitches. Win rates, between 22.9 and 24.0 per cent for three quarters, reached 31.4 per cent in the September quarter.

Three beliefs then failed. The first was that the apps were self-contained: twenty-three of the sixty-one wrote to platform tables or processed personal data, so Bengaluru inherited them whether anyone asked or not. The second was that the cost was being measured. Engineering logged 1,942 hours against those twenty-three; the other thirty-eight have no row in that ledger, which is not no cost.

The third surfaced on 14 August 2026, when Bahri's reviewers completed the review of artefacts filed to 30 June. They raised one finding: a nightly price extract had gone to storage outside the client's tenant for forty-one days, 12 May to 22 June. Bunyaad's Mumbai counsel had separately flagged a dealer-onboarding app at an Indian cement distributor capturing proprietor photographs and PAN images with no retention rule and a consent notice the consultant wrote himself. Asked how many Bahri apps were live without the notice, services answered six of nine.

5. The people

Eight people in six offices hold pieces of the answer (Figure 2).

Jhelum Randeria, 41 — Chief Product Officer, Pune
Owns Monday's paper, and no position. Her FY2027 bonus is sixty per cent on platform retention and forty on services margin, and the two pull apart here. She has not told the board she authorised the first six licences.
Jinesh Rawal, 52 — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune
Wants one answer by Monday. A growth fund's questionnaire asks what share of Bunyaad's shipped code is AI-generated; he does not know and has not said so.
Jaimin Rupani, 38 — VP Platform Engineering, Bengaluru
Wants new apps frozen and the twenty-three in-scope ones absorbed into Khaka; he is measured on the roadmap Exhibit 4 says has slipped nine items. Four of his engineers have used Cursor and Claude Code on platform code since February under no policy, and nobody has separated those hours from the 1,942 he cites.
Jaswandi Raniwala, 45 — SVP Professional Services, Pune
Wants it scaled and priced as an offering; she is measured on services margin and utilisation, both of which it lifted. She signs the statements of work, three promising maintenance for unowned apps.
Jairaj Rungta, 49 — SVP Sales, Edison, New Jersey
Wants forty more apps this quarter, as the only differentiator in a mid-market bake-off. The Exhibit 5 tag that supports him is set by his own account executives, two of whom he asked to retag closed deals.
Jonaki Rakhecha, 34 — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto
Argues the comparison cannot be made with the data that exists. Her telemetry misses the thirty-eight out-of-scope apps too, so the blind spot is partly hers.
Jenil Rajkotia, 36 — Principal Designer, Berlin
Counts eleven date pickers and four renderings of a rejected claim across the sixty-one apps, and argues clients pay in confusion what Bunyaad saves in rupees. Six are his own team's.
Jeevika Rasiwala, 39 — Director of Customer Success, Singapore
Holds the Bahri renewal conversation and counts fifty-four client-visible apps, not sixty-one. Two of her managers asked consultants for edge apps as save plays, so some have no commercial record.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“I am not arguing the apps are bad. Twenty-three are now mine, I did not choose them, they have no tests, and only eleven have anyone on the rota. If a claim queue dies at two in the morning in Dubai, whoever gets paged cannot read it.”

— Jaimin Rupani, architecture council minutes, 1 October 2026

“One thousand three hundred and seventy-one consultant hours since January — under twenty lakh of time — has produced sixty-one working applications at thirty-eight clients. Through Bengaluru that was the whole FY2028 roadmap. Ask me to stop in writing, and tell the three clients whose statements of work I signed.”

— Jaswandi Raniwala, email to Jhelum Randeria, 2 October 2026, 23:14 IST

“Engineering's own ledger says eighty-four hours an app. Sixty-one apps is 5,148 hours, more than the platform team spent on the whole Khaka release. Say that out loud to the board.”

— Jairaj Rungta, #edge-programme thread, 6 October 2026, 08:41 in Edison (18:11 IST)

“Jairaj, the base is wrong, so rebuild the whole sentence, not the multiplier. The 84.4 hours is a mean over 23 in-scope apps, not over 61. The ledger's total is 1,942 hours, all there are; multiplying its mean by 61 invents a little over 3,200 hours nobody worked. Across all 61 it is 1,942 over 61, or 31.8 hours — honest only if the 38 apps with no row consumed nothing, which nobody can show.”

“Put those 31.8 hours at the platform rate and you get ₹0.67 lakh an app, more than the ₹0.63 lakh Exhibit 3 says the whole thing costs. Add the 8.6 consultant rework hours it also leaves out, at ₹0.12 lakh, and Route A is ₹1.42 lakh — so Route B is 3.7 times Route A, not eight. Now per client: ₹5.29 lakh over 184 clients is ₹2,875 a client, while ₹1.42 lakh serves one, which makes the platform about forty-nine times cheaper. Both are correct, and that is the trouble with the exhibit.”

— Jonaki Rakhecha, same thread, 09:02 in Toronto (18:32 IST), and a note that evening

“Nobody has asked what the dealer sees. Eleven date pickers, four ways to show a rejected claim — and my team built six of them.”

— Jenil Rajkotia, design review, 7 October 2026, 11:20 in Berlin (14:50 IST)

“Bahri's head of IT has asked twice for the artefact list; I have sent it twice with a different count.”

— Jeevika Rasiwala, call notes, 8 October 2026, 17:40 in Singapore (15:10 IST)

8. The options as Jhelum sees them

Scale it. Price edge apps as an offering, hire fifteen consultants, target a hundred and fifty apps by March 2027. Jaswandi and Jairaj want this. It assumes Exhibit 3's cost curve holds at two and a half times the volume, and that twenty-three in sixty-one does not rise.

Freeze and absorb. No new apps; Bengaluru takes the twenty-three in-scope apps into Khaka over two quarters. Jaimin wants this. It assumes, untested, that the functionality generalises: one client's credit-note screen may have no second client.

Govern it. Keep building behind a gate: a template, a review, a named owner, a contract-notice check. Jhelum's instinct sits here. It assumes the gate can be staffed without eating the capacity the programme freed, and that three-day cycles survive a twenty-day notice.

Separate the tools from the question. Jonaki's position, uncosted: decide what Bunyaad sells, then pick a tool per job — Replit Agent for a demo that dies on Friday, v0 for a screen on an existing API, Claude Code in a repository with tests, Lovable for anything carrying client data and therefore not a fast decision.

All four are written as choices about tools. In the margin Jhelum has a note to herself: are we deciding what to build with, or who decides what gets built? She does not know whether that is a sharper framing or an evasion.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday 12 October 2026, 16:00 IST. Two of five directors join from New Jersey, where it will be 06:30.

Money. Fifteen consultants would cost about ₹3.92 crore a year at ₹26.10 lakh each; absorbing the twenty-three apps is, on Jaimin's estimate, two quarters of four engineers.

People. Ninety-six solution consultants at 31 March (Exhibit 1), forty-one now holding tool licences. No approved platform headcount for FY2027 H2.

Regulation. The DPDP Act, 2023 makes Bunyaad's clients data fiduciaries and Bunyaad a processor with obligations on retention and consent. One app has neither a retention rule nor a reviewed consent notice.

Contract. Twenty working days' notice per artefact at Bahri; six apps live without it; the next review falls in November. Notice due 30 November 2026 on an account worth 12.0 per cent of FY2026 revenue.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is each tool in Exhibit 2 for, and which apps should not have been built with the tool that built them?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 are each consistent and lead to opposite conclusions. What does each measure, and what would settle between them?
  3. Exhibit 5 shows the win rate rising 8.5 percentage points from Q1 FY2026 to Q2 FY2027. What must be true for the programme to be the cause, and what cuts against?
  4. Six of nine apps at Bahri went live without the contractual notice. Who is accountable — the consultant, the services head who signed the statement of work, the engineering head who owns the pipeline, or the CPO who authorised the licences? What does that imply for the gate?
  5. Jonaki reverses the services conclusion using the same cells. Which denominator is right, and what does that assume about demand for any given app?
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October 2026. What does Jhelum do before four o'clock, what does she say to the board, and what single number goes on the slide?

At a quarter past one she reopened the list of sixty-one apps, sorted by requester. Against nine the column was empty. She could not tell whether nobody had asked or nobody had written it down. Outside, the first Diwali hoardings had gone up along the Mumbai highway. The notice was due in seven weeks; the board in fifteen hours. She turned off the second screen and left the first on.
exp40v2-tech.ai.build:
AI-assisted building

Why the hours these tools save are not the hours that bind.

1. Two decisions, nine days apart

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, in a shed-floor office in Nagpur, Jayashri Kamat had a spreadsheet on one screen and a browser on the other. She is vice-president of product at Jalnidhi Meter Works, which builds ultrasonic bulk water meters and the utility-side software that reads them. Jalnidhi had won a lot in a Nagpur Municipal Corporation replacement programme: 14,000 meters, each surveyed before installation for pipe diameter, chamber condition, two photographs and the consumer identifier. Surveys were on paper, re-keyed at nine minutes a form — 1,26,000 minutes, or 2,100 hours, of typing. The ₹2.4 crore milestone required the survey complete by 31 December 2026.

Her two software engineers, Keya Thakar and a firmware specialist, were locked until Monday 9 November on firmware changes required for Legal Metrology approval, and that date would not move. On the second screen was a field-survey application that Jeevika Rao, who manages support operations and has never written production code, had produced over four evenings with an AI app builder. It captured a survey, worked offline, uploaded photographs and looked about right.

Nine days later, on Thursday 17 September, in Bengaluru, Kaushik Vaidya faced a narrower version of the question. He heads product at Khoj Talent Systems, which sells recruiting software to large employers and has 86 enterprise customers. Twenty-three wanted a bespoke adapter into their own human-resources system, each worth about 12 per cent of expansion on an average ₹18 lakh contract — ₹2.16 lakh a year each, ₹49.68 lakh across the 23. At 110 engineer-hours an adapter the backlog was 2,530 hours, which Lalit Mhatre, his chief technology officer, would not fund. An agent inside Khoj's repository could draft one in a day and a half; but every adapter moves candidate names, phone numbers and salary history, which put Komal Vartak, the security lead, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 in the path.

Neither decision is about whether the tools work. Both turn on one fact: they have collapsed the cost of producing code and barely touched the cost of becoming confident it is right.

2. The idea, and the four camps

AI-assisted building is the production of working software by instructing a large language model — a system trained to predict useful continuations of text and code — in ordinary language, using a tool that executes or hosts the result so the author can inspect it and correct the instruction. Three things are bundled: a model that drafts, a harness that runs, and a loop that lets a human steer.

The ambition is old. "Automatic programming" meant, in the 1950s, what we now call a compiler. Fourth-generation languages in the 1980s and the CASE tools after them promised applications from specifications and largely failed, because the specifications were the hard part. The spreadsheet, the most successful end-user programming system ever shipped, won by shrinking the problem instead, as no-code did later inside a vendor's component set. What changed from about 2021, with editor completions, and decisively from 2023, when tools began taking a whole repository as their unit of work, is that the output became general-purpose source code rather than someone else's blocks.

The camps are best stated by what each will and will not sign.

The leverage camp holds that the bottleneck was never thinking but typing. It will sign: a domain expert with these tools delivers a useful internal tool faster than any correctly prioritised backlog. It will not sign: that generated code may touch customer data unreviewed.

The verification camp holds that software cost is dominated by the cost of being sure, so generation relocates work rather than removing it. It will sign: the binding constraint after adoption is review capacity. It will not sign: that the tools are a fad — the drafting saving is real and large.

The substrate camp cares where the artefact lives. It will sign: the first question about a build tool is what you own when you stop paying. It will not sign: that exportability makes tools equivalent, since exported code with no tests is a liability transferred.

The apprenticeship camp worries about the pipeline. It will sign: an engineer who never wrote a first draft will review one badly in five years. It will not sign: restriction, since these are the best tutor a junior ever had.

These are not four flavours of one view: the first two make opposite predictions about throughput in month four, and a firm that cannot say which it believes will be surprised by whichever is true.

3. Mechanics: what the five tools are for, and where the hours go

What matters about each tool is not its quality but the unit of work it takes and what you hold at the end.

Tool (maker)Unit of workWhere code livesRight jobWrong job
LovableA whole applicationVendor project, exportableA first working versionChanging a large system
v0 (Vercel)A screen or componentPasted into your repositoryInterface variantsBusiness logic
Cursor (Anysphere)A few filesYour repositoryAn engineer editing their own codeNon-engineer autonomy
Replit AgentAn app plus hostingVendor workspaceShort-lived internal toolsAnything under security review
Claude Code (Anthropic)A task across many filesYour repositoryMulti-file changes with testsWork nobody can review

Table 1. Categories, not rankings; the middle columns move slowest.

Two properties trade off: the more of the loop a tool owns, the faster the first result and the dearer the exit.

Expert practice runs a loop easy to describe and easy to under-resource: assemble context, instruct, run, inspect, correct, and — the step no tool supplies — verify against something other than the model's own output. Three parts are left implicit. Context assembly is putting before the model what it cannot know: the real schema, two dozen genuine survey forms with the handwriting and missing fields, the rule that a surveyor must never see another ward's data. Jeevika's first attempt produced a generic form because she had not said a Nagpur consumer identifier carries a ward prefix. The harness is the tests the output is judged against; without it, "it works" means "it did not crash". The environment is where it runs and who can reach it.

Keya then decomposed the field app into six components, estimating for each the conventional engineer-hours, the drafting hours with an agent, and the hours to review and correct that draft to a standard she would sign. The first column includes peer review.

ComponentConventional hrsDrafting hrsReview & rework hrsAssisted hrsRatio (conv. ÷ assisted)
Survey form, offline120931403.00
Photo capture60414183.33
Meter serial scan90630362.50
Supervisor approval queue80519243.33
Billing-system sync1401062721.94
Roles and audit log100753601.67
Total590412092502.36

Table 2. Jalnidhi field-survey app, 11 September 2026. Assisted hours are drafting plus review: 41 + 209 = 250. The ratio row divides the totals.

Three readings matter. The headline: 590 hours become 250, a factor of 2.36, nothing like the tenfold figure a weekend demonstration suggests. The composition: 209 of the 250 assisted hours, 83.6 per cent, are verification; only 41, 16.4 per cent, are what people mean by "building". And the ratio is not uniform — 3.33 on the visibly testable photo pipeline and approval queue, 1.67 on roles and audit logging, where correctness means the absence of something unseeable. What prices review is how far a mistake travels.

The second-order effect decides Jayashri's case: cost is not her constraint, reviewer time is. Two engineers at 30 productive hours give 60 a week, so the conventional route takes 9.8 weeks of work — but cannot start until 9 November, putting completion near 17 January 2027, seventeen days past the deadline. The assisted route needs 209 reviewer-hours, and only one person can judge access control. At Keya's spare 12 hours a week that takes 17.4 weeks: cheaper and much slower. The crossover is arithmetic — 209 ÷ 9.8333 is 21.25 — so the assisted route wins the calendar only above 21.25 reviewer-hours a week.

In money, at a loaded ₹1,400 an hour for Jeevika and ₹2,600 for an engineer, the conventional route is 590 × ₹2,600 = ₹15,34,000 and the assisted route at internal rates ₹57,400 + ₹5,43,400 = ₹6,00,800. The option that hits the deadline splits the review — 105 hours from Keya, 104 bought at ₹3,200 — giving ₹57,400 + ₹2,73,000 + ₹3,32,800 = ₹6,63,200. Her purchase is not software; it is 104 hours of someone else's judgement.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable claims; the protagonists score differently.

Claim 1: the saving is large where the blast radius is small. Jalnidhi's photo pipeline scores 3.33, its audit log 1.67. Khoj's adapters all carry personal data, so none is a small-radius surface — which is why Kaushik's per-adapter ratio, 110 ÷ 52, is only 2.12.

Claim 2: the saving is large where a specification exists in verifiable form. Khoj passes emphatically: each of the 23 target systems has a published interface and 40 recorded payloads to judge against. Jalnidhi half passes — the survey form is specified by the tender, but the billing sync is defined by an undocumented eleven-year-old system, the component scoring 1.94.

Claim 3: the tools convert spare verification capacity into output, not spare ambition. Jalnidhi fails until it buys 104 hours; Khoj passes, with eleven engineers who read code for a living.

Claim 4: you must own the artefact where your engineers already work. Khoj passes by construction; Jeevika's app does not, and converting it is part of Jalnidhi's cost.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where the work is integration with a system the model has never seen, it will confidently invent the interface and free drafting is worthless. Where correctness is defined by a regulation rather than a test — a Legal Metrology tolerance, a DPDP consent record — passing tests is not evidence. And where the cost sits in the last five per cent, the tools accelerate the first ninety-five and leave the schedule where it was.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature firms actually do

In a multi-product company the characteristic failure is silent duplication. Khoj's agent, asked for an adapter in two repositories, wrote two different retry behaviours for the same vendor interface; six weeks later one retried four times and the other once, and the tickets looked like a vendor outage. Generation is cheap enough that shared components stop being shared.

In a two-sided business the blast radius crosses a trust boundary: a screen leaking one side's prices to the other is a breach of the market's premise.

In a regulated business the problem is explanation, not code. Kutumb Benefits Group, an employee-insurance intermediary, found its IRDAI-facing auditors asked not "does it work" but "why is it designed this way", and generated code arrives with no rationale. Its answer: a one-page design before generation, which improved the output.

In hardware plus software the asymmetry is brutal: Jalnidhi's survey app can be fixed in an afternoon, its meter firmware, once in 14,000 chambers, cannot. Hence a hard line at the device boundary.

In AI-native products the generated code itself calls a model, so output is non-deterministic and one passing test proves nothing. Jugalbandi Labs, which builds a clause-extraction product in Pune, replaced pass-or-fail tests with a scored set of 300 documents: a change must hold accuracy above the baseline or it does not merge.

At the organisational seam, what mature firms do differs from policy. Policy says all generated code goes through standard review. Practice is three-part: an allow-list of surfaces where anyone may build and ship — internal, read-only, no personal data; a registry entry for each such tool naming an owner and an expiry date, commonly 90 days, after which it is deleted unless renewed; and a rule that anything else joins the engineering queue with its origin declared. Firms skip the second part, the one that stops unowned systems accumulating.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The ratio you are quoted is a verification ratio in disguise. Jalnidhi's 2.36 says nothing about the model; it says how much of the work was reading. The tell is a ratio quoted with no review line beside it. One tool scored 3.33 and 1.67 on two components of one application.

Blast radius prices the review, not line count. A 900-line screen may review in two hours; a 30-line change to a permission check can take a day. The tell is a team estimating review by diff size.

A prototype is a specification only if someone throws it away. Kept, it becomes the architecture by default, inherited by engineers who never chose it. The tell is a pull request reproducing the prototype's folder structure. Reuse saves time only when what is reused was chosen.

Context assembly is the skill, not prompting. Jeevika's second attempt, with the real schema, 24 scanned forms and the ward rule, needed a third of the corrections of her first. The tell is an expert gathering inputs for longer than they write instructions.

The harness is the deliverable. What survives is not the code, which will be regenerated, but the tests and recorded payloads any version is judged against. The tell is a team whose golden files predate its implementation. Treat the code as the asset and every regeneration is fresh risk.

Exit cost is a product decision. A tool that owns hosting and the database is a future migration chosen in advance — for a 90-day internal tool, obviously correct. The tell is a team that can say what it would do if the price tripled.

The second week is the test, not the first weekend. First versions are uniformly impressive; the diagnostic is the twelfth change against code the author cannot read. The tell is an owner still editing by instruction three weeks in, unable to find the logic by hand.

Generated code defeats the reviewer's instincts. Human code carries signals — hesitant naming, a defensive comment, odd style around the hard part — while generated code is uniformly confident, so the eye has nothing to catch on. The tell is a reviewer who slows down on generated diffs: competence, not obstruction. And whatever the model gets wrong is something your organisation knows and never wrote down — each correction is a free audit of institutional memory.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

ContextWhat generation is genuinely forWhat prices the review
ConsumerInterface and onboarding variantsScale; store policy; personal data
B2BAdapters, demos, back officeContractual security terms
EnterprisePrototypes inside a governed processAudit explanation and change control
Platform / marketplaceOne side's operational toolingTrust boundaries; money movement
HardwareEverything off the deviceIrreversibility; certification
AI productsScaffolding around the model callNon-determinism; statistical tests

Table 3. The loop is identical everywhere; only the last column changes.

Say plainly where the difference is not real: the loop and the context-assembly discipline are the same in a four-person startup and in a bank; only the price of verification and of exit changes. A pre-product-market-fit company should accept a weak foundation deliberately — Jugalbandi Labs rewrote its first product entirely and was right to. A scaling company has the hardest version, its generation capacity having outrun its review capacity unnoticed. A mature company's problem is inventory, not quality: employees create systems faster than any registry records them, which is why the 90-day expiry matters more than the checklist.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Jalnidhi, succeeding with a condition. The saving — ₹15,34,000 down to ₹6,63,200, or ₹8,70,800 — was never in doubt; the deadline was, and it turned on buying 104 reviewer-hours.

Khoj, a clean and unglamorous win. Twenty-three adapters at 110 conventional hours is 2,530 engineer-hours, or ₹65,78,000 at ₹2,600. Assisted, each takes 14 drafting hours from a consultant at ₹1,500 and 38 review hours from an engineer: 52 against 110, a ratio of 2.12.

LineBasisAmount (₹)
Consultant drafting, 23 adapters322 hours at ₹1,5004,83,000
Engineer review and hardening874 hours at ₹2,60022,72,400
Total, assisted route1,196 hours27,55,400

Table 4. Khoj adapter backlog, assisted. 322 + 874 = 1,196 hours; the cost ratio is ₹65,78,000 ÷ ₹27,55,400 = 2.39.

Against ₹49.68 lakh of annual expansion revenue, ₹27,55,400 pays back in 0.55 of a year, or 6.7 months. Note what did not change: 874 of the 1,196 hours, 73.1 per cent, are still engineering. Kaushik cut the engineering constraint by 65 per cent, from 2,530 hours to 874 — enough to change Lalit's mind.

Lohit Metals Exchange, a failure. Lohit is a two-sided market in Raipur matching small steel re-rollers with construction buyers. Its founder, Kedar Bhagwat, built a seller-onboarding and quotation tool with an app builder and put it live on Thursday 14 May 2026, eleven days after starting; nineteen days later, on 2 June, it came down. The generated quotation path took a price sellers entered in rupees per kilogram and treated it as rupees per tonne. Of 1,482 quotes issued, 311 — 21 per cent — carried the error, and 168 of the 311, 54 per cent, were accepted at an average under-quote of ₹7,400.

ConsequenceBasisCost (₹)
