Table 5. Lohit, 14 May to 2 June 2026. Against a conventional estimate of seven engineer-weeks, ₹7,28,000, and a build cost of ₹96,000, the claimed saving was ₹6,32,000.

The failure cost ₹35,07,200 to save ₹6,32,000 — 5.5 times the saving, and ₹28,75,200 worse than not trying. The reason is not "AI wrote bad code": nobody had written down which unit sellers quote in, because every human at Lohit knew, so the model could not know and no test disagreed. The recovery kept the generated interface and rewrote only the pricing path by hand, behind a golden-file test of 400 historical quotes that would have failed all 311 bad quotes first time. Lohit still generates most of its code; it no longer generates the two paths where being wrong is expensive.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Review debt. Generated code merges faster than reviewers read it, visible as a lengthening queue two to three weeks in. Diagnostic: how many reviewer-hours a week do we have, and what is the backlog? Caught late, it arrives as a cluster of incidents whose only common feature is their origin.

The undocumented rule. The sign is a reviewer saying "obviously it should be per kilogram". Diagnostic: name three rules every employee knows and no document states, then ask whether a generated path depends on them. Lohit's late catch cost ₹12,43,200 in honoured quotes.

Orphaned tools. The sign is a tool whose author has changed teams and whose hosting sits on a personal account. Diagnostic: who is paged when it breaks, and what is its deletion date?

Architecture by default. The sign is an engineer unable to explain why data is stored where it is. Diagnostic: ask the builder to describe where data lives and who can read it; inability is the finding. Caught late it is a rewrite — at Jalnidhi's scale, roughly the 590 hours supposedly saved.

Capability atrophy. A team generates for eighteen months and finds its juniors cannot review; the sign is comments that only concern style. Diagnostic: ask a two-year engineer to explain a generated permission check line by line.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the prototype a specification or an anchor? The specification camp points to Jalnidhi, where Jeevika's four evenings removed most of the discovery the conventional 590 hours assumed, and argues that a running artefact communicates intent better than any document. The anchor camp replies that Lohit's recovery kept the interface and threw away the logic, and that inherited structure costs more than it saves: engineers reviewing a working thing ask "is this right" rather than "is this the right shape". It would be wrong if teams starting from a prototype showed no more rework at twelve months than teams starting from a document.

Should non-engineers build things that reach production? The leverage position is that the person holding the problem is the right author, and that gatekeeping costs more in unbuilt tools than it saves in defects. The restriction position is that Table 2's 83.6 per cent verification share shows the author was never the expensive part, so letting non-engineers author merely loads the scarce resource. It would be wrong if firms that opened building widely showed no rise in reviewer load per feature. Both agree on the allow-list and disagree about its width.

Does review cost scale with volume or with exposure? The volume view holds that unread code is a liability per line. The exposure view holds that Table 2 settles it: 100 conventional hours of audit logging cost 53 review hours while 60 hours of photo handling cost 14. The volume camp's best evidence is drift — Khoj's divergent retry behaviours were a volume failure, and no reviewer saw both.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can name the five tools. Someone who has internalised it budgets review before generation, in hours, from a named person's calendar; asks what the worst wrong behaviour costs before asking how fast the build will be; names the two paths that must never ship unreviewed; invests in the harness, expecting code to be rewritten and tests to survive; and treats every model error as a documentation defect of their own. The signature is unglamorous: they generate less than they could, with more confidence.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Tuesday 29 September, Jayashri took the assisted route with a written condition: the project was funded for 209 review hours, 105 from Keya and 104 from a contract reviewer at ₹3,200 an hour, and if that reviewer was not engaged by 9 October it reverted to the November start and Jalnidhi renegotiated the milestone. Jeevika's prototype was declared a specification and its code discarded; the app was rebuilt in Jalnidhi's own repository, firmware off-limits. Budget ₹6,63,200 against ₹15,34,000, completion mid-November rather than mid-January.

On Friday 2 October, Kaushik funded six of the 23 adapters rather than all: the 65 per cent cut in engineering hours was worth having, but the 874-hour review load was real and he would rather learn its true cost on six. His instruction was narrow — draft against the recorded payloads, never the specification alone.

Discussion questions. First: Jayashri's binding constraint was one person's attention, not money. What else in her organisation is priced in Keya-hours, and what should she stop doing? Second: Kaushik cut engineering hours by 65 per cent and funded a quarter of the backlog — prudent sequencing, or a failure to take his own numbers seriously? Third: name the rule in your product that everyone knows and nobody wrote down, and say why it is still unwritten.

13. Going deeper

  • How web and mobile apps work — Figure 1's axes depend on it.
  • Choosing the right AI build tool — Table 1 as a procedure.
  • Prompting a builder from a spec — context assembly, practised.
  • Deploying a web product — the step hosted tools hide.
  • Adding an LLM feature — building with a model versus shipping one.
  • AI-native teams — allow-list and registry as an operating model.
  • When building gets cheap and deciding does not — the sequel to 83.6 per cent.
  • APIs and integration basics — why the billing sync scored 1.94.
  • Data modelling for PMs — the schema is your best input.
  • Databases, storage and caching — where your data actually went.
  • Cloud infrastructure basics — what exit cost means.
  • Reading an architecture diagram — review shape, not only code.
  • Scalability and performance — what a prototype cannot tell you.
case20v1-tech.ai.build:
Anvik Textile Exchange: Build, Prototype or Wait

A decision case in AI-assisted building

1. Opening

At 11:00 India time on Tuesday 3 November 2026, Ihita Pancholi, head of product at Anvik Textile Exchange, joined a video call from her desk in Surat. It was 06:30 in Berlin, 13:30 in Singapore and 09:30 in Dubai. On the Dubai line, the procurement head of Anvik's largest export client repeated a request he had first made in September: a live portal showing where each of his firm's consignments stood. He wanted a working demonstration by Friday 20 November. Without it, he said, the annual agreement due for signature on 30 November would go to a competitor that already offered tracking.

Ihita had until Thursday 5 November to tell the chief executive, Ishwin Pujara, how Anvik would answer. She had a full engineering roadmap, a five-hour experiment from the previous Sunday, and three possible courses of action.

2. Company background

Anvik, founded in Surat in 2017, is a business-to-business marketplace on which fabric mills and traders sell to garment makers and exporters. In the year to March 2026 it handled goods worth ₹640 crore and earned a 2.3 per cent commission, or ₹14.72 crore. An export desk, which consolidates fabric and garment shipments for buyers in the Gulf, contributed ₹3.2 crore of that, about 22 per cent. Payments run over UPI and bank transfer, invoices follow GST e-invoicing rules, and the company is a data fiduciary under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

Its rivals are Udaan and Bizongo for online ordering, and, more stubbornly, the telephone-and-WhatsApp trade of Surat's Ring Road markets. The company employs eleven engineers, seven in Bengaluru and four in Pune.

3. The situation

The Dubai client, a garment re-exporter, has bought through Anvik's export desk for three years. Its revenue to Anvik rose to ₹128 lakh (₹1.28 crore) in 2025-26, and, as Exhibit 1 shows, so did the burden of its questions: the average consignment now generates more than three status queries to the Singapore desk.

Assuming the export desk earns a 25 per cent gross margin, the account is worth about ₹32 lakh a year in gross margin. The cost of engineering time is the competing figure: Anvik treats an engineer-week as ₹0.6 lakh, a fully loaded ₹30 lakh a year over fifty working weeks. Building the portal from scratch, engineering estimates, takes nine engineer-weeks, and the roadmap through December is already committed to e-invoicing changes and the festival-season ordering peak. Up to two engineers could start in the first week of January.

On Sunday 1 November, Ihita spent five hours with Lovable, a browser-based tool that generates a working web app from a written description. She produced a clickable shipment list and a status timeline, filled with invented data. On Monday, Inderpal Parmar, the engineering lead, tested it. The screens were convincing; the login was decorative, and any visitor could see every shipment.

The views from the edges differ. In Berlin, where it was still early morning, Ishvi pointed out that the portal would be used by logistics clerks on phones in Dubai. In Singapore, Ishir said the Dubai client's 640 status queries last year had nearly all been answered by hand. The Dubai procurement head, when asked, said he did not care how the portal was built, only that his clerks could see it working before signing.

4. The people

Ihita Pancholi, Surat, owns the roadmap and the client relationship. She wants to keep the account without mortgaging the engineers' quarter.

Inderpal Parmar, Bengaluru, leads engineering. His team already uses Cursor and Claude Code, which work inside an existing codebase, to speed up refactoring. He does not object to AI tools; he objects to anything reaching a client without passing his review, and he notes that the consignee contacts in the data are personal data.

Ishvi Parekh, a product designer in Berlin, drew the original portal screens in September. She likes seeing them alive but fears a generated interface will harden into the product before anyone has designed it properly.

Ishir Pitroda, who leads customer success from Singapore, absorbs the Dubai client's 640 status queries. He wants anything live as soon as possible.

Ishwin Pujara, the chief executive, wants the renewal and does not want a security incident to follow it.

5. The options

Option A: join the queue. One engineer builds the portal from scratch from 4 January, finishing on 5 March. It is the safest build, and it costs ₹5.4 lakh of engineering time. But it misses the 20 November demonstration, and the client has said that is the test.

Option B: prototype, then build. Ihita uses Lovable or v0, a similar interface generator, to turn Sunday's experiment into a demonstration with anonymised data by 12 November, and writes the prototype up as the specification. Two engineers then build the production version from 4 January with Cursor and Claude Code, the six engineer-weeks Exhibit 2 prices, and it reaches production on 22 January. It adds ₹0.6 lakh of tool spend. It also asks Ihita to spend her own week on a throwaway.

Option C: ship the prototype. Ihita, with Replit Agent to host and wire it, extends the Sunday app to read a nightly export of the client's rows and puts it live by 17 November, with one engineer-week of review from Inderpal himself. It is the cheapest option and the fastest to production. It also leaves untouched the login, database, data-separation and alert work in Exhibit 2, and it places client data on a platform Inderpal has not assessed.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly does the client need by 20 November, and what does he need by 22 January? Does either need production software?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, which parts of the portal did Ihita's five hours remove, and which did they leave untouched?
  3. Match Lovable, v0, Cursor, Replit Agent and Claude Code to the jobs in this case. Which belong to Ihita and which to Inderpal?
  4. Rank the three options in Exhibit 3 on cost, speed and risk to the account. Which would you take to Ishwin Pujara on 5 November, and what condition would you attach?

7. A note for the learner

This case rests on a distinction that cheaper building does not erase: the cost of producing screens has collapsed, but the cost of deciding what to build, and of making it safe, has not. Think of the tools by what they are for. Interface generators such as Lovable and v0 turn a description into a clickable app in hours. Replit Agent goes further and hosts a small full-stack app. Cursor and Claude Code work inside an existing codebase under an engineer's supervision. A product manager can therefore build a convincing demonstration alone today. She cannot yet build, alone, the login, data separation and database connection that make a demonstration a product.

One defensible path is Option B, run with conditions. Ihita builds the 12 November demonstration using only anonymised data, and shows it to the client as a preview. She hands the prototype to Inderpal as the specification, which Exhibit 2 prices at three engineer-weeks saved, one third of the build. Production follows on 22 January, and the renewal is signed on 30 November on the strength of a visible plan. Inderpal owns the release gate.

Option A fails the stated test. Option C is attractive: ₹0.9 lakh against ₹4.2 lakh. But 5.0 of the 6.0 remaining weeks, 83 per cent, sit in work the prototype never touched, and one engineer-week of review cannot replace them. Saving ₹3.3 lakh while putting a ₹128 lakh account's data on an unassessed platform is a poor trade. Ishir's queries and Ishvi's design concerns are best met by B, which gets something live sooner than A and keeps the product designed rather than generated.
exp20v2-tech.ai.build:
AI-assisted building

1. The queue and the calendar

On Monday 14 September 2026, Anjali Chaturvedi, head of product at Bharani Exchange, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. Bharani is a Pune-based business-to-business marketplace that connects small manufacturers with institutional buyers. The sheet listed 1,800 suppliers waiting to be onboarded. Each took the operations team about 25 minutes of copying documents between email, a shared drive and the admin panel. That is 45,000 minutes, or 750 hours, of clerical work before a single supplier could be shown to a buyer.

The fix was a supplier self-service portal: a form, a document upload, a status page. Engineering had room for it, but only from Monday 21 December, fourteen weeks away. Bhavesh Chandak, the engineering lead, estimated twelve engineer-weeks once it started. Meanwhile Chitra Anand, a business analyst with no engineering background, had spent the weekend describing the portal to an AI builder and had a working demonstration running in a browser.

The decision was not whether the tools were impressive. It was whether a demonstration made in a weekend changed what Bharani should do about a fourteen-week wait, and what it would cost if Anjali mistook one for the other. Ship the weekend version unreviewed and supplier documents might leak. Dismiss it and the 750 hours of clerical work, and the buyer demand waiting behind it, would simply continue. This page builds the understanding she needed.

2. The idea

AI-assisted building means using software, driven by a large language model (a system trained on vast amounts of text and code that predicts useful continuations), to produce working software from instructions written in ordinary language. The problem it addresses is old: the distance between knowing what you want and having a program that does it. Spreadsheets, no-code form builders and templates each narrowed that distance for narrow cases. Language models widened it by writing general-purpose code on request. Their usefulness for code became visible from about 2021, when GitHub Copilot began suggesting lines inside editors, and tools that take whole applications as the unit of work followed from 2023 onward.

The tools are not interchangeable, and the learning objective is to know what each is for. The table sorts five well-known ones by the job they do best. Products change quickly, so treat it as a map of categories rather than a verdict on brands.

Tool (maker)Best understood asTypical userOutput
LovableDescribe an app, get a hosted prototypeProduct manager, founderFull web app
v0 (Vercel)Describe a screen, get interface codeDesigner, front-end developerInterface components
Cursor (Anysphere)A code editor with an assistant insideWorking developerEdits to an existing codebase
Replit Agent (Replit)Build, run and host in one browser workspaceLearner, small teamRunning app with hosting
Claude Code (Anthropic)An agent working in a codebase from the terminalDeveloper, technical PMMulti-file changes, tests

Table 1. Categories, not rankings; capabilities overlap and shift month to month.

The sentence Anjali could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "These tools make the first working version cheap; they do not make the decision about what to build, or the responsibility for running it, any cheaper."

3. How it actually works

Every tool in the table runs the same loop, shown below. The person writes a request. The model drafts code, often across several files. The tool executes the code or renders the screen. The person looks at the result and writes a correction. The loop repeats until the output is acceptable.

Three steps are usually left implicit. First, the model has no memory of your business; whatever it needs must be in the request or in files it can read. Chitra's early attempts produced a generic form because she had not said that Bharani suppliers hold a GST registration (the Goods and Services Tax identification number) and a Udyam certificate (the government registration for small enterprises). Second, "running" means somewhere: a hosted preview, a laptop or a server, and the data it touches must live somewhere too, typically a managed database. Third, the tool judges its work by whether the code runs, not whether it is safe or correct for your suppliers.

The tools differ mainly in how much of the loop they own. Lovable and Replit Agent own most of it, including hosting, which makes them fast and hard to inspect. Cursor and Claude Code sit inside a codebase you already have, so they suit changes to a real product. v0 owns only the interface. Choosing a tool is choosing how much of the loop you wish to hand over.

A useful habit follows from this: write the request as if briefing a capable contractor on their first day. State who the users are, what data they hold, what must never happen, and what done looks like. Chitra's second attempt, which named the two registration documents, the three status values and the rule that a supplier must never see another's files, behaved far better than her first. The improvement came from clearer thinking, not from a cleverer tool.

4. A worked example

Anjali asked Bhavesh to cost one more month of work on the weekend prototype, with an engineer reviewing it. Tooling costs are illustrative monthly assumptions; time is valued at a loaded cost per hour.

ItemBasisCost (₹)
App-builder subscription1 month2,000
Editor assistant1 month1,700
Agent usage1 month8,300
Hosting and database1 month4,000
Chitra's time40 hours at ₹1,50060,000
Engineer review12 hours at ₹2,50030,000
Total, assisted route1,06,000

Table 2. Assisted route. The first four lines sum to ₹16,000; the two time lines add ₹90,000.

The conventional route is twelve engineer-weeks at ₹90,000 per engineer-week, or ₹10,80,000 (₹10.8 lakh). The assisted route at ₹1,06,000 (₹1.06 lakh) costs about a tenth: 10,80,000 divided by 1,06,000 is 10.2.

The second pass changes one input. Bhavesh's review finds that uploaded documents sit in a publicly readable store, and that status pages can be guessed by changing a number in the address. Hardening takes three engineer-weeks, which is ₹2,70,000. The assisted route becomes ₹1,06,000 plus ₹2,70,000, or ₹3,76,000 (₹3.76 lakh). The saving falls from ₹9.74 lakh to ₹7.04 lakh, and the cost ratio from 10.2 to 2.9, since 10,80,000 divided by 3,76,000 is 2.87. It is still a clear saving, and the conclusion survives. What changed is that the headline ratio was never the right figure: the cost of making the prototype safe was the figure that mattered, and nobody knew it until a person who understood storage and access looked.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Prototype is not product

A prototype demonstrates that an idea can work; a product survives real users, bad data, failures at 2 a.m. and staff changes. The tools erase most of the cost of the first and almost none of the cost of the second.

Generated code is not reviewed code

The model optimises for code that runs and looks right. Hidden faults, such as missing access checks, stay invisible in a demonstration. Review is a human skill that scales with the stakes.

Ownership outlasts creation

Someone must fix it when it breaks in March. If the builder was a product manager who has moved teams, the software is orphaned. Ask who owns it before asking whether it works.

Platform lock-in

Some tools keep code and hosting inside their own environment. Ask whether you can export the code to a repository (a versioned store of source files) your own engineers control, and what happens if the price changes.

Confusion with no-code

No-code builders constrain you to components the vendor built. AI builders emit ordinary code you can read and extend, which gives more freedom and more ways to be wrong.

What the tool cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether suppliers want a portal, whether the document rules satisfy a regulator, or whether the workflow is the right one. Those questions need interviews and data. It builds what you asked for, not what you needed.

Where the tools struggle

Large existing systems, unusual integrations, strict performance needs and anything involving money movement or personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 are where unaided outputs are least trustworthy.

6. How it differs by product type and company size

ContextBest use of AI buildingPrincipal risk
ConsumerFast experiments on landing pages and onboarding flowsScaling to millions of devices; app-store rules
B2BInternal tools, dashboards, customer demosCustomer data, access control, contractual security terms
MarketplaceSupplier or seller tooling and back-office screensTwo-sided trust; payments; disputes
Early stageWhole product, built by foundersA fragile foundation that must later be rewritten
Large companyPrototypes and internal tools inside a governed processShadow systems outside security review

Table 3. The same tools, different failure points.

In a consumer product the interface is the product, and v0-style tools speed up iteration, but reliability under load is untouched. In B2B, buyers' security questionnaires apply to anything that touches their data, however it was built. In a marketplace such as Bharani, the prototype is safest when it serves one side's operations rather than moving money between sides. A start-up with four people can accept a weaker foundation to find out whether anyone wants the product. A large firm has the opposite problem: employees can now build tools faster than the security team can find them.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the demonstration as the estimate. The symptom is a plan that says "done in a weekend" with no line for review or hosting. The misunderstanding is that the loop's first four steps are the whole job. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask what happens at step five, and who does it.

Prompting for a feature rather than a behaviour. The symptom is a portal that looks right and handles only the happy path. The misunderstanding is that the model knows your edge cases. The diagnostic is to feed it five real, messy supplier submissions before showing anyone.

Letting the tool choose the architecture. The symptom is a database and hosting arrangement nobody on the team can explain. The misunderstanding is that defaults are neutral. The diagnostic is to ask the builder to describe, in two paragraphs, where data is stored and who can read it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Chitra's weekend result is labelled a prototype and shown to eight suppliers within a week. Anjali writes a one-page request naming the owner, the data it will hold and the point at which it is retired. Bhavesh reviews it against a short checklist of storage, access and logging, and an engineer is allocated for three weeks of hardening. The prototype is the specification: it shows the engineers exactly what is wanted, saving much of the twelve weeks of discovery. Product and engineering spend their time on judgement, not typing.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Anjali decided to treat the prototype as a specification and a pilot, not a release. On 16 September she told the leadership team that Bharani would run it with eight suppliers behind a login, fund Bhavesh's three weeks of hardening, and release it generally only after review. The expected cost was ₹3.76 lakh against ₹10.8 lakh, and the portal would not wait for 21 December. Her reasoning was that the tools had changed the price of the first version, so the cost to guard against was no longer building the wrong thing slowly but releasing the wrong thing quickly.

To go further, learn how web and mobile apps work, then how to choose among these tools, how to prompt a builder from a specification, how to deploy a web product and how to add a language-model feature. The final topic, when building gets cheap and deciding does not, follows directly from the argument above.

Two questions to sit with. If Chitra can build in a weekend what once took twelve engineer-weeks, what should the engineering team's time now be spent on? And in your own organisation, who would own a tool someone built on a Saturday, a year from now?
exp20v2-tech.client.server:
How Web and Mobile Apps Work

What actually happens when a user taps a button, and why a product manager should be able to say so precisely.

1. Opening: the cart that took three seconds

On 28 September 2026, Gauri Hegde, the product manager for the shopping app at Gulal Grocery Exchange, opened a chart she had been avoiding. Gulal connected about 4,000 neighbourhood grocery stores in Pune and Nashik to households, and its festive sale was due to begin on 19 October, 21 days away. The chart showed the "View cart" screen. Fenil Shah, the analyst, had measured it on the phones customers actually carried, and the median load time was 3.2 seconds.

The app recorded about 80,000 cart views a day. Of these, 60 per cent, or 48,000, came from phones on weak mobile networks. Among those users, the share who went on to attempt payment, which Fenil called the proceed rate, was 62 per cent. Among users who saw the cart in under 2.5 seconds, it was 71 per cent. Farooq Ansari, the engineering lead, wanted to spend the next two weeks on a new store-ratings feature. Greta Olsen, a contract backend engineer working from Tallinn, suspected the cart's problem lay in how the screen talked to the server, and said so in a message that Gauri could not fully evaluate.

That was the real difficulty. Gauri could read the chart but could not say what happened between a thumb touching glass and the cart appearing. Without that, she could not tell whether Greta's suspicion was plausible, whether Farooq's priority was defensible, or what to ask for. This page builds the picture she needed.

2. The idea: client, server, API, database

Almost every web or mobile product divides its work between two machines that never meet. The client is the program on the user's device, a browser tab or a phone app, which draws the screen and reacts to touches. The server is a program on a computer in a data centre, which holds the rules and answers questions. A database is the server's organised long-term memory: the stores, prices, carts and orders. An API (application programming interface) is the agreed menu of requests the server will accept and the shape of the replies it will give.

The arrangement solved a problem of control. Software installed on each user's machine could not be corrected centrally, and shared information could not live on any one user's device. Tim Berners-Lee's work at CERN between 1989 and 1991 produced the web's version: a browser asks for a page by address, using HTTP (hypertext transfer protocol), and a server replies. Roy Fielding's 2000 doctoral dissertation described the style, called REST, that most modern APIs follow. The iPhone in 2007 and the app stores that followed in 2008 put the same conversation inside installed apps.

Gauri's sentence for meetings became: "Every tap that needs shared information is a conversation across a slow network, and our job is to decide how many sentences it takes."

3. How it works, step by step

Follow one tap on "View cart". First, the client's code notices the touch and decides it needs the cart contents, which live on the server. Second, unless a connection is already open, the phone must establish one. It looks up the server's numeric address through the domain name system (DNS), opens a channel with TCP, and agrees encryption with TLS. Each of these three steps costs one round trip, the time for a message to reach the server and a reply to return. Practitioners rarely mention this setup, yet on a weak network it is often the largest single cost.

Third, the client sends a request: a method such as GET (fetch) or POST (change), an address such as /cart, and credentials proving who is asking. Fourth, the server checks the credentials, runs its own logic, and asks the database for the rows it needs. Fifth, the server assembles a response, usually structured text called JSON, together with a status code such as 200 for success. Sixth, the client receives the response, interprets it and finally draws the screen. The user perceives only the total.

Two implicit points matter later. The phone and the server are separated by a latency, the delay per round trip, that bandwidth cannot buy back, because latency is set by distance and congestion while bandwidth is merely how much data flows per second. And a screen that needs several pieces of data may make several requests, one after another, each paying the full round trip.

4. A worked example, line by line

Greta opened the app's network log and found that "View cart" made four sequential calls: the cart items, the saved address, the delivery slots, and the price breakdown. She assumed a poor mobile network with a 300 millisecond round trip and a bandwidth of 2 megabits a second, which is 250 kilobytes a second, or 4 milliseconds per kilobyte. Setup costs three round trips, 3 × 300 = 900 ms, paid once because the connection is reused. Each call then costs one round trip, plus the server's working time, plus the time to transfer its payload.

Table 1. Four sequential calls on a 300 ms network. Transfer = payload in KB × 4 ms. Total = round trip + server + transfer.
CallPayload (KB)Round trip (ms)Server (ms)Transfer (ms)Total (ms)
Cart items203009080470
Saved address103007040410
Delivery slots30300160120580
Price breakdown40300220160680
Total1001,2005404002,140

Add the 900 ms setup and 150 ms for the phone to draw the screen, and the tap costs 900 + 2,140 + 150 = 3,190 ms, the 3.2 seconds Fenil measured. Notice that 1,200 ms of the call time, plus the setup, is pure waiting for round trips. Only 540 ms is the server working. Greta's suspicion was right: the problem was the number of conversations, not the server's speed.

Her proposed change was one new endpoint returning all four pieces together. The server could gather them in parallel, taking as long as the slowest, 220 ms, and send the combined 100 KB, which transfers in 400 ms. The second pass varies the network and the design.

Table 2. Same screen under two designs and two networks. Total = setup + calls + render.
ScenarioSetup (ms)Calls (ms)Render (ms)Total (ms)
A. Four calls, 300 ms round trip9002,1401503,190

Scenario C is one call costing 300 + 220 + 400 = 920 ms. Scenario B recomputes the four calls at 100 ms each: 270, 210, 380 and 480, summing to 1,340. The batching therefore cuts the weak-network time by 1,220 ms, to 1,970 ms, under the 2.5 second threshold, while a faster network alone only reaches 1,790 ms in B. Notice that the design change matters most precisely where the network is worst.

The business arithmetic, which Gauri built with Fenil, was deliberately cautious. The cohort gap was 9 points (71 less 62), but the groups differed in other ways, so they halved it to 4.5 points. That gives 48,000 × 0.045 = 2,160 extra orders a day. At an average order of ₹640, that is ₹13,82,400 of daily order value. At a 6 per cent contribution margin, it is ₹82,944 a day. The work needed three engineers for ten working days at ₹10,000 a day each, or ₹3,00,000, repaid in roughly 3.6 days of sales at that uplift.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Latency is not bandwidth

A faster plan raises bandwidth, but each round trip still takes as long as distance and congestion dictate. In Table 1, round trips account for 1,200 ms and transfer only 400 ms.

The client is not trustworthy

Code on a user's phone can be inspected and altered. Prices, discounts and permissions must therefore be decided on the server. A client can display a discount; only the server may grant it.

Apps and websites cache differently

A cache is a stored copy that avoids a trip. A website can rely on the browser's cache and updates instantly. An installed app can hold its own copies, but old versions linger on phones for months, so the server must serve many client versions at once.

The API is a contract

Once apps ship, changing a reply's shape breaks installed versions that expect the old one. Hence the new batched endpoint is added beside the old ones, not substituted for them.

Success hides in the average

The median hides the users in the tail. A slow ten per cent may sit on exactly the cheap phones and weak coverage your growth depends on, so ask for the 90th percentile as well as the median.

Correlation is not the uplift

The proceed-rate gap came from comparing different users. Halving it was a judgement, not a measurement. Only an experiment, where a random half sees the fast cart, tells you the true effect.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products, early and late

In consumer products like Gulal's, the binding constraint is the weakest network among your users, so the number of round trips dominates. In B2B products, users sit on office broadband but ask for heavy work: a report over millions of rows. There the database and server time in Table 1's third column dominate, and the question shifts to whether the query should run at all while the user waits.

A marketplace has two clients, here the shopper's app and the store owner's order screen, talking to one server. A change that helps one side can break the other, so the API contract matters doubly. Early-stage companies often run a single server and one database, and can change anything quickly. Large companies split them into many services, each with its own owners, and a single tap can cross several of them. At that scale, the PM's skill is knowing which team owns which slice of the milliseconds.

7. Common mistakes

Blaming "the server" for everything

Symptom: a slow screen produces a ticket titled "backend performance" and nothing improves. Misunderstanding: that time is spent at the server. Diagnostic: open the network log and add the columns of Table 1 for that screen; it takes ten minutes.

Testing only on office Wi-Fi

Symptom: the team says the screen is fast while customers say it is not. Misunderstanding: that the developer's network represents the user's. Diagnostic: throttle the connection to a 300 ms round trip and use the screen once.

Treating a ship date as a deploy date

Symptom: a fix is released yet complaints continue for weeks. Misunderstanding: that every user runs the new client. Diagnostic: ask what share of sessions run the latest app version.

Quoting an uplift as a fact

Symptom: a business case promises a precise gain from a speed fix. Misunderstanding: that a correlation measures a cause. Diagnostic: ask whether anyone has run a randomised test, and haircut accordingly.

8. What good looks like

A PM handling this well begins with the network log, not an opinion. She can name the calls behind a screen, state the round trips and the server time, and say which of the two Table 2 levers applies. She asks engineering for the 90th percentile as well as the median, and agrees a threshold, here 2.5 seconds, before work begins. She sizes the benefit conservatively, as Gauri did, and proposes a randomised rollout so the real effect is measured rather than assumed.

9. Closing: the decision and what to learn next

Gauri took the numbers to Farooq on 30 September. She did not ask him to drop the ratings feature; she asked for ten working days of three engineers, at ₹3,00,000, ahead of it, with the new endpoint added beside the old ones and released to a random half of users first. Her reasoning was that the cost was repaid in about 3.6 days of the cautious uplift, that the sale was 19 days away, and that the test would convert her estimate into a measurement before the sale's heaviest traffic. Farooq agreed, and ratings moved to November.

To go further, learn APIs and integration next, because the batched endpoint is an API design decision, and then data modelling, which governs the database's share of the milliseconds.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of one screen in a product you know, and ask how many sequential calls it plausibly makes, and what you would need to see to find out. Second, if the randomised test showed an uplift of only 1 point, what would you do with the other two weeks of engineering time?
exp40v2-tech.client.server:
How Web and Mobile Apps Work

Dependency chains rather than call counts, the handshake as a pre-payable tax, idempotency as a product choice, and who may commit a fact.

1. Two taps, two companies, one week in October 2026

On Thursday 1 October 2026 Nandika Pathare, group product manager for the learner app at Nukkad Learning Network in Indore, read a measurement her engineering lead did not believe. Nukkad sells live classes in Hindi and Marathi for ₹349 a month to 7,40,000 monthly active learners, nearly all on Android phones with two or three gigabytes of memory in towns where the network is excellent at eleven in the morning and unusable at eight. The app records 2,60,000 "Join class" taps a day across nine class bells. Purnima Aklujkar, the analyst, had started the timer at the touch rather than at the load balancer: the median cold join took 2,355 milliseconds, the ninety-fifth percentile 6,900. Parimal Nene's instrument disagreed — the API's own ninety-ninth-percentile response was 240 milliseconds. Nuno Ferreira, a performance engineer in Lisbon, read both and wrote: "Your problem is depth, not width." Nandika had five engineers and six weeks.

In Pune on Tuesday 29 September, Pranika Sahasrabudhe met the same subject from the other end. Parvat Elevator Works maintains 48,600 lifts in fourteen cities with 2,150 technicians, and 19,400 of those lifts carry a telemetry box on the controller. Technicians work in basements with no signal, and their app was a thin client: every submission was a request, and a request without a network fails. In September the fleet logged 2,90,250 service visits, of which only 1,97,370 reached the server on the first attempt. Nilay Phadtare, the chief technology officer, and Naveen Thatte, head of field operations, wanted it rebuilt offline-first. Padmanabh Ranade, who leads controller firmware in Coimbatore, objected to one line: a technician must never mark a lift returned to service while out of contact, because a state electrical inspectorate reads that record after an accident.

Both decisions turn on one picture, and the argument here is that it is an accounting system: it says where a unit of time, a unit of trust and a unit of truth sit.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that disagree

Define the terms. A client runs on hardware the user controls, a server on hardware the operator controls. A request names a method, a resource and credentials; a response carries a status and usually a body. A round trip is one message out and one back, and its duration, the latency, is set by distance and congestion, not by how much data moves. A database is the server's durable memory; an API the contract of accepted requests and promised replies.

The arrangement solved a problem of control. The client-server wave of the late 1980s moved presentation to the desk, leaving data in a shared database. Tim Berners-Lee's work at CERN between 1989 and 1991 produced HTTP, in which the server forgets you between messages, and Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation named that style REST. XMLHttpRequest, in Internet Explorer 5 in 1999 and used by Google Maps and Gmail in 2004 and 2005, made the browser a real client; the iPhone in 2007 and the app stores from 2008 put the same conversation inside software the operator could not update at will. HTTP/2 in 2015 let requests share a connection, and HTTP/3 over QUIC, standardised in 2022, cut the setup cost priced below. Meanwhile Marc Shapiro and colleagues published conflict-free replicated data types in 2011, and Martin Kleppmann and co-authors argued in 2019 for "local-first" software.

Four schools disagree, and what each will not sign is the useful part. The server-authoritative school signs that the server is the single source of truth and the client a cache of it; it will not sign that a client may declare a business fact while out of contact. The local-first school signs that the device holds a writable replica and reconciles later; it will not sign that every write needs central validation before the user is told it worked. The client-shaped-API school — Falcor, GraphQL from 2015, backend-for-frontend — signs that a screen should fetch exactly its data in one round trip, even at the price of an endpoint per screen. The event-driven school signs that request and response is a special case of a stream both sides subscribe to. Nandika's problem sits between the first and third, Pranika's between the first and second.

3. Mechanics: the handshake tax and the dependency chain

Purnima's trace of a cold join on an ordinary urban connection — a 180-millisecond round trip at 1.6 megabits a second, which is 200 kilobytes a second, or 5 milliseconds a kilobyte — decomposes as follows. The first four round trips do no product work: DNS, TCP, and two for TLS.

Table 1. One cold "Join class" tap, 1 October 2026, at a 180 ms round trip and 5 ms per kilobyte. Payloads were 6, 18, 4 and 25 KB, totalling 53 KB. The last row's work is on the phone; row and column totals agree at 2,355.
StepRound tripsNetwork wait (ms)Work (ms)Transfer (ms)Step total (ms)
DNS lookup118000180

Three facts fall out. First, 1,440 of the 2,355 milliseconds, 61 per cent, is network waiting, against 650 milliseconds of computation. Second, the four product steps are dependent: the token cannot be requested until the class is identified, nor the class until the session resolves. Since HTTP/2 six independent requests share one connection and cost one round trip between them; six dependent requests cost six. What floors a screen's latency is its longest dependency chain times the round-trip time, plus the work along it. Third, Parimal's 240 milliseconds measured first byte at the load balancer to last byte leaving it; DNS, handshake, radio queue and layout are invisible to it.

Two levers follow. Pre-pay the handshake by keeping a connection warm when the app reaches the foreground, removing four round trips. Then collapse the chain with one endpoint, POST /join, resolving session, class and token server-side, where the three run in parallel and cost the slowest, 110 milliseconds, rather than their sum of 240. The payload is still 28 kilobytes, and the media connection stays separate.

The weak-network case falls from 4,858 to 2,208 milliseconds, a saving of 2,650, which is 55 per cent of 4,858; the urban case falls from 2,355 to 1,145. The design is worth more than twice as much where the network is worst, which is the cohort Nukkad's growth depends on.

A second-order effect follows. At the seven o'clock bell 34,000 learners join within ninety seconds, which is 377.8 joins a second. Under the old design each consumed 240 milliseconds of server work, so the fleet needed 90.7 core-seconds every second; at Nukkad's 55 per cent utilisation target that is 165 virtual CPUs standing ready. Under the single endpoint each join consumes 110 milliseconds, or 41.6 core-seconds a second, needing 76 — removing 89 virtual CPUs from the peak, about ₹2.18 lakh a month at ₹2,450 per virtual CPU-month.

4. When the picture applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: user-felt time is dominated by chain depth, not server computation. Divide network waiting by the total: for Nukkad's join, 1,440 over 2,355, so the claim holds decisively. For Parvat's console it fails — the status query takes 38 milliseconds of database work and office connections are fast, so capacity binds and fewer round trips is the wrong target.

Claim two: the server can arbitrate every decision at the moment the user acts. Trivially true at Nukkad; false at Parvat for roughly a third of visits, and all of Pranika's difficulty follows from it.

Claim three: the client may be trusted with nothing. Sound about prices and permissions; misleading at Parvat, where an offline client must mint identifiers and order its own events. The client may not be the authority on a fact, but it may be its author.

Claim four: a faster network would fix it. Table 2 refutes it: moving every learner to a 180-millisecond link reaches 2,355 milliseconds, while changing the design reaches 2,208 on the bad link. The picture also misleads when the delay is on the device, when the server is a third party such as a payment gateway, and when the medium is real-time video.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Parvat is at once a hardware company, a two-sided product and a regulated one. The telemetry boxes do not make requests; they emit events. Modelled as pollers at one heartbeat every thirty seconds, 19,400 boxes commit you to 38,800 requests a minute, or 646.7 a second, before a human touches anything — hence an ingestion pipeline for devices, a request API for people.

The two sides disagree about truth. A technician who closes a job offline believes it closed; the manager's console still shows the lift down. Mature firms make staleness explicit rather than picking a winner — Parvat's console prints "as of 14:06" beside every status, and the decision becomes the seconds in the budget.

The regulated seam is sharper. Under the Indian lift regime a return-to-service record carries evidentiary weight, and Bureau of Indian Standards practice assumes a single authoritative log, so an offline-committed return to service is a liability even where the engineering is sound. What mature organisations do, as against what their diagrams say, is partition by consequence: most of the form goes offline, one field does not. The organisational seam is where this leaks — the sync queue belonged to the mobile team, deduplication to the platform team and the definition of a completed visit to operations, and none believed they owned it. AI features add a fourth pattern: Parvat's fault-summary inference takes 2 to 9 seconds, too long to sit inside a request a user waits on.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Round trips, not requests, are the unit of account. The tell is an engineer reporting that a screen's calls fell from nine to four without saying whether any were sequential. Connections multiplex, so width is cheap; what costs is the chain in which each call needs the previous answer.

The handshake is a fixed tax, and it can be pre-paid. The tell is a respectable median beside a ninety-fifth percentile three times worse with no slow query to blame: the tail is cold starts paying 720 milliseconds of setup. Nothing is intermittently slow; something is intermittently new.

"The server" is a chain, and availability multiplies. A tap crossing five services each at a 99.9 per cent target succeeds 99.50 per cent of the time, because 0.999 to the fifth power is 0.99501 — fifty failures in ten thousand taps. The tell is every team meeting its objective in a month when user-visible success fell.

Caching converts a speed question into a staleness question. Parvat's sixty-second cache cut request load by 94 per cent and created a window in which a stopped lift reads as running. The tell is that nobody can state the staleness budget in seconds.

Idempotency is a product decision in engineering clothes. A client-minted key lets the server recognise a retry rather than a new action, and somebody must define "the same" — the same visit, the same lift that day, the same technician within ten minutes. The tell is a rule in a code comment.

An installed client is a population, not a version. Nukkad released 4.12 on 15 June 2026; twenty-one days later, on 6 July, 64 per cent of sessions ran 4.12 or later, 27 per cent one of five previous builds and 9 per cent something built before 1 May. The tell is a fix that "shipped" and a metric that ramps for a month, then stalls.

The API contract outlives the organisation chart. Adding POST /join beside the three old endpoints means owning four. The expert sign is a retirement rule tied to client versions — Nukkad's is that an endpoint may go once fewer than two per cent of sessions need it.

Where the work happens is a cost allocation. Computation on the device is free on the operator's balance sheet and dear on the user's battery; on Nukkad's cheapest handsets it decides between a smooth class and a hot phone. The tell is a decision justified entirely on server cost.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer mobile products the binding constraint is the worst network among users who matter, so depth dominates and the instrument is a client-side timer on real handsets. In enterprise web products users have good connections and ask for heavy work, so server and database time dominate, and the question becomes whether a query should run while a human waits. In platforms and marketplaces the contract matters twice over, because two clients on different release cycles share one set of shapes. For hardware the model covers the people, not the devices; for AI products the response is long, variable and metered, which pushes work out of the synchronous path.

Where the difference is overstated: the fundamentals do not change by stage, since a seed-stage company and a listed one pay the same handshake tax. What changes is the number of seams. Early on, one team owns client, API and database and a chatty screen is fixed in an afternoon; at Parvat's size the same endpoint needs three teams to agree, and the manager's skill becomes knowing who owns which slice of the milliseconds.

8. Three worked examples

The launch screen that worked, and over-promised

Nukkad applied the pre-warm idea once before, to the launch path, in version 4.12 on 15 June 2026. Median time from icon tap to a usable home screen fell from 3,100 to 1,780 milliseconds. Across 1,12,000 new installs, seven-day retention rose from 31.2 to 33.4 per cent, a gain of 2.2 points, or 2,464 retained learners. The forecast had been 4.0 points, so the realised effect was 55 per cent of the model, which read the gap between fast and slow cohorts as causal. Purnima now halves any cohort-derived gap before it enters a case.

The retry that multiplied work orders

In March 2026 Parvat shipped a minimal fix for lost submissions: retry a failed POST on reconnection. Between 9 March and 3 April, twenty-six days covering 3,01,860 submissions, it created 4,188 duplicate work orders, 1.4 per cent of submissions, because a request that timed out after the server had committed it was retried as a new visit. Each duplicate cost about ₹520 of coordination and 212 produced a second dispatch at ₹1,460: ₹21,77,760 plus ₹3,09,520, that is ₹24,87,280 in twenty-six days. The failure was the absence of identity, not the retry. The recovery was a client-minted idempotency key written locally before the first attempt and stored by the server, which returns the original result for any repeat. Between 11 and 30 April, across 2,32,200 submissions, duplicates fell to 139, or 0.06 per cent. The engineering took nine days; the argument over the definition took five weeks.

The console that polled itself down

On Tuesday 21 July 2026 a power disruption sent building managers to Parvat's console at once: 26,000 of the 31,400 registered accounts, about 83 per cent, within twenty minutes. Each tab polled a live-status endpoint every five seconds, so 26,000 tabs generated 3,12,000 requests a minute, or 5,200 a second, each running a 38-millisecond query: 197.6 core-seconds of database work every second against a cluster of 48 cores, 4.1 times capacity. The ninety-ninth percentile went from 240 milliseconds to 26 seconds and for 38 minutes most requests timed out, on the afternoon whose purpose was to say which lifts were stopped. Credits came to ₹18.6 lakh. The recovery replaced polling with a server-pushed update behind a sixty-second cache: volume fell from 5,200 to 310 a second and the cluster was resized from 48 cores to 14, saving ₹83,300 a month at ₹2,450 per core-month. Polling load scales with tabs open, event load with things that happen.

9. Failure modes, warnings, and the cost of late diagnosis

The lengthening chain. Each release adds a dependent call to a popular screen and nobody notices, because no one release is slow. The warning is a call count rising through release notes; the question is "how deep is the chain here, not how many calls?" Caught late it cost Nukkad 2,650 milliseconds on the cohort it is now spending six weeks to recover.

Measuring the server's clock. The warning is the shape of Nandika's October: a healthy server percentile beside users describing a six-second wait. The question is "does the timer start at the tap or at the load balancer?" The companion test is the ninety-fifth percentile on a 420-millisecond link on a two-gigabyte device, which no office network will show you. Caught late it costs a quarter of misdirected work.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Who may commit a fact. The server-authoritative position rests on the difficulty of reconciling conflicting writes; its evidence is Parvat's own first attempt, which produced 4,188 duplicate work orders. It would be wrong if conflict rates were as low in practice as the 0.06 per cent idempotency keys achieved, and if merges could be made intelligible to a technician in a basement. The local-first position rests on the cost of insisting on the server — Parvat's leakage runs at ₹61.51 lakh a month. It would be wrong if even one offline-committed fact could create a statutory liability, which is Padmanabh Ranade's case.

One general API or one endpoint per screen. The REST position holds that a general resource API survives a decade of client churn while per-screen endpoints multiply until nobody can reason about the surface; the client-shaped position holds that Table 2 prices the refusal to serve the screen. The first fails when screens change faster than resources, the second when clients multiply faster than teams. A related split: Nukkad's stay rates of 80, 75, 65, 50 and 20 per cent across ascending join times read as a gradient, while those who believe in cliffs call that an artefact of bucketing.

Whether the manager needs the mechanics. One camp holds that half a model argues badly with engineers and that outcomes should be stated instead; the other points to Nandika, whose leverage came from knowing the fix lay in chain depth, not server speed. The first is wrong if half-knowledge improves prioritisation.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this can draw four boxes. Someone who has internalised it asks which clock a number came from before discussing it; asks for a screen's dependency chain, not its call count; names the staleness budget whenever a cache is proposed; treats the definition of a duplicate action as theirs to write; partitions by consequence rather than doctrine; and haircuts every cohort-derived estimate, having watched a 4.0-point forecast land at 2.2.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Monday 5 October 2026 Nandika committed the six weeks to the join path, on a conservative case. It should move 60 per cent of the 1,04,000 taps now taking longer than three seconds into the two-to-three-second band, which on the observed band rates yields 12,792 additional engaged attendances a day, or 4.9 per cent of 2,60,000 taps. Over thirty days that is 3,83,760 attendances across the 2,96,000 learners on weak connections, 1.30 extra classes each. Purnima's regression suggested 0.9 points of monthly renewal per additional class; halved by rule to 0.45, that is 0.58 points on 2,96,000 learners, or 1,717 retained learners a month, each worth ₹663.10 at ₹349 a month, a 38 per cent margin and five further months of tenure. The monthly benefit is ₹11,38,543. Five engineers for six weeks at ₹1,85,000 a month cost ₹13,87,500, and ₹2,60,000 of load-balancer capacity brings the project to ₹16,47,500 — about 1.4 months of payback. The endpoint ships beside the old three under the two-per-cent retirement rule, to a randomised half of learners from 1 November.

Pranika decided on 1 October: a partition rather than a direction. The technician app becomes offline-first for every part of a visit except one: the return-to-service declaration stays synchronous and server-authoritative, and a technician who cannot reach the network must walk until they can. Every other record is written locally with an idempotency key, queued, and reconciled with the server resolving ties by key rather than arrival time. The console gains an "as of" timestamp and a sixty-second staleness budget. Twenty engineer-months at ₹2,10,000 plus ₹7,50,000 of device-lab cost come to ₹49,50,000, against leakage of ₹61,51,360 a month of which the design should recover 72 per cent, ₹44.29 lakh — a payback of about 34 days, which is why the argument was never about money.

First, if Parvat's lawyers accepted an offline return-to-service declaration signed with a timestamped device key, would you allow it, and what would you need to know about clock accuracy across 2,150 devices? Second, Nandika halves a cohort-derived gap by rule, and that rule was 55 per cent accurate once: what would change the haircut, and in which direction? Third, a building manager says sixty seconds of staleness is unacceptable when a lift traps a passenger: what is the smallest change that answers him, and what does it cost in requests?

13. Going deeper

  • APIs and integration basics — Nukkad's fix is an API-shape decision.
  • Data modelling for PMs — Table 1's 110 milliseconds is a data model.
  • Databases, storage and caching — the staleness budget, the 38-ms query.
  • Cloud infrastructure basics — the 48-core cluster, the 76 virtual CPUs.
  • Scalability and performance — chain depth as queueing theory.
  • Mobile platform constraints — battery and the version population.
  • Reading an architecture diagram — the chain multiplying to 99.50 per cent.
  • Identity: auth, SSO, roles and permissions — what a client may assert.
  • Security basics for PMs — why prices and statuses are server-side.
  • CI/CD, environments and deployment — release versus arrival.
  • AI-assisted building — prototyping an endpoint shape yourself.
  • Embedded systems and firmware basics — Parvat's boxes emit events.
