case40v1-tech.client.server:
Sopaan Technologies: Where Does the Tap Go?

An ambiguous case on clients, servers, APIs and databases — and on which measurement of a tap a contract actually means

1. The night before

At twenty past eleven on Thursday night, 15 October 2026, Devashri Kinariwala was still at the office in Baner, Pune, with two laptops open: on the left a one-page note due Monday, on the right a video of a salesman's thumb.

It had come from Dubai. A hand holds a cheap Android phone in a grocery in Al Quoz, the thumb presses Submit order, and then nothing: a spinner, a shop owner looking up, and at eleven seconds a green tick. Darshana Khatod had forwarded it with one line: "This is the clip going to the board."

On Monday 19 October, Sopaan Technologies had to serve or waive notice on renewal of its contract with Sanad Trading L.L.C., its largest and only Gulf account, and the board would ask what was wrong with Sopaan Beat. Devashri, vice-president of product, had four options, five exhibits, colleagues on three continents, and two figures for the same tap — 9.4 seconds of summed phases on the handset, 1.284 seconds at the gateway — that nobody could reconcile.

2. The company, and the decision of 2019

Sopaan Technologies was founded in Pune in January 2017 by Dhanraj Khinvasara and Divyesh Khandwala to replace the paper order book. Sopaan Beat runs on a salesman's Android phone and walks him through his beat: the daily route of shops, the stock each holds, the schemes he may offer, the order he books.

In June 2019, pitching for a North Indian confectionery distributor network, the founders made the decision that still governs the product. Rural beats in Bundelkhand had no signal, so Beat was built offline-first with a single bulk synchronisation: the handset holds a complete local copy of the masters, ships the day's work up in one request at shift end, and takes a fresh copy back. By March 2021 the clause "the Application shall function without connectivity" stood in Sopaan's standard contract.

That design is now the constraint, and Figure 2 sets it beside what followed. Beat has no incremental sync: no sending one outlet's order alone, no partial retry, no refreshing one credit limit. Every proposal on Devashri's desk is about that.

3. The industry

Sales-force automation in India is crowded and price-sensitive. Bizom and FieldAssist hold much of the branded-FMCG market, Zoho and Freshworks sell adjacent suites cheaply, SAP and Salesforce sit above. Buyers are brands, users are the distributor's salesmen — a gap that keeps prices low and switching costs lower than vendors admit. GST e-invoicing has made order-to-invoice a compliance artefact, so forking the order service per customer is dear.

Sopaan's Indian business is twenty-eight accounts in twelve states, served from a Mumbai cloud region with data kept in India under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Outside India it has three accounts in Singapore and Malaysia, two American pilots, and Sanad Trading, a Dubai distributor of packaged foods serving about 31,000 outlets in six Gulf markets. Sanad licenses 1,400 seats at more than twice Sopaan's Indian price per seat, and is the reference every Gulf prospect asks for.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Sanad signed in November 2023, going live in April 2024 with 400 seats on beverages. It worked. In January 2025 it extended Beat to all 1,400 seats and switched on a trade-scheme module pricing schemes per outlet. Sopaan had assumed Sanad's masters would resemble an Indian account's; its price-list table runs to 2,14,000 rows against 18,600 for the largest Indian account, eleven and a half times as many, and a Sanad handset's local database has a median size of 1.08 GB against 240 MB.

In November 2025 Sopaan shipped fast confirmation, which draws the tick as soon as the order reaches the local store. It is on everywhere but Sanad, whose contract requires the server to enforce a credit limit before the salesman leaves the shop; Sanad alone waits for a round trip.

In February 2026 Dhanika Khemka's team timed the on-device recompute at 1.2 seconds on the then-current model, charged and on Berlin wifi. That same month a data-minimisation pass dropped the device-model field from Beat's telemetry. In March Sanad refreshed its fleet to a cheaper handset with 3 GB of memory; nobody at Sopaan noted it, and nobody can now measure it. Sanad served its first service-level notice on 24 August, citing July, and sent its own September reconciliation on 5 October. Devang Kacholia circulated estimates on 1 October, the team met on 6 October, and on 9 October Deepali Kagzi unsettled the exhibit everybody quoted.

Four beliefs held in September are in doubt: that Sanad's data resembled anyone else's; that confirmed was defined; that the missing orders were a server problem; and that the offline design was an asset.

5. The people

  • Devashri Kinariwala, VP product, Pune. Needs a plan she can still hold in April. Unsaid: she can verify neither timing exhibit.
  • Divyesh Khandwala, co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru. The fault is on the client: a 1.08 GB database, a scheme engine recomputing on the phone. Unsaid: the 2019 design is his, and he approved the scheme module untested.
  • Devang Kacholia, platform engineering, Pune. The sync API is the fault; wants the rewrite he has twice proposed. Unsaid: his team is three short; the estimate assumes replacements.
  • Deepali Kagzi, data scientist, Toronto. Built both measurement systems, trusts neither here. Unsaid: the tracer's clock is never synchronised.
  • Dhanika Khemka, designer, Berlin. A wait with no feedback is a different problem from a wait; she has a prototype. Unsaid: tested only on Berlin wifi.
  • Darshana Khatod, customer success, Singapore. Sanad needs something visible this quarter; her pay sits on retention. Unsaid: Sanad's buyers have seen a competitor's demonstration.
  • Devdatta Kansara, sales head, New Jersey. Nothing should touch the offline claim before the American pilots convert; his quota excludes Sanad. Unsaid: one pilot wants the enforcement that makes Sanad wait.
  • Dhanraj Khinvasara, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai. Will not spend into a Gulf problem during a Series B. Unsaid: the lead investor's adviser has asked about single-tenant design.

6. Exhibits

Devashri began, in August, by asking Devang what happens when a salesman taps the button. His sketch is Figure 1. The app hands the order to the on-device scheme engine, which revalues the basket against the local price list; the result goes to the local store, so it survives a dead battery; the request crosses the carrier network to the Mumbai gateway, which checks the token and passes it to the order service; that service revalidates prices through the scheme service, reads credit limit and stock from the replica, and writes header and lines to the primary database in one transaction. The reply returns through steps 5 and 4 to the screen.

Exhibit 1 is the server's account of itself: gateway instrumentation for steps 5 to 9, a Pune beat against a Sanad beat.

Exhibit 2 is the handset's account of the same event, from a tracer Deepali built in September and Sanad installed on fourteen phones. Its phases map onto Figure 1: A is step 2, B step 3, C step 4 out and back, D steps 5 to 9 as the handset sees them, E step 1.

The two do not agree. Phase D says the server took 1.9 seconds at the median; Exhibit 1 says 1,166 milliseconds by step sum and 1,284 end to end. Devang argues phase D must be swallowing the gateway queue wait, which sits in Exhibit 1 at 61 ms and cannot bear 600. Deepali cannot locate the handset's phase boundary without a packet capture, which Sanad forbids. Divyesh says the fourteen are the complainers. All three fit both exhibits.

Exhibit 3 is the month Sanad is arguing about.

Read one way it is a good month: 3,660 of 4,12,660 taps never confirmed, or 0.9 per cent. Read as Dharmesh Khakhar, Sanad's group IT head, reads it, 2,180 of the 51,420 taps at the key branches never confirmed, or 4.2 per cent — the outlets whose owners telephone Sanad's commercial director. What the account is worth is in Exhibit 4.

That reading is a money question. Sanad's service level requires 99.5 per cent of submissions to be confirmed within five seconds, with a credit of 5 per cent of the quarterly fee per 0.1 percentage point below, capped at 25 per cent. The quarterly fee is a quarter of ₹9.80 crore, or ₹245 lakh. Of the 3,84,100 first-attempt confirmations, 3,80,644 landed inside five seconds: 99.1 per cent, 0.4 points short, twenty per cent of the fee, ₹49 lakh. Over all 4,12,660 taps the same 3,80,644 is 92.2 per cent, 7.3 points short, past the cap at ₹61.25 lakh. Measured on the handset there is no figure at all: the tracer reports phases, whose medians sum to 9.4 seconds, and never a whole tap. The contract says confirmed and not where.

7. Voices

"Your gateway is not where my salesman's thumb is. I have 312 branches whose owners now ask my men to telephone the order instead. I am not interested in milliseconds, but in whether the tick means the order exists."

Dharmesh Khakhar, group IT head, Sanad Trading, 5 October 2026, 09:12 Gulf time (10:42 IST)

Devdatta Kansara: "Dubai is eighteen per cent of our ARR and we are discussing a six-week rewrite for it while the American pilots wait."

Devang Kacholia: "Both halves are wrong. Sanad is ₹9.80 crore against ₹61.50 crore, which is 15.9 per cent, not eighteen. And no rewrite on my sheet is six weeks: the incremental sync is 54 person-weeks, sixteen weeks elapsed at my staffing, and that is option A alone."

All-hands call, Tuesday 6 October 2026, 18:30 IST — 15:00 Berlin, 09:00 Toronto and New Jersey, 21:00 Singapore

"We are arguing which box on Devang's diagram is guilty. Nobody in Al Quoz has a diagram. The salesman taps, the screen does nothing, the shop owner turns away. Give him a tick and a queue he can see."

Dhanika Khemka, same call

"Stop quoting 9.4 seconds as the company's number. It is the sum of five phase medians over 1,610 traces, from fourteen phones Sanad picked because those salesmen had complained. It is not a population estimate, and its phase D cannot be set against Exhibit 1 until somebody tells me where the handset starts its clock."

Deepali Kagzi to Devashri Kinariwala, Friday 9 October 2026

Divyesh Khandwala: "A gigabyte of SQLite on a 3 GB phone recomputing 2,14,000 price-list rows. That is the story."

Darshana Khatod: "Berlin's 1.2 seconds was the old model, charged, on wifi. Exhibit 2's 3.1 seconds is a field median on this one. I cannot take either to Sanad."

Engineering channel, Saturday 10 October 2026

8. The options as Devashri sees them

In the form of Exhibit 5 they are a question about where in Figure 1 to spend money. Option A attacks the 2019 design and would let one outlet's order travel alone; it is also the only one that cannot land before the term ends on 17 January. Option B should shorten phases C and D, the 2.4 and 1.9 seconds of Exhibit 2, and leaves phase A alone. Option C attacks phase A, the largest in Exhibit 2 and one Exhibit 1 cannot see. Option D changes nothing in the request path and everything the salesman sees, at the price of a tick before the credit limit is enforced.

Written that way the list invites a reader to pick a point on a line from cheap to structural. Devashri had twice crossed it out and started again. The five-second test has no stated measurement point, and defining it in the renewal letter would change the quarterly credit by ₹12.25 lakh. And she does not know whether Sanad is building a case to leave or to pay less.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Notice is due on Monday 19 October 2026, ninety days before the term ends on 17 January 2027; silence renews the contract on existing terms, including the five-second clause. Sopaan held cash of ₹14.6 crore at 30 September 2026 against a monthly burn of ₹1.9 crore, a runway of 7.7 months from 1 October, with a Series B in diligence. Of thirty-four engineers, eleven can touch the sync path and eight are on the Diwali roster of 4 to 11 November. A Gulf region would take Sanad's data out of the Mumbai footprint Sopaan describes to Indian buyers under the DPDP Act. Credits of ₹49 lakh to ₹61.25 lakh, depending on the reading, are accrued and not invoiced, and Sanad has not said which it will apply.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Walk through Figure 1 for one tap. At each step, name the measurement that would show whether that step is the problem, and which exhibit could produce it.
  2. Exhibit 1 reports 1,166 milliseconds and Exhibit 2 reports 1.9 seconds for the same stretch of path. List every explanation consistent with both, and what would eliminate each.
  3. Exhibit 3 supports both 0.9 per cent and 4.2 per cent. Which denominator belongs in a renewal letter, and what does that imply about what the clause measures?
  4. Exhibit 5's dates assume each option runs alone from 26 October. What would any two together cost in time, people and cash, and which column do you now distrust?
  5. Option D removes the wait but not the latency. When is that an improvement, and when a misrepresentation to the shopkeeper and to Sanad?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Devashri send, what does she tell the board, and which colleague will say afterwards that she was warned?

The office lights had gone to half. Devashri played the clip once more with the sound off, watching the thumb rather than the spinner, unable to decide whether she was looking at a slow server, a loaded phone, a bad road to Mumbai, a screen that said nothing, or a contract that never said where to put the stopwatch. The note still had a title and no first sentence.
case20v1-tech.client.server:
Rozana Mart: The Slow Tap Before Diwali

A decision case on how an app actually answers a tap

1. Opening

At 9:00 on Thursday evening, 15 October 2026, Chaitya Jethwa closed the laptop lid halfway and opened it again. As head of product at Rozana Mart, she had until Monday 19 October to tell the steering committee how the company would spend the eleven days left before the engineering freeze on Monday 26 October. The Diwali sale would open on Monday 2 November. Diwali itself fell on Sunday 8 November.

Two months earlier, during the Independence Day sale, the app had slowed to a crawl. Shoppers tapped "Place order" and watched a spinner. Many gave up. Nobody in the company disagreed that this must not happen again, least of all the chief executive, who had asked for one page and one recommendation. They disagreed, loudly, about where the slowness lived.

2. Company background

Rozana Mart, founded in 2019 in Ahmedabad, delivers groceries and household staples to 140 towns, mostly tier-2 and tier-3, where Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart do not yet reach and where JioMart, BigBasket and DMart Ready compete on price. It had 38 lakh monthly active users and recorded gross merchandise value of ₹1,260 crore in 2025-26. The average basket was ₹640. Customers paid mostly by UPI, with Razorpay processing the payments, and the company stored customer data in a Mumbai cloud region to stay inside the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's expectations.

The company ran its own app on Android and iOS, a web storefront, and a back end hosted in the cloud. Sales were its growth engine: three or four a year, each timed to a festival and each answering the Big Billion Days and Great Indian Festival campaigns that dominate October.

3. The situation

Chaitya had never written code, and in August she had asked an engineer to explain what happens when a shopper taps the button. The answer, sketched in Figure 1, was a chain. The app on the phone, the client, builds a request. It travels over the mobile network to a gateway, which checks who is asking. The gateway hands it to an application server, which applies prices and offers. The server asks the database to check stock and record the order. The reply retraces the same path, and the phone draws the confirmation. Every link adds time, and a slow tap means one link has grown.

Chaya Jhunjhunwala, the data scientist in Toronto, had instrumented each link during the Independence Day weekend. Exhibit 1 shows her median timings for the order call, which ends before the UPI payment screen opens, so Razorpay and NPCI do not appear.

The database accounted for 1,060 of the 1,465 extra milliseconds, or 72 per cent. Exhibit 2 shows what that cost in orders.

The Berlin designer, Carla Jagetia, had watched session recordings and seen shoppers tap the button three and four times, each tap sending another order request to the same struggling database. She wanted the button to disable itself after one tap, a small client-side change, and she wanted a progress message in plain Hindi and Gujarati rather than a bare spinner.

The argument had split along geography. Pune and Bengaluru traded messages most mornings, Chitrangda insisting that "the server fell over" and Charvik replying that the phone was making the server's life harder than it needed to be. Chaitya found that each side was describing something true, and that neither description told her what to buy.

4. The people

  • Chitrangda Jobanputra, vice-president of engineering, Pune. She owns the back end and argues the database is undersized for a festival. She wants budget for a bigger instance and read replicas, copies of the database that serve reading only.
  • Charvik Jajoo, Android lead, Bengaluru. He notes the checkout screen makes seven separate calls when it opens, and wants them merged into two. This means a new app release. He distrusts any plan that depends on a server alone.
  • Chaya Jhunjhunwala, data scientist, Toronto. She is nine and a half hours behind Ahmedabad, so her analysis arrives overnight. She wants a load test before anyone spends a rupee.
  • Carla Jagetia, designer, Berlin, three and a half hours behind until 25 October. She wants shoppers shown honest progress, not a blank spinner.

5. The options

Chaitya reduced the debate to three courses, costed in Exhibit 3. She assumed the freeze could be waived for server-side changes and for the waiting room, but not for an app release. The build-and-release times come from Chitrangda and Charvik. The share of users reached comes from the last app release, which was running on 54 per cent of sale-day sessions seven days after it reached the stores.

Option A attacks the biggest measured delay and reaches everyone at once, but replicas ease reading only; the 370 ms of writing remains. Option B is the cleaner design, yet an app fix only reaches users who update, and it arrives after the sale begins. Option C is cheap and fast, but it tells festival shoppers to wait, at a moment when rivals promise speed.

Chitrangda added one condition: the replicas would sit in the same Mumbai region as the primary database, so no customer data moved elsewhere. Charvik conceded that Option A, unlike his own, did not depend on a customer tapping "Update" in the Play Store, but warned that it would leave the seven calls untouched.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which links of the chain did the sale weekend barely touch, and which did it stress? What does this suggest about where the slowness lives?
  2. Why can a server-side change reach every user on a given day while a client-side change cannot? How does the 54 per cent figure bear on Option B?
  3. In Exhibit 2, what denominator is used for completion, and how would you test Chaitya's ₹16.2 crore projection before relying on it?
  4. Which option would you take to the steering committee on 19 October, and what result on a load test would make you change it?

7. A note for the learner

This topic frames a vague complaint, "the app is slow", as a question about a path. Each tap crosses a client, a network, a server and a database, and each owner can truthfully say their part is fine. The measurement in Exhibit 1 settles the argument: the phone and the network moved by 105 milliseconds together, while the database moved by 1,060. A product manager does not need to tune a query, but must ask which link grew, and whether the fix lives where it can reach users in time.

A well-reasoned answer ranks the options on three tests: does it address the measured cause, can it reach users before 2 November, and what does it leave unsolved?

One defensible path is Option A now, with Option B scheduled for the January release and Option C held in reserve. Option A targets the 1,060 ms database increase (72 per cent of the added delay), but its replicas can remove only the reading part: 720 ms, or 49 per cent, on this assumption. It ships on 23 October, three days before the freeze. If the replicas return reading time to 60 ms (an assumption, from the normal-day database figure), database time falls to 430 ms and the call to 1,345 ms, at August load, still more than twice a normal day. That residual explains why A should not stand alone. Chaitya should ask Chaya for a load test at 2.2 times August traffic by 24 October, and agree in advance with Chitrangda that if the median call exceeds 1,500 ms, about 2.5 times a normal day, the waiting room goes live on 29 October. Option B is right in design, wrong in timing; Carla's one-tap lock can ride along in the January release or an earlier small update. The costs of A and a possible C total ₹31 lakh, against a possible ₹16.2 crore shortfall.
exp20v2-tech.ai.choose:
Choosing the Right AI Build Tool

Delivery & Technology, Technical Fluency: UI-first, code-first, full-stack and agentic tools, and which job each one fits.

1. A nine-week window

On Monday 14 September 2026, Eshwar Pillai, head of product at Eklavya Labs in Pune, opened a spreadsheet he had been avoiding. Eklavya sold fee-and-attendance software to 214 coaching institutes across Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana. The admission season for its largest customers opened on Monday 16 November, exactly 63 days away, and 31 institutes had told Dilip Nambiar, the head of customer success, that they would renew only if parents could see instalment schedules and receive reminders on WhatsApp. Those 31 renewals carried an average annual contract value of ₹1,40,000, or ₹43,40,000 in all. Losing them would hurt badly.

Eshwar had four ways to start. A prompt-to-app builder could produce a working parent dashboard by Friday. Farida Mansuri, the engineering lead, preferred to write the feature herself in the existing codebase with an AI assistant inside her editor. A full-stack generator could create the screens, database and hosting in one pass. And an autonomous coding agent could be given the ticket and left to work overnight.

The decision looked like a question about which tool was best. It was really a question about what kind of job this was, because the four tools give different parties control over different parts of the work. A wrong choice would show up only in early November, when a demo-quality prototype met real fee data, real parents and a payment gateway. This page builds the mental model Eshwar needed.

2. The idea

An AI build tool is software in which a language model, a system trained on very large amounts of text and code to predict what comes next, produces working software on a person’s behalf. The category has four working types, and the distinction between them is the idea this page rests on.

UI-first tools turn a plain-language description or a sketch into a running interface, usually inside a browser, with the plumbing hidden. Code-first tools sit inside a developer’s editor and suggest, explain or rewrite code that the developer still owns and reviews. Full-stack tools generate the whole chain: interface, server logic, database and deployment. Agentic tools accept a goal, break it into steps, read and edit many files, run tests, and loop until they believe the goal is met. An agent, in this sense, is a model allowed to take actions and observe their results rather than only emit text.

The problem these tools addressed was the cost of the first working version. Code completion arrived for ordinary developers around 2021 with GitHub Copilot. Chat assistants followed in 2022 and 2023. Browser-based generators of the kind sold by Vercel (v0), StackBlitz (Bolt) and Lovable appeared from 2023 onward, and editor agents such as Cursor and Claude Code spread in 2024 and 2025. Practitioners converged on a simple test: who holds the pen, and who will hold it in six months? Eshwar could say it in any meeting without sounding glib, because it asks for a name, not a preference.

Figure 1 shows the central trade. Moving right buys speed to a first demonstration but costs you the ability to take the result over later, because you did not make those decisions. Agentic tools sit left of full-stack ones because they usually work inside a codebase a human already owns.

3. How it actually works

Beneath all four types the mechanism is the same: the model receives a prompt plus whatever context the tool gives it, and returns code. The categories differ in three implicit choices that practitioners rarely state.

The first is context, meaning how much of your existing system the model can see. A UI-first tool sees only what it has generated. A code-first tool sees the open file and some neighbours. An agent can search the whole repository, read logs and run commands. The second is the loop: whether a human checks every suggestion, as with code-first tools, or the tool checks itself against tests and error messages, as with agents. The third is the destination: whether the output lands in your repository as ordinary files you can edit, or in the vendor’s hosted environment from which you may be able to export only part of what you need.

Applied to Eklavya, the walk-through is as follows. The parent dashboard needed Eklavya’s fee ledger, which lives in a PostgreSQL database behind an internal service. It needed WhatsApp messages through an approved Business API provider. It needed instalment due dates that obey each institute’s own rules, such as a 5 per cent late fee after a ten-day grace period at some centres only. The ledger needs context a UI-first tool lacks. The late-fee rules need a loop that tests edge cases. And the integration needs a destination inside Eklavya’s own repository, where Farida’s team could review and deploy it.

An implicit step deserves naming: every tool needs a definition of done outside the tool. A model will report success when the screen renders; whether an instalment of ₹12,500 split across three due dates sums back to ₹12,500 only a test can know.

4. A worked example

Eshwar scored the four tool types against five criteria, weighting each by its importance to this particular job. Scores run from 1 (poor fit) to 5 (strong fit). The weights total 100, so a weighted score is the sum of weight times score, divided by 100.

Exhibit 1. Pass one: the real parent-dashboard job. Weighted score = sum of (weight × score) ÷ 100.
CriterionWeightUI-firstCode-firstFull-stackAgentic
Custom logic (late fees, splits)302434
Integration with ledger and WhatsApp251534
Maintainability by Eklavya’s team204332
Speed to first demo155342
Handling of student and fee data102533
Weighted score (260, 400, 315, 320 ÷ 100)1002.604.003.153.20

The sums are shown line by line. For UI-first: 60 + 25 + 80 + 75 + 20 = 260. For code-first: 120 + 125 + 60 + 45 + 50 = 400. For full-stack: 90 + 75 + 60 + 60 + 30 = 315. For agentic: 120 + 100 + 40 + 30 + 30 = 320. Code-first wins because the heaviest criteria, custom logic and integration, together carry 55 of the 100 weight points, and code-first scores 4 and 5 on them.

The scores are judgements, so Eshwar checked them against money. The code-first route was estimated at 120 engineer-hours at ₹1,800 per hour, which is ₹2,16,000, plus three editor licences at ₹1,700 per month for two months, which is ₹10,200, for ₹2,26,200 in all. The UI-first route needed 30 hours (₹54,000) and a platform fee of ₹8,000 per month for two months (₹16,000), a subtotal of ₹70,000. But if it later had to be rebuilt in code, that rebuild was estimated at 90 hours, which is ₹1,62,000, giving ₹2,32,000. The expected cost of the UI-first route is therefore ₹70,000 plus the probability of rebuild times ₹1,62,000. At a 50 per cent chance of rebuild this is ₹1,51,000; at certainty it is ₹2,32,000, which is ₹5,800 more than the code-first route. Break-even sits at a rebuild probability of 1,56,200 ÷ 1,62,000, about 96 per cent. Integration requirements made a rebuild nearly certain, so the cheap-looking route was not cheaper.

Second pass. Eshwar then changed one input: the purpose. Suppose the job were only a throwaway pilot to show five institutes a mock-up before committing. The scores stay the same, but the weights shift to custom logic 15, integration 10, maintainability 15, speed 50 and data 10, still totalling 100.

Exhibit 2. Pass two: a throwaway demonstration. Same scores as Exhibit 1, new weights.
Tool typeSum of weight × scoreWeighted score
UI-first3703.70
Code-first3553.55
Full-stack3503.50
Agentic2602.60

UI-first, which scored last in pass one, now leads, for example 30 + 10 + 60 + 250 + 20 = 370. Nothing about the tools changed; only the job did.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Speed to first demo is not speed to production

The early part of the work is a small fraction of the total. A tool that halves the time to a demo may leave hardening and security review untouched.

Autonomy is not accuracy

An agent that runs for an hour can produce a large change, and a large change takes longer to review than a small one. If review capacity is the bottleneck, the throughput is wasted.

Lock-in lives in the destination

Before using a hosted builder, ask whether the output can be exported as ordinary source code, whether the database is yours, and what happens to your application if the vendor changes its pricing. A cheap platform fee does not offset a forced rewrite.

The tools do not know your rules

No tool knows that one Eklavya institute waives late fees for scholarship students. Writing such rules down as tests is work no tool performs for you.

Data and compliance set a floor

Student and fee records are personal data under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Pasting production records into a tool whose data handling you have not read is a decision, not a convenience.

What the scoring cannot tell you

The weighted scorecard in Exhibit 1 ranks fit; it does not tell you whether the feature deserves building, or whether the scores are right. Before relying on it, ask who set the weights, and whether the answer changes when the weights move by ten points.

6. How it differs by product type and company size

In consumer products, experience quality and scale dominate, so UI-first tools suit concept tests with a few hundred users but not the performance work after. In B2B products like Eklavya’s, integration, permissions and audit trails dominate, so code-first and agentic tools score well. In marketplace products, errors cost real money on both sides, so generated code needs the most review and tests.

A five-person start-up with no codebase has little to integrate with, so full-stack and UI-first tools carry less risk and the prototype may become the product. A company with fifteen years of code and a security team has the opposite problem, so tools that operate within the existing repository dominate; UI-first tools stay useful in a sandbox, with the rule that nothing built there reaches customers.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the prototype as the product. The symptom is a demo that impresses and a launch date that keeps slipping. The misunderstanding is that a working screen implies a working system. The cheapest diagnostic is to make the prototype process one awkward real record, such as a part-paid fee with a waived late charge, in week one.

Choosing by enthusiasm. The symptom is that the tool in use matches the loudest advocate. The misunderstanding is that tools are ranked rather than fitted. The diagnostic is to write the criteria and weights before anyone names a tool.

Starving the review. The symptom is a growing queue of unmerged machine-written changes. The misunderstanding is that generation was the bottleneck. The diagnostic is to compare reviewer-hours per week with changes proposed.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the decision takes one afternoon and produces a short page. It names the job in a sentence, states the weights, scores the options with a reason for each, and records who holds the pen at launch and six months later. It separates the throwaway from the durable, lists the definition of done as testable cases, and names a date on which the choice will be reviewed. The target is a traceable pick that a colleague could challenge line by line.

9. Closing

Eshwar scheduled a review on Friday 25 September. He chose a split. Dilip’s team received a UI-first mock-up for the five pilot institutes within a week. Farida’s engineers built the real feature code-first, with an agent allowed only to draft tests for the late-fee rules, never to merge anything. His reasoning was written on a single slide: the throwaway job and the durable job were different jobs, so they deserved different tools. Seven weeks and three days remained before the season opened, enough for the durable build only because the demo bought customer confidence early. Next to study: AI-assisted building, which this topic builds on, then evaluating AI output, since every route depends on someone judging whether the result is correct.

Two questions to sit with. First, in your own organisation, who will hold the pen six months after a tool-generated feature ships, and do they know it? Second, if you shifted your scoring weights by ten points, which choices would flip, and what does that say about how much you actually know?
case40v1-tech.ai.choose:
Dhaneri Systems: Four Tools, Nine Days, One Signature

Delivery & Technology › Technical Fluency — an ambiguous case for discussion

1. Bani Park, Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday 11 October 2026, Labdhi Thanawala sat at her dining table in Bani Park, Jaipur, the garba drums still going in the lane behind, with a one-page note she had rewritten four times. It was headed AI build tooling: recommendation. The recommendation line was blank.

At nine the next morning she would tell 164 engineers which AI build tool Dhaneri Systems would standardise on. The quotes expire on 31 October; the board meets on Thursday 22 October, and has already approved an envelope of ₹85 lakh. Behind it sat two dates: a manufacturer's new warranty-claims interface, live on 31 January 2027, and a Dubai dealership group's go-live on 1 February 2027, with a delay clause attached.

Four tools had been trialled over nine working days from late September. Her engineering director circulated the scoreboard under the subject line clear winner. Her chief financial officer sent different hours for the same nine days, four days later.

2. Dhaneri Systems, 2015 to 2026

Dhaneri Systems Private Limited was founded in Jaipur in 2015 by Lalji Totla, who had spent eighteen years in his family's Maruti Suzuki dealership in Ajmer. Its product, DealerDesk, runs a dealership end to end: showroom enquiries, vehicle invoicing, Vahan portal paperwork, workshop job cards, spare parts, warranty claims and collections.

At 30 September 2026 Dhaneri served 180 dealer groups operating 1,240 outlets, at annual recurring revenue of ₹96 crore, with 740 staff. Of those, 164 were engineering staff — 96 in Bengaluru, 44 in Pune, 24 in Jaipur — 14 of them quality engineers.

One decision from March 2019 shapes what is possible today. Dealer groups competing in the same city refused to share a database, and that year's largest prospect made single-tenancy a condition. Dhaneri chose one database and one application instance per dealer group, with most business logic written as stored procedures. An internal audit in 2024 put 41 per cent of that logic inside 2,340 of them. The estate now runs to 1.86 million lines across 118 live deployment branches, each feeding between one and six of the 180 instances. Seventeen of the instances sit on hardware in the dealer's own premises, and those 17 groups account for ₹21.8 crore of recurring revenue.

3. The industry around the decision

Indian automobile retail is consolidating and digitising at once: the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations counts single-outlet dealers selling out to multi-brand groups, and every acquirer inherits three or four systems. Maruti Suzuki, Hyundai, Tata Motors, Mahindra, Hero MotoCorp and TVS each publish their own dealer interfaces and change them at will. Ather and Ola Electric brought company-owned stores; Cars24 and Spinny pull the used-vehicle transaction away.

Regulation arrives on a similar rhythm. GST e-invoicing swallowed the vehicle invoice. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 made the dealer fiduciary for the buyer's phone number and identity document and Dhaneri the processor; 42 contracts now carry an India-only residency clause. Channel finance runs under Reserve Bank of India rules and showroom insurance under the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority's.

Dhaneri's global exposure is thin but sharp: one Dubai dealership group, holding three franchises and exporting used vehicles into East Africa, signed in January 2026 for ₹14.4 crore over three years — the largest contract Dhaneri has signed, and its only one outside the rupee.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

On Thursday 9 July 2026 the manufacturer that accounts for 512 of Dhaneri's 1,240 outlets published a replacement warranty-claims interface, to cut over on 31 January 2027. For a workshop, claims are the margin. Dhaneri's claims logic sits in the stored procedures of 2019, and all 118 branches need it.

In August, Labdhi ran an experiment. Three engineers in Pune were given an agentic tool — one that plans, writes across files and runs its own tests — and asked to rebuild the parts-return flow, estimated at nineteen engineer-days. On Friday 14 August they demonstrated it working, six engineer-days in — about two calendar days for the three of them. By the end of August the number was in a board paper.

What has since turned out to be wrong is instructive. The August build ran against a mocked version of the manufacturer's interface, the sandbox credentials not having arrived, and the tests the tool wrote were the tests by which its output was judged. When the sandbox opened in September, integration took eleven further engineer-days and produced 23 defects. Seventeen engineer-days against nineteen estimated is a saving of two, not thirteen. Lalji Totla was still quoting six in October.

The bake-off ran nine working days, Tuesday 22 September to Monday 5 October — Gandhi Jayanti on 2 October not counted — with eight engineers in two squads. Procurement anonymised the four as Vendor U (UI-first, prompt-to-screen), Vendor C (code-first, in the editor), Vendor F (full-stack: application, database and hosting) and Vendor A (agentic). Exhibit 1 is Lipakshi Tolat's scoreboard; Exhibit 2 sets the nine days against the dates that constrain them.

Three things were not visible on 6 October. The tracks were not given the same work: U and F built against a greenfield mock, C and A on a live client fork. “Accepted by QA” meant demonstrated-and-signed-off on the greenfield tracks and merged-to-branch on the other two; Exhibit 4 shows how many reached staging. And on 10 October Linisha Talati found 109 hours in the finance timesheet that Jira had never seen (Exhibit 5). Exhibit 6 draws the consequence.

5. The people

Labdhi Thanawala, Vice-President, Product, Jaipur. Owns the roadmap; no engineering background beyond two years as an analyst. Thinks a discount calendar is forcing the decision. Not saying: the six-day figure in the August board paper was hers.

Lalji Totla, co-founder and Chief Executive, Jaipur. Wants the agentic tool: he saw the demonstration, and migrating 2,340 stored procedures by agent is a Series C story. Not saying: that round needs a clean Dubai go-live.

Lipakshi Tolat, Director of Engineering, Bengaluru. Ran the bake-off; argues for UI-first on 10.67 Jira hours per accepted feature. Her headcount plan promises the gain. Not saying: she chose which tracks got the mock.

Lavneet Thirani, Principal Engineer, Pune. Has kept the stored procedures since 2019 and knows why 40 of them cannot be touched at month-end. Wants code-first. Not saying: that architecture makes him irreplaceable.

Linisha Talati, Chief Financial Officer, Jaipur. Produced Exhibit 5 and the envelope; indifferent between tools, hostile to pricing she cannot forecast. Not saying: the envelope predates every quote.

Liya Tanna, Product Designer, Berlin. Built the UI-first prototypes and logged no Jira time, because designers at Dhaneri never have. Wants the tool out of production. Not saying: she has rebuilt two by hand.

Lavisha Tapadia, Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Owns the Dubai account and the 17 on-premises groups; opposes full-stack on residency grounds. Not saying: their IT director has twice asked for hosting.

Lekhraj Tulsyan, Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Six prospects ask about AI in the first meeting; his commission favours new logos. Not saying: two are also evaluating a competitor he once worked for.

6. Exhibits

The exhibits were produced by four people for four purposes, and they do not agree.

7. Voices

Engineering review, Bengaluru, 6 October

“Under eleven hours a feature, against fifteen for the editor tool. I have run this organisation's estimates for six years and never seen a gap like that. We should sign on Monday.” — Lipakshi Tolat

Reply in the same thread, Pune

“Against a mock. My track lost two days to a column used by a stored procedure nobody has read since 2021. Give U the fork and the live interface and we can compare. Until then this compares two different jobs.” — Lavneet Thirani

Chat, 7 October, 7.00 pm IST / 3.30 pm Berlin

“Forty-eight hours of this work are mine, and they are not in your system because nobody gave designers one. The screens were fast because I had already drawn them. The hours you are calling the tool's speed are my hours.” — Liya Tanna

Leadership call, 9 October, 7.00 pm IST / 9.30 am New Jersey

“We cannot be the company that slips Dubai. Thirty-five lakh a month, so four crore twenty if we lose the year.” — Lekhraj Tulsyan

“Thirty-five lakh per completed month of delay, capped at six months. A full year's slip costs two crore ten, not four crore twenty. I would rather argue about the two crore we can actually lose.” — Linisha Talati

Same call, ten minutes later

“Six engineer-days for nineteen days of work. I watched it happen.” — Lalji Totla

“Six engineer-days to the demonstration. Eleven more to integrate, and twenty-three defects. Seventeen against nineteen.” — Labdhi Thanawala

“Then we learned how to do it properly, and the next one will be six.” — Lalji Totla

Email, 10 October, 9.10 am IST

“He will ask you about a hosted option. For 42 contracts the answer has to be no, and seventeen groups have the box in their own server room.” — Lavisha Tapadia

8. The options as Labdhi sees them on Sunday night

Standardise on code-first (Vendor C). ₹57.93 lakh, inside the envelope, first on the finance measure at 16.50 hours, and the fewest staging defects per promoted feature of the three tracks that got that far, 9 on 8. It asks the engineers to change least, which is also the case against it: nothing in it addresses 2,340 stored procedures by 31 January.

Standardise on UI-first (Vendor U). The cheapest at ₹46.02 lakh, and first on the measure the engineering director circulated. All of that advantage rests on a greenfield mock and on 62 unlogged hours of design and analyst work the scoreboard did not count, 48 of the 109 being Liya Tanna's. She wants the tool out of production.

Buy full-stack (Vendor F). The Dubai module is the one genuinely new piece of work, and this is the tool built for that. At ₹88.41 lakh it is ₹3.41 lakh over the envelope, a rounding error against a ₹14.4 crore contract. It never reached staging, and its runtime collides with 42 residency clauses and the hardware in 17 server rooms.

Bet on agentic (Vendor A). The only option that treats the migration as a volume problem rather than a staffing one, and the only one the chief executive has endorsed publicly. It costs ₹125.36 lakh, 2.7 times the cheapest option and ₹40.36 lakh over the envelope; it is highest on both hour measures; it produced 27 of the 47 staging defects on 6 of the 19 promoted features; and its August evidence was a mock.

Labdhi had written the four as one choice because procurement's note was one choice and the discount lapses on a single date. At midnight she read the chat from Berlin and the reply from Pune again, and then Exhibit 4, where fourteen quality engineers had absorbed 47 staging defects from 19 features in nine days. She could not see which of the four paragraphs in front of her changed that row.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money. ₹85 lakh approved for the year against the quotes in Exhibit 3, and metered agent charges are the line Linisha Talati will not forecast. Engineering payroll runs to roughly ₹36.9 crore a year, against which even the dearest tool is 3.4 per cent — Lalji Totla's favourite argument.

People. 164 engineering staff, 14 of them quality engineers, and a hiring freeze until the Series C. Lavneet Thirani is a single point of failure.

Time. No deployment to any outlet between 19 October and 13 November, the festive peak. Between the freeze lifting on 16 November and the handover on Friday 29 January lie 55 weekdays, 51 after Dhaneri's declared holidays.

Regulation and contract. India-only residency in 42 contracts under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; on-premises deployment for 17 dealer groups worth ₹21.8 crore of recurring revenue; the manufacturer's cut-over on 31 January 2027 for 512 outlets; the Dubai go-live on 1 February 2027, at ₹35 lakh per completed month of delay capped at ₹2.10 crore; quotes expiring 31 October.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 measure, and what would make 10.67 hours per accepted feature a fair description of Vendor U?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 5 cover the same nine days and rank the tools differently. Which goes to the board, and what do you say about the other one?
  3. Vendor F's row in Exhibit 4 is empty. Is an untested option safer or more dangerous than a tested one that performed badly, and how should that be priced?
  4. Dhaneri has two jobs of different shapes: a bilingual greenfield product, and a migration of 2,340 stored procedures. Does “which tool should we standardise on” survive that, and what replaces it?
  5. Lalji Totla's six-day figure is wrong and he keeps using it. What should a vice-president of product do about a chief executive's number already in a board paper?
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday 12 October and 164 engineers are waiting. What does Labdhi say, what does she commit to before the quotes lapse, and how will she know in ninety days whether she was right?

The drums stopped after midnight. Labdhi read the procurement line again — one tool, one seat count, one signature — and began a fifth version under a new heading: what we are actually buying. By half past one she had three paragraphs and no recommendation line, and the Bengaluru squad leads were already awake, waiting to be told.
case20v1-tech.ai.choose:
Choosing the Right AI Build Tool at Chandlo Retail Systems

A decision case in Delivery & Technology: Technical Fluency

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Kinjal Sarda arrived at Chandlo Retail Systems' Ahmedabad office with a decision due by Friday. As Head of Product, she had to name the AI build tool her four-engineer squad would use for the next twelve working days. The squad was to build a Scheme Claim Tracker, and the first pilot was promised to three anchor distributors for Monday 16 November, immediately after the Diwali closure.

Four tools had been tried the previous Wednesday. Each had impressed someone. None had been tried against the live system, and her colleagues in four cities disagreed about which to trust. She would announce the choice on a Friday call at 7:30 pm IST, which was 4:00 pm in Berlin and 10:00 am in New Jersey.

2. Company background

Chandlo, founded in Ahmedabad in 2016, sells an order-taking, billing and collections app to FMCG distributors, the stockists who supply kirana stores in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. At 30 September 2026 it had 1,850 distributor clients, annual recurring revenue of ₹38 crore, and 212 staff. Fifty-eight were engineers, 34 in Ahmedabad and 24 in Pune.

Its rivals are mixed. Marketplaces such as Udaan and Jumbotail pull retailers towards their own ordering apps. Tally and Zoho Books own the accounting desk, and ONDC promises open retail networks that distributors are only beginning to test. Chandlo competes by knowing the distributor's day: the van route, the cheque that bounces, the monthly argument with a manufacturer.

3. The situation

That argument was the origin of the new product. Manufacturers such as Amul, Parle Agro and Asian Paints fund trade schemes, and distributors pass the discount to retailers and then claim it back. Claims fail when an invoice, a GST credit note and a scheme circular do not match. Chandlo audited 40 distributors' September 2026 claims: ₹3.60 crore was filed and ₹41 lakh rejected, a loss of 11.4 per cent of claim value. A tracker that matched documents before filing could recover part of that. The data is also sensitive, since it carries retailer names and GST invoice details, which the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act obliges Chandlo to handle with care. Chandlo planned to charge ₹1.2 lakh per distributor per year, and 46 distributors had asked to join the pilot, a run-rate of ₹55.2 lakh if all signed.

On Wednesday 14 October, Kirit Shroff, Vice President of Engineering, had four engineers each take one tool category and attempt the same brief: a claim-status screen with three filters and a CSV export, built over an anonymised copy of production data. The results are in Exhibit 1. The UI-first tool produced a handsome screen in thirty minutes, but it had invented its own data layer and passed 6 of the 38 existing tests. The full-stack tool also built its own database and hosting, and Chandlo's large-client contracts require data to stay in AWS Mumbai. The code-first assistant, working inside the existing repository, was slowest to a first screen but passed 31 tests. The agentic tool planned the work, edited several files and ran the tests on its own; it passed 29 but touched two files outside the brief.

Kinjal also noticed what the trial could not show. Exhibit 1 measured one screen, whereas the tracker's hard part is matching claims to invoices and credit notes, where an error costs a distributor real rupees.

The weeks ahead are short. Exhibit 3 shows that the squad has twelve working days, because the office closes from Saturday 7 to Wednesday 11 November. Exhibit 2 turns the trial into estimates. Only two senior engineers, who sit outside the four-person squad, may approve code bound for production, and each can give 40 per cent of twelve days to review. That is 2 × 12 × 0.4 = 9.6 review days, against a build capacity of 4 × 12 = 48 engineer-days.

4. The people

Kirit Shroff, Vice President of Engineering in Ahmedabad, owns the codebase and its security. He wants nothing in production that his seniors cannot explain line by line.

Kunjal Saraiya, a product designer in Berlin, who is 3.5 hours behind IST until 25 October and 4.5 hours after, wants to test a clickable version with distributors within days. She favours the UI-first tool, which let her change layouts herself.

Kritesh Somani, head of sales in New Jersey, made the promise to the three anchors. He saw the agentic tool's demo and wants the fastest route to something he can show.

Kavan Sutaria, customer-success lead in Singapore, will handle the calls from distributors. A wrong claim amount, he warns, becomes a dispute with a manufacturer within a day, and it lands on his team.

5. The options

Option 1: UI-first. Build the tracker in the interface tool and have engineers connect it to the real system. Exhibit 1 shows the fastest first screen, and Kunjal could refine it herself. But Exhibit 2 puts its senior review at 13 days against 9.6 available, so the plan cannot be approved in time without dropping the review.

Option 2: Code-first. The four engineers work in the existing repository, each with an AI assistant suggesting and editing code under their eye. It needs 25 engineer-days and 5 review days, and costs ₹3.15 lakh all-in. The cost is that engineers type and think more than with the other tools, and the screens will look plainer.

Option 3: Agentic. Hand whole work packages to an agent that plans, edits and tests. It needs the fewest engineer-days, 22, but costs ₹3.52 lakh all-in, and its 9 review days leave 0.6 of a day spare. One late defect would break the schedule, and the two senior engineers would be reviewing code that nobody on the squad wrote.

The full-stack category was set aside, because Chandlo's contracts rule it out.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the job here: a demonstration, a pilot, or a production system? How does each answer change the right tool category?
  2. Which constraint in Exhibits 1 to 3 binds first: engineer-days, review capacity or data location? Why does it matter more than tool cost?
  3. Kritesh, Kunjal and Kavan each want something different from the tool. What is each really optimising, and what would you say to each of them?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what evidence would make you change your mind during the first week?

7. A note for the learner

The topic frames the choice as a matching problem, not a ranking. UI-first tools suit exploring an idea, code-first tools suit changing a system that exists, full-stack tools suit a new self-contained app, and agentic tools suit well-specified work that is easy to check. Asking which tool is best gets nowhere. The useful question is what this job is and which tool fits it.

Here the job is a pilot inside a live product, using client data that must stay in Mumbai, with review as the scarce resource. The cost spread across the options is ₹0.45 lakh, against ₹55.2 lakh of annual run-rate if all 46 sign at ₹1.2 lakh each, so cost should not decide it. Only Options 2 and 3 fit within review capacity.

One defensible path is Option 2 for the build, with 4.6 review days spare for the surprises. Kunjal builds a one-day UI-first prototype herself on 26 October, to be thrown away after distributor testing, so her need is met without touching the repository. The agentic tool can later take narrow, checkable jobs such as writing tests, once the squad has seen how it behaves on Chandlo's code. Kritesh gets a demo from the prototype, and Kavan gets a tracker whose figures a senior engineer has checked.

Kinjal should also tell the squad what would change her mind: if by the end of the first week the code-first squad has missed its pace, she can shift narrow work to the agentic tool while review stays within capacity. Other answers are defensible if they explain how review capacity is protected. An answer that picks the tool with the best demo and does not mention the 9.6 days is not.
exp40v2-tech.ai.choose:
Choosing the Right AI Build Tool

Delivery & Technology › Technical Fluency. UI-first, code-first, full-stack and agentic tools — and the arithmetic that decides between them.

1. Two decisions, two days apart

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Malati Vengurlekar, chief product officer of Nupur Diagnostics Network, sat in the company’s Pune office with three build requests and one engineering team of nine. Nupur was a consumer marketplace: a customer booked a blood test on the app, a phlebotomist from one of 412 partner laboratories collected the sample at home, and the report returned through Nupur. In the twelve months to 31 August 2026 the app was installed 8,40,000 times, and 1,00,800 of those, or 12.0 per cent, produced a first booked test.

Exhibit 1. Nupur Diagnostics Network, twelve months to 31 August 2026. Each rate is measured against the stage above it; the last column restates it against installs.

The three requests were unrelated in everything but timing. Marketing wanted campaign and offer pages for the Diwali health-check push, which opened on Monday 2 November, 55 days away, and ran twenty-one days to Sunday 22 November. Clinical operations wanted a report explainer in the app, turning a lipid panel into plain Marathi and English. Partner operations wanted a portal for the 412 laboratories, coordinated until then over WhatsApp and email by six staff. Nihar Pattanaik, the principal engineer, observed that the team could build one well and all three badly.

Two days later, on Thursday 10 September, Osheen Thakkar faced a narrower decision in Chennai. Munim Works, where she was vice-president of product, sold receivables-reconciliation software to 63 mid-market manufacturers at an average annual contract value of ₹9,40,000, for annual recurring revenue of ₹592.20 lakh. Some 2,74,000 invoice lines a month passed through Munim’s matching engine, and 4.2 per cent of them — 11,508 lines — fell out as exceptions a clerk resolved by hand at about six minutes each, or 1,150.8 clerk-hours a month across the base. Eleven customers, whose contracts totalled ₹115.50 lakh of ₹592.20 lakh, or 19.5 per cent, wanted an exception console: a screen that proposed matches between bank credits and GST e-invoices and recorded the human decision.

Osheen had the same four-way choice as Malati, and both had been told the answer was obvious by somebody confident. The choice turns not on which tool is better but on arithmetic most teams never perform: the cost of the twenty-fourth change, not the first.

2. The idea, and what the schools actually disagree about

An AI build tool is software in which a large language model — trained to predict text and code — produces working software on a person’s behalf. Four classes have settled out. UI-first tools turn a description or sketch into a running interface and hide the plumbing. Code-first tools sit in an engineer’s editor and propose code the engineer still owns and merges. Full-stack tools generate interface, server, database and deployment in one pass. Agentic tools take a goal, read and edit many files, run tests and loop until they judge it met.

The class boundaries are not about model quality. They turn on three structural questions: how much of your system the tool can see (its context), who closes the correctness loop, and where the output lands — your repository, as ordinary files, or the vendor’s runtime.

None of this is new as an ambition. The computer-aided software engineering tools of the late 1980s promised generated systems from diagrams and foundered on what practitioners then called the round-trip problem: once a human edited the generated code, diagram and code diverged and the tool could no longer regenerate. Rapid application development, visual web editors from 1997, framework scaffolding and the low-code platforms that followed each rediscovered that boundary. Statistical code completion reached ordinary developers in 2021, chat assistants in 2022 and 2023, browser-based generators from 2023, editor-resident agents through 2024 and 2025. What changed was fluency, not the round-trip problem — which is why the 1980s failure mode still bites.

Three schools give genuinely different advice. What each will and will not sign:

The substrate school signs this: a tool whose output you cannot read as ordinary source files in your own repository is acceptable only for work you are willing to discard. It will not sign that hosted builders are unfit for production; plenty of internal tools run in a vendor’s runtime for years.

The amendment-economics school, to which this page is sympathetic, signs: choose the tool that minimises the cost of the twenty-fourth change, not the first. It will not sign that the first version’s cost is irrelevant, since the first version is often what buys permission to attempt the next twenty-three.

The learning-rate school signs: until you know what to build, the only cost that matters is the cost of being wrong about the requirement. It will not sign that prototypes should be built with production tooling; making the throwaway durable is the commonest way to waste a quarter.

3. Mechanics: the amendment curve, worked

Expert practice reduces to drawing two cost lines and finding where they cross. Define an amendment precisely: a change that alters behaviour visible to a user or an integration. Copy edits are not amendments; a new tax rule, a new permission, a new field in a payload are.

For a route with first-version cost a₀ and marginal cost a₁ per amendment, total cost after n amendments is a₀ + a₁n. Two routes cross at n* = (b₀ − a₀) ÷ (a₁ − b₁), and the crossover runs in the expected direction only when the cheap-to-start route is also the expensive-to-amend one.

Osheen costed her console four ways over twenty-four months, assuming three substantive amendments a quarter, so twenty-four in all: GST schema revisions, two bank statement formats, per-customer tolerance rules. Munim’s blended cost was ₹1,20,000 an engineer-week. Migration — abandoning the route and rebuilding in Munim’s own stack — was ₹22.00 lakh in every case; only its probability differed.

Exhibit 2. Munim Works console, cost by route over twenty-four months and 24 amendments. Weeks per amendment include review. Labour = total weeks × ₹1.20 lakh; expected migration = probability × ₹22.00 lakh; the last column sums the three money columns.

UI-first builder1.81.1028.233.845.280.7015.4054.52
Code-first assistant7.00.5520.224.242.880.051.1028.22

UI-first reaches a working console in 1.8 weeks against 7.0 for code-first, an advantage of five weeks that in September looked decisive. But it carries 1.10 engineer-weeks per amendment against 0.55, because each change to the matching rules must be expressed through the builder’s abstractions rather than in code, and cannot be unit-tested in the usual way. Over twenty-four amendments that is 26.4 engineer-weeks against 13.2.

Set migration aside and take labour plus fees. The UI-first line is ₹7.44 lakh + ₹1.32 lakh per amendment, the code-first line ₹11.28 lakh + ₹0.66 lakh. They cross at n* = 3.84 ÷ 0.66 = 5.82 amendments, at ₹15.12 lakh each. Below six amendments the builder is cheaper; above it code-first wins, the gap widening by ₹66,000 per amendment. At the planned twenty-four it is ₹39.12 lakh against ₹27.12 lakh.

Restore migration risk and the picture does not merely shift — it loses its crossover. Expected migration of ₹15.40 lakh on the UI-first line and ₹1.10 lakh on the code-first line raises the intercepts to ₹22.84 lakh and ₹12.38 lakh. The cheap-to-start route now begins higher and rises faster, so no amendment count exists at which it wins. The second-order effect matters more than the first: migration probability is itself a function of how many amendments you expect, each one another chance to find something the builder cannot express.

Two implicit steps deserve naming: estimating n by counting amendments to the nearest comparable surface, and holding a definition of done outside the tool. A model reports success when the screen renders; only a test knows whether an instalment of ₹12,500 split three ways sums back to ₹12,500.

4. When the arithmetic applies, and when it misleads

The model rests on three claims, each testable and each worth applying to both protagonists.

Claim one: the amendment count is knowable in advance to within a factor of two. True at Munim, where the comparable surface, the existing matching engine, had taken 24 substantive changes in the preceding twenty-four months — three a quarter, the rate Osheen carried forward. False for Nupur’s report explainer: nobody knew whether clinical operations wanted two test panels explained or forty.

Claim two: the per-amendment cost ratio is stable across the surface. Here the model earns its keep by reversing. Amendments to Nupur’s Diwali campaign pages are copy, layout and offer mechanics — what UI-first tools are good at. Malati estimated 0.4 weeks to a first version and 0.06 per amendment with a builder, against 1.6 and 0.22 in code, with marketing expecting about 36 amendments. Including, over twenty-four months, a ₹22,000-a-month builder fee and ₹12,000 a month of editor seats, the builder line is ₹5.76 lakh + ₹0.072 lakh per amendment and the code line ₹4.80 lakh + ₹0.264 lakh. Here the crossover runs the other way: below five amendments the platform fee dominates and code is cheaper, above five the builder is, and at 36 amendments the builder costs ₹8.35 lakh against ₹14.30 lakh — a saving of ₹5.95 lakh. Same tools, same company, opposite answer, because the slope ratio flipped.

Claim three: migration cost is bounded and estimable. True for the campaign pages, a surface twenty-one days old whose disposal costs nothing but the fee. Dangerously false where the generated system becomes the system of record. The arithmetic actively misleads in two situations: when failure is irreversible — a wrong lipid-panel explanation is not a cost but a clinical event, and no crossover count speaks to it — and when the amendment is a discovery rather than a change, because a team still learning what its product is belongs with the learning-rate school.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

Nupur’s marketplace shows the two-sided problem. The consumer booking flow and the partner-lab slot inventory share one contract; when an agent was allowed, in a trial, to “make slot selection faster”, it quietly changed how a half-hour slot was represented, which would have overbooked the labs. Two-sided products hide their couplings in the data model, where UI-first tools cannot see them and agents only if tests say so.

Munim shows the regulated case. Its console touches GST e-invoice data and, for some customers, bank statements fetched under the Reserve Bank of India’s account-aggregator framework. Two constraints follow that no tool relaxes: personal data in those records falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, so production records cannot be pasted into a tool whose data handling nobody has read; and an auditor will ask who authorised a rule change. A route that cannot produce an attributable diff for every behavioural change is unauditable.

Hardware is the sharpest edge. Nabh Industries, a Nashik maker of cold-chain monitors, has 7,500 units in the field; its chief technology officer, Omkar Deshbandhu, notes that an over-the-air firmware update fails on about 0.8 per cent of them, or 60 devices, each needing a technician visit at roughly ₹2,200 — ₹1.32 lakh per release. Generation speed is worthless when cadence is set by truck rolls. Nabh uses agentic tools freely on its dashboard and never below the driver layer.

At the organisational seam the honest account differs from the stated one. Mature companies say they have a tool policy; what they have is a permission structure — hosted builders in a sandbox with synthetic data, agents allowed to open changes but never to merge, a named human accountable for each surface. Ask three engineers which surfaces it forbids: if the answers differ, you have theatre. Munim’s head of risk, Neerja Khilnani, wrote the rule that mattered in one line: any surface that writes to the ledger is code-first, whatever drafted it.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

The slope matters more than the intercept. The tell is a team quoting time-to-first-demo and nothing else. Faster is not better, because the intercept is paid once and the slope twenty-four times; at Munim the slope difference alone was 13.2 engineer-weeks, or ₹15.84 lakh. The corollary: aggressive tools where undo is cheap, conservative ones where it is not, never one tool for both the campaign page and the payout engine.

Autonomy is not accuracy, and throughput is not progress. The tell is a growing queue of unmerged machine-written changes. More generation against fixed review capacity raises inventory, not output. Measure reviewer-hours per week before lines per day.

The migration probability is endogenous. Novices treat it as a fixed risk percentage; it is a function of your roadmap, since the more amendments you plan, the likelier one is inexpressible in the tool. Read the next four quarters, then set it.

Lock-in lives in the data, not the code. The question is rarely “can I export the source?” but “where does the authoritative data sit, and can I move it with its history?” A surface rebuildable in a week is not locked in even if the vendor keeps the code.

The round-trip problem never left. The sign is a hand-edited generated file: once it exists, regeneration becomes destructive and the speed advantage dies quietly. Experts ask what happens to a human edit on the next generation.

Agents are context-acquisition machines first. Their advantage over code-first assistants is not autonomy but the ability to read a whole repository, run the suite and read the failure. In a codebase with no tests an agent loses most of its edge, which is why the first agentic task there should be writing tests, not features.

The tool cannot know your rules. None of them knows that two of Munim’s customers treat a 1.5 per cent short payment as settled. Writing such rules as executable cases is irreducible product work; a team that skips it has not saved time, only moved the cost into production.

Who reviews is a staffing decision disguised as a tooling one. The tell is a tool chosen by an engineer and reviewed by nobody with domain knowledge. Munim’s console depended for correctness on a reconciliation specialist reading the proposed match logic, not on the model that wrote it.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products surfaces are numerous, short-lived and reversible, so UI-first tools win more often than engineers expect: Nupur’s campaign arithmetic is the general case. In B2B and enterprise, integration, permissions and audit dominate, code-first and agentic routes win on amendment cost, and the binding constraint is often the customer’s security questionnaire. In platforms and marketplaces, errors reach parties who never consented to the experiment, which raises the review requirement more than it changes the tool. In hardware, cadence caps the value of generation speed. In AI-native products correctness is statistical, so the constraint shifts from build tooling to evaluation infrastructure; a team without evals gains little from any of the four.

By stage the difference is real at the extremes and overstated in the middle. A five-person company with no codebase has nothing to integrate with, so full-stack and UI-first routes carry little migration risk and the prototype may become the product. Fifteen years of code and a security review give the opposite arithmetic. Between those poles — where both Nupur and Munim sit — stage explains far less than surface does, and teams arguing about stage are avoiding the harder work of classifying surfaces.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Munim’s console. Osheen took the code-first route at ₹28.22 lakh over twenty-four months, against ₹115.50 lakh of contracts asking for it — plus one piece of the UI-first route: a clickable version built in two days and shown to four customers in the week of 21 September, which changed the layout before any production code existed.

Nupur’s partner portal. Malati chose the full-stack generator here — the route that loses in Exhibit 2 — and was right to. The portal was greenfield, served 412 known users rather than the public, and replaced six operations staff at ₹38,000 a month, or ₹27.36 lakh a year, with three. The build was 3.0 engineer-weeks, or ₹3.60 lakh; hosting ran ₹28,000 a month, ₹3.36 lakh a year, against a saving of ₹13.68 lakh a year. The annual saving net of hosting is ₹10.32 lakh, so the build pays back in 4.2 months; net of the one-off build too, the first year returns ₹6.72 lakh.

Omkara Field Services, and what failure costs. The Hyderabad maker of HVAC field-service software gave an agentic tool its scheduling and payout engine in February 2026. In eleven days the agent produced 23,800 lines across 214 files. Nirupama Chakraborty, the product lead, had two engineers reviewing eighteen hours a week each, 36 reviewer-hours in all; at the observed rate of 180 lines an hour the change needed 132.2 hours, or 3.67 weeks of pure review. Under pressure to ship, 141 of the 214 files, or 65.9 per cent, were merged unreviewed. The engine applied an overtime multiplier to the wrong base.

Exhibit 3. Omkara Field Services, cost of the February–March 2026 episode. March payouts affected: 1,180 of 3,460, or 34.1 per cent, at an average of ₹310.
