At a 99.9 per cent request-based objective over a 30-day month, the budget was 0.1 per cent of 4,32,00,000 requests: 43,200 permitted failures. September used 32,868, or 76.1 per cent. For Prabhat alone it is 1,296 against 4,140: 319 per cent, overspent 3.2 times. One number said the quarter was fine; the other that a customer had been failed.

Sensitivity of the aggregate to one tenant is simply si. Prabhat carried 3.0 per cent of traffic, so moving the platform figure one point needed Prabhat's rate to move 33.3 points. Pranali's rule — above 2 per cent over two consecutive five-minute windows — could not see Prabhat unless it failed two-thirds of its requests. The broken path ran 10 failures a minute: against 1,000 platform requests a minute that is 1.0 per cent, 1.07 with background; against Prabhat's 30 it is 33.3 per cent. At a 0.1 per cent budget rate the platform burned at 10.7× and Prabhat at 334×, against the standard 14.4× — the rate at which an hour, a 720th of a month, spends 2 per cent of budget.

Two steps are usually left implicit. The first: the window must scale inversely with traffic. At 1,000 requests a minute split as above, a five-minute window holds 2,000 requests for the largest chain, 150 for Prabhat, about 111 for a mid-size group and 19.4 for a single-site hospital. One error trips a 2 per cent threshold on 19.4 requests; a 10-error gate needs 10 of the 19.4, or 51.4 per cent, to fail first. The window is wrong, not the threshold: at sixty minutes it holds about 233 requests, where 10 errors is 4.3 per cent.

The second: rules multiply the chances of being wrong. Thirty tenants on five-minute windows give 288 windows a day each, 8,640 a month, 2,59,200 across the estate; at one chance in a thousand of a spurious breach per window that is 259 false pages a month. Two consecutive breaching windows cut the expectation to 0.001² × 2,59,200, about 0.26 a month, for five extra minutes of detection. Hence "for N minutes", N derived.

4. The conditions, stated so they can be tested

C1: the fault's signature is emitted at the grain at which the fault occurs. Pranali failed this cheaply: the tenant identifier was on every request, absent from every metric label. Mastul failed it irreparably — the connector-lock faults behind 46,494 of September's failures were invisible because the only sensor watching the lock was the controller that had failed.

C2: a human can act inside the time the alert buys. Pranali's repair took 38 minutes after detection, so cutting MTTD from 276 minutes to 8 cuts MTTR from 314 to 46 — 85.4 per cent. Mastul's median dispatch-to-repair is 660 minutes; cutting detection from 95 to 7 moves MTTR from 755 to 667, or 11.7 per cent. Nearly rational for one, nearly irrational for the other.

C3: the telemetry costs less than the loss it removes. Mastul's failed sessions, at 9.4 kWh and ₹18.50 per kWh, are worth ₹173.90 each: ₹1.97 crore gross across 1,13,400. Since roughly 60 per cent of drivers retry successfully within the hour, true lost revenue is 40 per cent of that, ₹78.88 lakh in September. The ₹29.29 lakh bill is 37.1 per cent of it, so the programme must remove more than 37 per cent of failures to pay for itself.

5. Hard edges: hardware, two sides, regulation, models and seams

When the observation channel shares a failure domain with the thing observed. Each Mastul site backhauls charging transactions and telemetry over one 4G router. Volume is trivial — 4,200 chargers at 1.4 MB a day is 176.4 GB a month, about ₹1,411 of SIM data at ₹8 a gigabyte. Correlation is the problem: the 28,350 network-class failures are the events the site cannot report. The answer was buffering on the charger plus an independent channel, the driver's phone. A signal is evidence only if it survives what it reports.

Two-sided products hold two incompatible definitions of working. One Mumbai mall site with 8 connectors recorded 2,765 unavailable connector-minutes out of 8 × 43,200 = 3,45,600: connector availability 99.20 per cent. In the same 30-day window it took 2,400 session attempts and failed 336: session success 86.0 per cent. The host's contract pays on the first, the driver lives the second, and the gap is structural — a connector can stand available and still refuse a vehicle.

Regulation turns logging into a liability. Pranali's most useful logs hold patient identifiers, which India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 makes expensive to keep searchable for years. Its compromise is where regulated teams converge: hash the identifier with a per-tenant salt before it leaves the service, so engineers count by patient without reading one. That keeps the cardinality and kills the readability that is the breach.

Organisational seams absorb the evidence. September's 18,144 payment-class failures reached the payments team's dashboard as 4,536, exactly a quarter, because the gateway in front counted the rest as client errors and dropped them. Each dashboard was accurate about its own scope. The missing 13,608 lived between two accurate dashboards, and such gaps are found only across the seam.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A device's self-report is not evidence about that device. The tell is an uptime figure sourced from the component it describes. Five in six of Mastul's charger-class failures — 38,745 of the 46,494, some 83 per cent — happened while the charger's status notification read "Available". The fix is a different sensor: delivered energy, from the revenue-grade meter, is independent of it.

Partially missing data is worse than bad data. Most teams eventually alert on a metric that stops arriving. Fewer catch the subtler case: when one dimension stops reporting — a firmware cohort, an app version, a region — the aggregate improves, the worst slice having left the denominator. The tell is an indicator improving after a deployment.

Small cohorts are invisible to percentiles by construction. Each of Pranali's single-site hospitals carries 0.39 per cent of platform traffic. Since 0.39 is below 1, every request from it could hang without moving the platform p99; it surfaces only at p99.9, 0.39 exceeding 0.1. Comparing percentiles across windows is the same error: a 7-day p95 and a 30-day p95 differ.

Burn rate is the grown-up threshold, and inherits the grain problem. "Consuming budget 14.4 times faster than sustainable" self-calibrates across volumes but does not fix the denominator. Pranali's platform burn rate of 10.7× was genuinely below 14.4; the same event per tenant was 334×. The tell is a burn-rate alert on an aggregate budget.

Cardinality is a product decision with a visible price. Mastul's metrics line was 2,40,000 active series at ₹1.29 each a month, ₹3.10 lakh. One session-outcome metric labelled by site, outcome and manufacturer is 1,050 × 6 × 14 = 88,200 series. Add firmware version, nine values, and it becomes 7,93,800 — 7,05,600 more series at ₹9.10 lakh a month, taking that line to ₹12.20 lakh and the bill from ₹29.29 lakh to ₹38.39 lakh, up 31.1 per cent. The tell is a request for "a breakdown by firmware" from someone who thinks it is free.

Sampling should be decided after the outcome is known. Mastul traced every API request at ₹4.72 lakh a month. Head sampling at 5 per cent cuts that to ₹0.24 lakh but is useless for attribution: a fault affecting one session in 2,000 yields 630 instances a month, of which 5 per cent is about 31 traces — across 14 manufacturers and 9 firmware versions, a quarter of a trace per cell. Tail sampling, keeping every failure and 1 per cent of successes, retains 1,24,866 of 12,60,000 at ₹0.47 lakh.

You can only observe what you deployed, which makes the version label the most valuable one you own. Instrumentation ships in the same pipeline as the code, so the newest and least-understood service is always the least instrumented. The tell is an incident whose first question — which build is this? — has no dashboard answer. Much of Pranali's 276 minutes went there.

The on-call human is a component with a measurable failure rate. Over April 2026 Mastul's rotation of six took 412 pages, of which 61 led to an action: precision 14.8 per cent, about 96 in an on-call week, 14 of them real. Below roughly a quarter precision, recall means nothing, since pages are closed unread. The tell is not complaint — people stop complaining — but a falling time-to-acknowledge and a rising share closed "no action".

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the dominant unanticipated dimension is the client — app version, device, network — so server telemetry is blind to a fault on one Android build. In B2B and enterprise products it is the tenant, since contract, renewal and escalation are per tenant. In platforms and marketplaces two indicators are needed, one per side: Mastul's 99.20 per cent connector availability and 86.0 per cent session success are a tension, not a contradiction. In hardware the constraints are sensor independence and the repair tail; in AI products failure is silent, so the indicator must be an outcome against ground truth arriving later.

Two claimed differences are not real. Regulated industries need differently shaped telemetry — hashed, retention-bounded, access-logged — not more. And consumer products need no lower latency than enterprise: Pranali's clinicians abandon a screen as fast as any shopper.

Stage changes the binding constraint, not the principle. Below about twenty engineers it is attention, and the answer to "should we add per-tenant objectives" is almost always no. From twenty to two hundred it is consistency, when a platform team starts to pay. Above that, cost: Mastul's ₹3.51 crore a year is 1.47 per cent of annualised energy revenue.

8. Three worked cases

Pranali's tenant-grain retrofit. Replay 8 September against a per-tenant rule: above 2 per cent for two consecutive five-minute windows, minimum 10 errors. The window opening at 11:50 holds three fault-minutes — 30 failures in 150 requests, 20 per cent; the next, to 12:00, 50 in 150, 33.3 per cent. The rule fires at 12:00, eight minutes after onset rather than 276. Holding repair at 38 minutes, restoration comes at 12:38: 460 failures instead of 3,140, Prabhat closing at 1,460 errors against a 1,296 budget.

Mastul's change of indicator. On 1 May 2026 Mastul replaced charge-point status with delivered energy per attempt, per site, over 60-minute windows with a volume gate. Across April 2026 the old scheme gave 412 pages of which 61 were actionable — 14.8 per cent precision — and found 23 of 46 customer-visible incidents first, an incident being 50 or more failed sessions at one site within an hour: 50.0 per cent recall. Across June 2026 the new scheme gave 97 pages, 54 actionable, 55.7 per cent precision, and found 35 of 41 first: 85.4 per cent recall. Pages fell 76.5 per cent, actionable pages only from 14.2 to 12.6 a week.

The case that failed: a model monitored by nothing. In February 2026 Mastul deployed a model predicting charge-point failure within 48 hours. Over April 2026 its 4,200 chargers gave 1,26,000 charger-days holding 1,890 real failures, a 1.5 per cent base rate. It flagged 9,240 charger-days, of which 1,134 were followed by a real failure: precision 12.3 per cent, recall 60.0 per cent. Every flag became a ₹2,400 dispatch, so April cost ₹221.76 lakh. A failed charger is down for the MTTR above, 755 minutes, or 52.4 per cent of a day; at 10 attempts a charger a day that is 5.24 attempts, of which 91 per cent would have succeeded — 4.77 sessions at ₹173.90, about ₹830 protected per averted failure. The model protected 1,134 × ₹830 = ₹9.41 lakh, or ₹23.56 of dispatch per rupee.

Firmware cohortCharger-days flaggedFlags followed by a real failurePrecision
4.x (shipped from January 2026)5,6001963.5%
3.x and earlier3,64093825.8%
Total9,2401,13412.3%

April 2026, 30-day window. The Total precision is 1,134 ÷ 9,240, not the cohort average.

Once someone segmented, the diagnosis was plain: the features came from the same status notifications the control-theory school calls unreliable, and firmware 4.x had changed how they were emitted. Nothing monitored the model's precision, so a fall from 25.8 to 3.5 per cent on a growing cohort produced no alert. On 12 May it was retired for a rule a graduate could write: zero kilowatt-hours in 24 hours while reporting itself available. Replayed over the same April data it flagged 2,016 charger-days of which 1,512 preceded a real failure — 75.0 per cent precision, 80.0 per cent recall, ₹48.38 lakh of dispatch, ₹12.55 lakh protected. Better on every axis, still ₹3.86 per rupee of protection.

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of lateness

Failure modeEarliest signDiagnostic questionCost if late
Aggregate-only indicatorsNo tenant selector on the dashboardWhich large customer had the worst month?Pranali: a ₹2.40 crore renewal in doubt
Self-reporting componentsThe uptime number comes from the componentCould this signal survive the failure?Mastul: 38,745 failures behind a healthy flag
Telemetry outgrowing its valueSpend rising faster than trafficWhat share of the loss prevented is this?A panic cut of the wrong stream
Unmonitored modelsNo chart of prediction quality vs outcomesIts precision last month, by segment?Mastul: ₹221.76 lakh to protect ₹9.41 lakh

In every row the early sign is visible without an incident; the cost is not.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Pre-aggregated metrics versus wide events. The metrics position rests on cost arithmetic of the kind above: 7,05,600 extra series for one label is ₹9.10 lakh a month, most never queried. The wide-event position rests on Pranali's failure being a dimension dropped at write time, an unbounded cost. The first is wrong if query-time aggregation becomes cheap enough that the write-time choice stops mattering; the second if the queries people run are few and predictable, as most query logs suggest. The same split decides buy against build: a bill dominated by volume favours self-hosting, one dominated by cardinality does not.

Symptoms only, versus leading indicators. The orthodox position — page only on user-visible symptom breaches — rests on evidence that cause-based alerts drive the noise behind Mastul's 14.8 per cent precision. The dissent rests on repair latency: when restoration takes 660 minutes because a technician must drive, a symptom alert comes too late, and a saturation signal, however noisy, is all that buys time. Both are right inside their own repair-time regime; the argument goes badly because neither states it.

Per-tenant objectives versus one platform objective. Pranali appears to settle this, but the strongest counter is not cost: 30 objectives mean 30 budgets and 30 negotiations, the smallest tenants consuming most attention per rupee because their windows are noisiest. A company that cannot defend a budget tenant by tenant ends with 30 nobody enforces, worse than one that is. It holds at Pranali because 90 per cent of traffic sits in eleven accounts.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this adds dashboards and congratulates themselves on coverage. Someone who has internalised it starts from the last three incidents and asks which signal, at which grain, in which window, would have fired — accepting the answer when it is "none, and here is the label we would need." They state the window before quoting a rate, know their alert precision as a number, treat each label as a purchase, and ask of any health signal whether it survives the failure it reports. And they will argue that faster detection is not worth paying for in a given product — the clearest marker, since it needs knowing what repair costs.

12. The decisions

Mitali Pradhan chose grain over coverage. Pranali would define per-tenant indicators and budgets for the 12 tenants above 5,00,000 requests a month, each with three rules — a five-minute error rate with a 10-error gate, a 60-minute burn rate, a missing-data rule — and give the 18 single-site hospitals one 60-minute rule each: 36 plus 18, or 54 new rules, alongside the 11 platform rules already running. Two engineers for a quarter, at the price of a delayed scheduling feature. Her case to her CTO Prashant Mhatre: September showed a measurement problem, not a reliability one.

She also took the harder item to Prabhat: the contract's 99.5 per cent availability clause does not say which availability it means. On a request basis Prabhat's September was 99.681 per cent, so no credit is due. On a time basis, the medication-order path being down 314 of September's 43,200 minutes, it was 99.273 per cent, triggering a 10 per cent credit of ₹2 lakh on the ₹20 lakh monthly fee — and 314 minutes is 7.3 times the 43.2 a 99.9 per cent objective permits. Mitali proposed paying it and defining the term in the renewal.

Mrinalini Prabhu refused the 20 per cent cut and offered 56.6 per cent instead, on condition that she could add a stream.

₹ lakh per 30-day month, rounded to ₹1,000; both totals are sums of their rounded columns and match the full-precision sums to within ₹1,000. Tail sampling keeps all failures and 1 per cent of successes. The saving is ₹16.59 lakh a month, ₹1.99 crore a year; the bill falls from 37.1 per cent of monthly lost revenue to 16.1 per cent.

Her reasoning, put to Praveen Mokashi and to Pritam Mandke, her reliability lead, who covers the European night from Lisbon: a 20 per cent target was easy and useless, since shaving every stream by a fifth preserves the structure that made 46,494 failures invisible.

Discussion questions. First, Pranali's rules were correctly configured and silent for 276 minutes: whose mistake, and when should the tenant label have been added? Second, Mastul's model was worse than a one-line rule on every axis — what follows for the governance of models, as against their quality? Third, if faster detection moves Mastul's MTTR by 11.7 per cent, what justifies the spend?

13. Going deeper

CI/CD, environments and deployment comes first: instrumentation ships in the same pipeline as the code. Incident management and postmortems is where detection becomes value; Pranali's 38 minutes of repair is a response number. SLAs, SLOs and error budgets formalises section 3 and supplies the language whose absence cost Prabhat ₹2 lakh. Model monitoring and drift generalises Mastul's failure: silent degradation, segment precision, late ground truth. How web and mobile apps work shows why client telemetry is a separate problem. APIs and integration basics covers the boundary where 13,608 failures vanished. Data modelling for PMs makes cardinality legible before it is an invoice. Databases, storage and caching explains the cost of high-cardinality queries. Cloud infrastructure basics gives the buy-versus-build vocabulary. Reading an architecture diagram is the prerequisite for seam faults.
exp20v2-tech.observability:
Logging, monitoring and observability: how the team knows before customers do

1. The Saturday that customers found first

On Saturday 12 September 2026, Dhruv Hiremath, head of product at Hariyali Fresh Exchange, a Bengaluru grocery delivery business, was at his daughter's school fair when his phone filled with messages. Hariyali handled about 12,000 order attempts an hour in its evening peak, at an average basket of ₹640. Since a little after 7:10 p.m., one in every twelve or so of those attempts had been failing at the payment step. The first person in the company to notice was not an engineer. It was a customer-support agent, at 7:52 p.m., who saw eleven near-identical complaints about UPI payments in twenty minutes and pinged a manager.

Forty-two minutes had passed. Dhruv later did the sum on the back of a school programme. Eight per cent of 12,000 attempts an hour is 960 failed orders an hour; 42 minutes is 0.7 of an hour, so 672 failed orders; at ₹640 each, that is ₹4,30,080 of baskets that never completed.

The engineering lead, Deepa Hosmani, was blunt in the Monday review. The servers had been up the whole time. Every dashboard on the wall was green, because the dashboards tracked whether machines were alive, and the machines were fine. A release that afternoon had broken how one Android build of the app passed a payment reference to the UPI intent, and nothing in the company was set up to see that. Harish Dongre, the chief technology officer, put the decision to Dhruv: fund a three-month observability programme, at the cost of delaying a loyalty feature, or keep buying more dashboards. What was at stake was whether the next failure, perhaps during the festival peak, would be found by the team or by Twitter.

2. The idea

A log is a timestamped record of one thing that happened, written by the software itself: "order 88213 payment callback received, status FAILED". Monitoring is the practice of watching a chosen set of measurements against known thresholds and alerting a human when one is crossed. Observability is a property of a system: the degree to which you can work out what is happening inside it, including things you did not anticipate, by examining what it emits.

The problem these ideas were invented to solve is simple to state. Software that runs on other people's phones and across dozens of cooperating services fails in ways its builders did not predict. Early monitoring tools asked whether a machine was up; Google's site reliability engineers, in the mid-2010s, argued the better question was whether users were succeeding. The word observability was borrowed from control theory, where it dates to Rudolf Kálmán in 1960, and was brought into software around 2017 by engineers including Charity Majors, who stressed that monitoring covers questions you knew to ask and observability covers the ones you did not.

Dhruv eventually reduced it to a sentence he could repeat in any meeting: "Monitoring tells us that something we feared has happened; observability lets us find out what happened when we did not fear it; and neither is worth anything unless a person is woken up in minutes rather than informed in hours."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a chain, and the diagram below shows it for Hariyali. The app and the services behind it emit three kinds of telemetry, meaning data about their own behaviour. Logs are the event records. Metrics are numbers counted over time, such as "checkout failures this minute". Traces follow a single request across services, with each hop timed, so that one slow or broken order can be followed from the phone to the payment gateway and back.

The telemetry lands in a store that can be queried. Hariyali used Grafana dashboards over a metrics store. The next step is the one practitioners leave implicit: someone must decide what counts as healthy. This is done by choosing a service level indicator (SLI), a measurement of user-visible success. The most common is an error rate, defined here as failed checkout requests divided by all checkout requests in the same time window. Then an alert rule says: if this indicator crosses a threshold and stays there for a stated period, page the on-call engineer, the person who carries the phone that week.

The last implicit step is routing. An alert that reaches a shared channel nobody owns is not an alert. Deepa's rule was that every alert must name a person, a first action and a dashboard link.

4. A worked example

Return to the Saturday. Hariyali's checkout normally ran at a baseline error rate of 0.4 per cent. Order attempts were 200 a minute, which is 12,000 an hour, matching the opening. In a five-minute window that is 1,000 attempts, of which the baseline accounts for 4 failures. Starting at 7:10 p.m., the broken Android build caused 8 per cent of attempts to fail.

QuantityWorkingResult
Attempts per 5-minute window200 × 51,000
Failures per window during the fault1,000 × 8%80
Error rate in that window80 ÷ 1,0008%
Proposed alert threshold5-minute error rate above 2%, sustained 3 minutes20 failures per window
Alert fires7:10 p.m. onset, first full window ends 7:15, plus 3 minutes7:18 p.m. (8 minutes)
Customer-found detection7:10 to 7:52 p.m.42 minutes

Failed orders are the same sum in both cases. At 200 attempts a minute and an 8 per cent failure rate, 16 orders fail each minute. Detected at 8 minutes, 128 orders fail, worth 128 × ₹640 = ₹81,920. Detected at 42 minutes, 672 fail, worth ₹4,30,080. The alert would have saved 544 orders and ₹3,48,160, and that is before counting the lost second orders.

Second pass: change one input

Now change the severity. Suppose the broken build had affected only a minority of users, so that 3 per cent of attempts failed rather than 8. Failures per window become 30, an error rate of 3 per cent, which still clears the 2 per cent threshold of 20, and the alert fires at the same moment. But suppose the team, having been burned by noisy alerts, had set the threshold at 5 per cent. The 3 per cent fault would never cross it, and the alert would stay silent while the customer-support queue filled. Neither setting is free.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Monitoring and observability are not synonyms

Monitoring answers questions fixed in advance. Observability is the ability to ask a new question of old data. The 2 per cent rule above is monitoring. Discovering that failures clustered on one app version, one Android vendor and one payment handle is observability, and it needs telemetry detailed enough to slice.

The three pillars answer different questions

SignalBest question it answersMain cost driver
MetricsIs something wrong, and how big is it?Number of distinct label combinations
LogsWhat exactly happened in this event?Volume of text stored and searched
TracesWhere in the chain did this request go wrong?Share of requests recorded

Cardinality is what breaks budgets

Cardinality means the number of distinct combinations of label values a metric carries. A checkout metric labelled by 40 endpoints, 12 status codes and 3 app versions produces 40 × 12 × 3 = 1,440 time series, which is trivial. Add a user identifier with 5,00,000 active users and it becomes 1,440 × 5,00,000 = 72,00,00,000 series, which is 720 million, and the bill or the database gives way.

Averages hide the people in pain

The p95 latency is the response time that 95 per cent of requests beat, so 5 per cent are slower. If average checkout time is 0.8 seconds but p95 is 4.5 seconds, one customer in twenty is waiting more than four seconds. Alert on percentiles, never on the mean alone.

Alert fatigue is a real failure mode

An alert's precision, defined here as the pages that required action divided by all pages in a 30-day month, measures whether people can trust it. If an on-call engineer received 60 pages in a month and 15 needed action, precision is 25 per cent, and the engineer will soon start ignoring pages, including the real ones.

Silence is not health

No alert might mean no problem, or a broken pipeline. A metric that stops arriving looks identical to one that is calm unless a rule explicitly watches for missing data.

What it cannot tell you

Telemetry shows what the software did, not what the customer wanted. A checkout can succeed technically while the wrong substitute is delivered. Observability also cannot say whether the fault matters commercially; that needs a target agreed with the business, which the next topics, service level objectives and error budgets, supply. As an example, a 99.9 per cent monthly availability target allows 0.1 per cent of a 30-day, 43,200-minute month, or 43.2 minutes of full outage. Hariyali's 42 minutes at an 8 per cent failure rate equals 42 × 0.08 = 3.36 minutes of full outage.

6. How it looks across products and stages

In a consumer product such as Hariyali, the unit of concern is the individual app version, device and network, so telemetry from phones, not only servers, matters. UPI payments add a dependency on banks whose outages show up as your errors. In a B2B product, there are fewer users but contracts attached: a monitored error rate per customer, rather than in aggregate, is what lets an account manager say, before the client does, that something is wrong. In a marketplace, both sides must be observed: a healthy buyer app can hide a silently failing seller-order feed.

Stage matters as much. A ten-person start-up needs three or four alerts on user-visible outcomes and one on-call rotation. A large company such as Flipkart or Jio runs thousands of services and needs standard instrumentation, sampled traces and a platform team, because telemetry itself becomes a budget line.

7. Common mistakes

Watching machines, not outcomes

The symptom is a wall of green dashboards during a customer-visible failure, as at Hariyali. The misunderstanding is that infrastructure health equals product health. The cheapest diagnostic: pick the last incident and ask which graph would have shown it; if none, you are watching machines.

Thresholds nobody revisits

The symptom is pages that everyone mutes, or silence during a known real fault. The misunderstanding is that an alert is configured once. The diagnostic: compute precision for the last 30 days, and replay the last three incidents against the rule to see whether it would have fired.

Alerts with no owner

The symptom is an alert firing in a channel while everyone assumes someone else has seen it. The misunderstanding is that visibility equals responsibility. The diagnostic: look at the alert and ask whether it names one person and one first action.

8. What good looks like

Imagine the same Saturday handled well. At 7:18 p.m., Deepa's rule on the checkout error rate pages the on-call engineer, Hamid Dastur, working from Lyon in the mid-afternoon. The page carries a link to a dashboard sliced by app version. Within four minutes he sees that all the failures sit on one build and that the traces end at the same hop. At 7:30 p.m. the product team halts the staged rollout, and by 7:45 p.m. the previous build is back. Nobody learned of the incident from a tweet.

9. Closing

Dhruv chose the programme, but narrowed it. The loyalty feature slipped by three weeks. In the first quarter the team would instrument only the order journey, with a checkout success alert, an app-version slice on every dashboard and one trace route from the phone to the payment gateway. It would measure itself on one number, the gap between when a fault began and when a human on the team knew, with a target of under ten minutes. His reasoning was that a narrow system the team trusted would teach more than a broad one nobody read.

What to learn next: incident management and postmortems, because detection only matters if response follows; then SLAs, SLOs and error budgets, which convert "how bad is bad" into an agreed number; then model monitoring and drift, where the same ideas apply to systems whose failures are quiet by design.

Two questions to sit with. First, what is the last customer-visible failure in your own product, and how many minutes passed before someone on the team knew? Second, if you set an alert threshold so that it never produces a false page, what faults have you chosen to miss?

Pravaham Systems: Four Ways to See the Same Failure

Hyderabad, November 2026

1. Sunday night in Hyderabad

At twenty past ten on Sunday, 15 November 2026, Bindushree Illikkal was the only person on the fourth floor of Pravaham Systems' office in Madhapur. On her screen was a four-page paper due at the board's technology sub-committee the next evening, Monday the 16th, at 18:30 IST — two in the afternoon for the designer in Berlin, eight in the morning for the sales head in New Jersey, nine at night for customer success in Singapore.

The board had asked a narrow question in September: why does this company find out about its own failures from its customers, and what will it cost to stop? Bindushree, vice-president of product, had arrived at four courses of action costing between ₹26 lakh and ₹149.7 lakh in the first year. The uncommitted part of the financial-year envelope was ₹84 lakh.

What unsettled her was not the money but that the four options agreed on what Pravaham could not see and disagreed on nothing else — and that Pravaham's measurement of its own reliability and its largest customer's measurement of the same service, both on her desk that month, differed by a factor of five in downtime.

2. How Pravaham got here

Pravaham Systems was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by two retail ERP engineers. Its product is an order-management and store-fulfilment platform: it holds the price and inventory master, and pushes invoices to the GST e-invoicing system. In FY26 it earned ₹63 crore from 142 retail customers and employed 310 people across Hyderabad, Bengaluru and a support floor in Jaipur, with small teams in Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey. The FY27 revenue plan was ₹81 crore. The platform carried 92 lakh orders in October 2026.

One decision from 2023 still governs everything. To win a Dubai-based grocery and general-retail group — now the largest single account at ₹486 lakh of FY27 contract value, 6.0 per cent of the revenue plan — Pravaham accepted a data-residency clause: all order, customer and operational data belonging to the UAE entity must be stored and processed in a UAE cloud region, and must not be exported. Pravaham therefore built its own log and metrics cluster and deployed it twice, in Mumbai and in the UAE region. That cluster, now carrying 10.2 crore log lines a day, costs ₹6.1 lakh a month. In March 2026 the client's legal team was asked for a side letter permitting telemetry export, and declined.

3. The industry

Reliance Retail and Flipkart set delivery expectations for Pravaham's customers; Meesho and Nykaa set price expectations; Zepto taught shoppers to treat ten minutes as normal. ONDC has added a second front: a retailer's catalogue now appears on buyer apps the retailer does not control, so a stale price is published to strangers.

Regulation bears on the product in two directions. The GST e-invoicing rules require invoices to be reported to the Invoice Registration Portal within thirty days of issue, so a stalled invoice queue becomes a compliance matter and not only a service one. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats the consumer phone numbers and delivery addresses passing through Pravaham's logs as personal data, with purpose and retention obligations, which makes what the company writes down a legal decision as much as a technical one.

Zoho, Freshworks and Postman set the Hyderabad and Bengaluru salary bands Pravaham pays. The observability vendors whose quotes sit in Bindushree's paper price in dollars, and Pravaham's planning rate had moved from ₹83.1 to ₹88.6 to the dollar since the 2024 budget — a 6.6 per cent increase before a single line of log was ingested.

4. The situation in detail

Exhibit 1 lists the seven customer-affecting incidents between 1 July and 12 November 2026. Four of the seven were found by a customer. Those four account for 44,050 of the 53,650 affected orders, or 82.1 per cent, and their mean time to detection was 160.8 minutes against 12.3 minutes for the three found by an internal alert.

Several incidents were also understood wrongly at the time. On 9 July, when the e-invoice queue stalled, the team believed the Invoice Registration Portal was slow; the cause was a deadlocked consumer in Pravaham's own queue. On 26 September the Dubai region's order-API timeouts were read as a cloud networking fault; on 28 October an engineer found connection-pool exhaustion in Pravaham's own service, visible all along in a metric that had no dashboard.

Figure 1 draws the 21 October incident to scale. A price-list publish job started at 10:58 IST and applied to part of the catalogue. From 11:04 stores served stale prices. At 11:26 an automated data-quality check in Toronto flagged a 0.4 per cent price mismatch; it wrote to a channel nobody owned. At 12:40 a category manager at the Dubai group telephoned Singapore, and that call is the first moment a Pravaham engineer knew.

Prices were corrected at 15:10 and the incident was declared closed that evening. On 1 November, reconciling GST credit notes, finance found that 2,960 SKUs — 0.4 per cent of the 7.4 lakh SKUs on the platform — had stayed at stale prices for eleven days, across 4,100 orders, for a net under-recovery of ₹6.3 lakh and 1,870 credit notes. None of that tail appears in Exhibit 1.

On 3 November the Dubai group sent its own quarterly availability report. Exhibit 2 sets it beside Pravaham's.

5. The people

Bindushree Illikkal, vice-president of product, Hyderabad, owns the paper and the recommendation. She says she wants the cheapest option that changes who finds out first. She does not say that she has twice asked for the service catalogue to be reassigned and been told it is not a product matter.

Bineesh Irumpanam, head of platform engineering, Bengaluru, wants Option A and is the person paged at night. He does not say that two of the eleven services in the catalogue have had no named owner since his predecessor left in April.

Benoy Iddya, chief financial officer, Hyderabad, quotes Option A at ₹149.7 lakh against ₹84 lakh uncommitted. He wants Option D, which is cheapest in year one. He does not volunteer that the comparison he has circulated runs for one year only.

Bhagyashri Injodey, customer-success lead, Singapore, took the 12:40 call on 21 October at 15:10 her time and wants Option C, a health view each large account can read for itself. She does not say that such a view would also show her team's own response times.

Bitasta Ittyerah, data scientist, Toronto, computes four data-quality signals over the platform's event streams. On 9 November she wrote that these would have caught five of the seven incidents, with as much as three hours of warning on the longest. She does not mention that the thresholds were chosen after reading the incident reports.

Bibin Immatty, product designer, Berlin, built the status and health screens Option C would ship. He is the only person who has read the Dubai group's probe configuration, and he points out that it counts any response over five seconds as a failure. He does not say that the screen he designed uses Pravaham's definition, not the client's.

Bharatendu Ilanthodi, sales head, New Jersey, is carrying the Dubai renewal. He wants whatever the client can see before its procurement committee meets on 10 December. He does not say that he has already told the client's chief operating officer that a health dashboard is coming this quarter.

7. Voices

Bineesh Irumpanam, platform review, 13 November: "Everyone keeps saying one-forty-nine. Net of the Mumbai cluster we retire, A runs at fifty-two lakh a year. We are arguing about money we already spend."

Benoy Iddya, same meeting: "We retire the cluster in April 2027. The envelope closes on 31 March. Show me the year in which both those things are true."

Bhagyashri Injodey, chat thread, 12 November: "Not one client has asked us for traces. Four have asked why they heard it from their own store manager. Those are different products."

Bitasta Ittyerah, email, 9 November, 21:40 IST: "Five of the seven are already visible in data I compute every fifteen minutes. The signals exist. What does not exist is anyone whose telephone rings when they move."

Bibin Immatty, comment on the health-screen design, 13 November: "Whose number goes on the screen? If we publish ours, Dubai will put theirs beside it, and the gap in Exhibit 2 becomes a slide in their procurement committee."

Bharatendu Ilanthodi, call with Bindushree, 14 November: "Their committee is on the tenth of December. Anything that goes live on the eighteenth is a promise, not a fact. I have made enough promises."

8. The options as Bindushree sees them

Option A puts logs, metrics and traces from every service into one vendor platform. It gives the team one place to look and retires the Mumbai deployment. It also cannot lawfully hold the UAE entity's telemetry, because the vendor has no UAE region and the 2023 clause bars export.

Option B instruments what the contracts promise: twelve objectives across four order journeys, each with a threshold, a measurement window and a named engineer who is paged. It explains nothing about causes, and whatever lies outside the twelve stays as dark as the connection pool did on 26 September.

Option C gives the eight largest accounts a health view they can read themselves. It is the fastest and the only option a client can see. It also publishes an availability number, computed on Pravaham's basis.

Option D spends nothing on seeing more and everything on breaking less: staged rollouts and automated release gates. Pravaham's change log ties five of the seven incidents in Exhibit 1 to a change made that day. It is the cheapest of the four in year one.

Bindushree had opened the service catalogue twice that week. It lists eleven services and nine owners, and she had not found a name sitting against an order journey from end to end.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at 18:30 IST on Monday, 16 November. Of the FY27 platform envelope of ₹180 lakh, ₹96 lakh is committed — ₹73.2 lakh of cluster running cost and ₹22.8 lakh of security work — leaving ₹84 lakh. The platform team is four engineers and the two open requisitions are frozen until the February review, so A and D cannot run together, and B followed by D puts D's go-live in May. The Dubai group's procurement committee meets on 10 December and the renewal must be signed by 15 January; ₹19.2 lakh of credits is contested. The data-protection officer's note of 5 November requires a purpose and retention statement before collection widens.

Bindushree reread her first page at a quarter to midnight. It opened with the sentence the board had used in September — why do we hear it from our customers? — and she could not decide, reading it again, whether her four pages answered it. She closed the file without saving the last paragraph, and switched off the lamp.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly does each availability column of Exhibit 2 measure, and what would Pravaham have to build before the two could be compared at all?
  2. Work out what each option in Exhibit 6 costs in FY27 and in FY28. Which envelope binds the decision?
  3. Using Exhibit 4, what are Bitasta's four signals worth to Pravaham, and what would the company be buying along with them?
  4. Figure 1 shows a signal firing at 11:26 and a telephone ringing at 12:40. Which option closes that gap, and which merely shortens what follows 12:40?
  5. Bindushree has framed the decision as a choice about tooling and cost. Is that the right frame? Restate the decision in the terms you think are central, and say which of the four options survives the restatement.
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November. What does Bindushree do before the 18:30 call, what does she recommend, and what does she tell the board she will be able to prove by the time the Dubai renewal is signed?
